Code and white paper

What does infrequent averaging do to the answer?

Local-SGD / DiLoCo-style averaging of heterogeneous quadratic workers has a closed-form fixed point: a weighted mean of the workers' optima with weights 1−(1−ηai)H that saturate, so it is exactly unbiased at H=1, forgets curvature as H grows (converging to the unweighted mean), and is non-monotone in between. Weighting by ai/wi removes the bias exactly; if the server trusts claimed step counts, a low-curvature worker moves the fixed point from 0.50 to 0.91 by claiming 100 steps instead of 5, tying communication savings to verified work. Wall-clock-optimal H under a bias tolerance is 5.7× faster than H=1 at moderate comm cost, with a non-interval feasible set. Noise formulas match Monte Carlo. Pure-Python, 8 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

How much can a provider steal by serving a cheaper model?

A decentralised inference provider substitutes a cheaper model on a random fraction p of queries; a verifier re-scores a fraction f under an anytime-valid mixture e-process. Detection delay scales as 1/(f p² χ²), so the profitable attack is a slow leak: undetected savings grow as √N rather than N (measured ×7.75 for ×64 queries). Closed-form audit rate to cap theft, cost-optimal check rate (hK/2Nc)2/3, and a substitute close enough to the claimed model that even checking every response cannot cap the theft. Seeded Monte Carlo, pure-Python, 10 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

How precise should a training-contest leaderboard be?

In a winner-take-all contest ranked on a noisy holdout of m samples, equilibrium effort is V·an√m/s with a2=a3=1/(2√π) exactly, but the formula stops being an equilibrium once V/σ² passes a ceiling (12.35, 7.78, 6.11, 5.60, 5.80 for n=2, 3, 5, 10, 20) that sits below the zero-rent limit and falls to half of it at n=20. The organiser's optimal holdout is min(mcap, (wVan/2sκ)²): when evaluation is cheap the ceiling, not cost, binds. Quadrature checked against Monte Carlo and brute-force best replies. Pure-Python, 11 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

What do risk-averse verifiers report under proper scoring?

Proper scoring rules are truthful only for risk-neutral agents. For a CARA verifier the log score yields reported odds exactly equal to true odds^(1/(1+k)), k = αb; the Brier score yields logit p = logit r + k(2r−1), which the principal can invert exactly. Summing reported logits under-extremises (log-loss 0.332 vs 0.214 at k=2); correcting with the mean k under heterogeneous verifiers is worse than not correcting; a log-score report needs true belief 0.964 to clear a 0.9 accept threshold at k=0.5. A binarised lottery rule is truthful for every increasing utility at a 2.6–27% certainty-equivalent cost. Pure-Python, 12 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Do free retries break hash-derived spot checks?

When an audit challenge is the hash of the prover's own commitment, a cheater simply re-rolls until the challenge misses its corrupted steps, so expected profit is exactly G−c/p (p = C(T−k,q)/C(T,q)) and the stake plays no role. Deterrence needs q ≈ ln(G/c)·T/k opened steps against ln2·T/k for a post-commitment beacon: 10×–60× more for G/c = 210…260. Proof-of-work on the challenge has a closed-form optimum x* = v/λp − c0. Real SHA-256 grinding matches the geometric law. Pure-Python, 12 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

What does not knowing the horizon cost a market maker?

An LMSR with liquidity b routes like Hedge with rate 1/b, but the tuned b needs the horizon T. A bt = c√t schedule with c* = 1/(2√ln N) pays exactly √2 over the horizon-aware bound (1.36 rising to 1.41 measured); the doubling trick is 1.70× worse than the continuous schedule against a price-reactive adversary; and self-tuning liquidity bt = Δt−1/ln N makes the subsidy equal the accumulated mixability gap (1.3 against 102 on easy data) with regret at most 2Δ. Regret analysis only. Pure-Python, 10 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Is load balancing a congestion price?

Capacity-constrained expert routing is a softmax with a per-expert price, the Lagrange multiplier of its capacity, and the dual is smooth and concave. Any price vector gives a computable upper bound and, after repair toward the uniform assignment, a feasible lower bound, so a verifier certifies near-optimality from prices alone (gap below 10−4 at the optimum, always above the true suboptimality). Sign-update balancing has a sampling floor of about 2.5/√B in max relative overload that no step size removes, plus a step-proportional limit cycle on a fixed batch (22.6% at γ=0.2, 1.2% at 0.01). Two-expert Gaussian price of balance is closed form with price shift equal to the median gap; a Hoeffding audit of ln(2N/δ)/(2ε2) tokens covered 400 of 400 trials. Synthetic scores only. Pure-Python, 10 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Can stake shorten a challenge window when proposers can be bribed?

In optimistic verification a fraud pays G unless a challenge is included within w blocks; the attacker controls each proposer w.p. ρ and otherwise pays b to censor. The exact attacker recursion V(n) = ρV(n−1) + (1−ρ)max(−S, V(n−1)−b) gives a closed-form deterrence window (0 mismatches in 5000 instances; Monte Carlo agrees) with a gamble-first, bribe-last optimal attack. A luck-only analysis underestimates the window 100–170×; with an exogenous bribe price the window is 63 blocks for every stake from 10 to 1600; if the bounty is paid as a priority fee the price becomes θS and S·w ≈ G/((1−ρ)θ). Pure-Python, 9 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

What does a verifier's silence tell you?

When reporting costs c, a truthful verifier paid the score gain over an anchor α abstains exactly when |p−α| < √c (Brier) or KL(p‖α) < c (log), so silence is an interval of signals and carries evidence unless the anchor is a symmetric prior. At prior 0.1 the outcome rate among reporters is 0.57; an aggregator that drops silent verifiers has log-loss 0.62 against 0.02 for one that uses silence at n=12 (it worsens as verifiers are added); a stale anchor makes silence point at the wrong state. Quadrature and seeded Monte Carlo, pure-Python, 12 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

How do you price the tail of benign drift?

A drift tolerance is a quantile, but compensation depends on expected shortfall, which is not elicitable alone (a mixture moves ES 1.6→2.24). The scale-free score ln e + (v + (x−v)+/(1−α))/e − 1 elicits (VaR, ES) jointly with exact excess law; misreporting ES by a factor r costs ln r + 1/r − 1 (0.307 at ½, 0.193 at 2), matched to quadrature within 2·10−5. A quantile-only tolerance leaves ES/VaR = a/(a−1) uncovered under Pareto drift (6× at a=1.2); auditing needs ~2,000 samples for a 20% understatement at index 4 and the CLT plan fails for index ≤ 2. Pure-Python, 10 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Should you pay verifiers for their calibration?

A verifier reporting expit(aL+b) for the true posterior logit L is overpaid-for-error by exactly E[(r−p)²] under Brier and E[KL(p‖r)] under log score. Brier is bounded (a hard 0/1 report still beats the prior at μ=1) but log is not: raw log score ranks a higher-resolution verifier first only for slope a in (0.264, 2.49), so at a=4 a weaker calibrated verifier wins, while recalibrated scores never reverse. Recalibrating on n outcomes costs about tr(HI−1)/2n excess Brier (0.264/n, simulation within ~10% for n≥100), beating raw pay beyond n≈20–80. Quadrature and seeded simulation, pure-Python, 12 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Is risk tolerance the learning rate of a wealth market?

When agents bet a fraction λ of wealth Kelly-style, the clearing price is the λ·wealth-weighted mean belief, total wealth is conserved, and λ=1 is exactly the Bayes mixture. Market log-loss exceeds expert i’s by at most ln(1/si)/λi on any sequence (loose on i.i.d. data), the growth-optimal fraction is (π−p)/(q−p), and moving the price against calibrated others costs Vχ²(p0‖p): equal to LMSR b·KL at b=2V for small shifts but 7.5× stiffer at p=0.99. On a truth that switches regimes, full Kelly is wrong about half of every segment (regret about 1630 at T=4000) while λ of 0.1–0.2 cuts it 3–7×. Binary events, static experts. Pure-Python, 11 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

What does a slippage limit give away in a prediction market?

A searcher who buys before and sells after a victim's LMSR trade extracts exactly the victim's slippage tolerance times its fair cost (εC0, error 1.4×10−14 over 216 instances), with a closed-form front-run of about εb/(1−p) shares, so return on capital falls as 1/b. A proportional fee of about v(1−p)/(2b) makes it unprofitable at any tolerance; the victim's optimal tolerance grows only like √log of the stakes; pro-rata batching keeps 0.989–0.999 of the extraction and uniformly random ordering cuts it exactly 3×. Pure-Python, 13 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Should a verifier's continuous drift report be scored by CRPS or log score?

For Gaussian reports N(m,s²) both rules have exact expected scores. Overconfidence costs at most σ(√2−1)/√π = 0.234σ under CRPS but is unbounded under log (4995 nats at s=0.01σ); mean errors cost linearly versus quadratically; CRPS is 1-Lipschitz in the realised outcome (log slope 75/σ in our example); a plug-in fit from n samples costs 5σ/(8√πn) versus 1/n; and per-round score variance is finite for Student-t tails ν>2 (CRPS) versus ν>4 (log), which matters for sequential tests. Gaussian family, one verifier. Pure-Python, 9 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Should a pipeline replicate stages or skip them?

A microbatch crosses L stages held by workers that come and go. The drop probability is the exact binomial tail P(Bin(L,q)>s) with stage outage q = ρ + (1−ρ)(1−a)r, so replicas cannot lift success above the shared-domain floor (1−ρ)L: at L=48, ρ=10−3 no r reaches a 1% drop rate, but allowing one skipped stage makes r=3 enough. At a=0.9 a four-stage skip budget cuts the workers for a 10−3 drop rate from 240 to 96; under a per-skip quality loss κ the cost-optimal design is skip-heavy for cheap skips and moves to replication as κ grows (gain over no-skip 2.9× down to 1.08×). Independent outages, multiplicative skip penalty. Pure-Python, 11 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Can a verifier be paid for reporting drift variance?

Not from one re-execution (variance’s level sets are not convex), but two independent ones suffice: D=(y1−y2)²/2 is unbiased with variance σ4(κ+1)/2. Brier excess is exactly (r−σ²)²; the scale-free loss D/r+ln r has excess 1/λ+ln λ−1, so halving the report costs 0.307 and doubling 0.193. Catching a 10% misreport at 95% takes about 2–4 thousand tasks (2z²(κ+1)/(λ−1)², simulated 0.93–0.97); disjoint pairs are 1.8× worse than the sample variance at n=10; with Pareto tail index 3 the error decays like m−1/3, not m−1/2. Pure-Python, 10 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

What if the referee itself is noisy?

When verifiers are paid against a judge whose label flips with rates e0, e1, any proper score elicits the noisy probability e0+γp (γ=1−e0−e1), the Brier incentive shrinks by γ², and rankings of truthful verifiers reverse at η*=0.25. The backward-corrected surrogate score is exactly unbiased for the true loss, at a 1/γ payment spread and (balanced case) 1/γ² more evidence; misestimated rates produce a closed-form affine bias whose cost falls as 1/m in gold checks. Pure-Python, 12 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Does agreement pay reward shared laziness?

Multi-task peer prediction pays 2G·Cov of two reports. If lazy verifiers copy a shared per-task default (the same public model’s guess) pay becomes 2G[aiajpq + (1−ai)(1−aj)d(1−d)], effort is a coordination game with threshold a* = (k/2G + s)/(pq + s), and the all-lazy profile is always an equilibrium paying 2G·d(1−d): equal to honest pay when the default matches the prior, 1.19× it at p=0.3, d=0.5. Closing it with gold checks needs payment mass (2Gs+k)/(1−accD), larger than the honest pay itself. Pure-Python, 9 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Can audits be predictable without corrupting scores?

If truth arrives only on audited tasks and the audit rate depends on the report (say g(r)=a+br), “score when audited” is no longer proper: the verifier shades by about −bp(1−p)/(2(a+bp)) and, for steep b, hides at r=0 (Brier excess 0.25 at p=0.5). Weighting the audited loss by 1/g(r) is exactly proper for any audit rule, at variance E[B²]/g−L² and payout cap 1/gmin; the Neyman audit allocation minimises variance but gains only 3–11% over uniform. Pure-Python, 9 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Can two verifiers be compared while the data streams in?

For fixed reports rA, rB and binary outcomes with frequency q, the Brier difference is a two-point gamble and A is better exactly when q is on A’s side of the midpoint π=(rA+rB)/2. Betting a fraction λ of wealth on it gives an anytime-valid e-process whose best bet grows at exactly KL(q‖π), so the expected decision time is ln(1/α)/KL. A z-test checked after every task falsely declares a winner in 19–38% of null runs at nominal 5%; a uniform mixture over bets stays at or below 3.8% and costs 15–41% extra tasks; a bet twice too large has negative growth. Fixed reports, i.i.d. outcomes. Pure-Python, 7 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

How noisy is peer-prediction pay with finitely many tasks?

The plug-in multi-task payment (agreement minus the agreement implied by empirical frequencies) is exactly twice the sample covariance of two verifiers’ reports, so its variance is available in closed form and matches full enumeration; it is √2 less noisy than drawing fresh penalty tasks and pays a constant reporter exactly 0. Under limited liability a verifier who does no work still collects a noise rent ≈ σ/√(2π) (0.020 against 0.208 honest at n=100). A deductible removes it in closed form, but killing 99% of the rent costs the honest verifier 54% of its pay. Detection needs 56–329 tasks for g=0.7–0.3 (simulated power 0.94–0.95), and ranking two close verifiers takes ~870. Binary conditionally independent reports. Pure-Python, 9 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

Can the log score be made payable?

Log score is ideal for rare faults but a confident wrong report costs unbounded stake. Extending the log generator past [ε,1−ε] by its second-order Taylor polynomial gives a strictly proper score, identical to log up to a constant inside, with worst-case payment exactly ln((1−ε)/ε)+1/(1−ε). Per unit of payment range it has 63× Brier’s curvature at p=10−3 but loses to Brier above a closed-form crossover (≈0.07), and ε=p is the best cutoff for truth p.

Code and white paper

How should Shapley payments be sampled and audited?

In a saturating contribution game v(S)=1−exp(−Σwi) every estimator variance is exact. Permutation sampling always pays out exactly v(N) but is noisy; size-stratified sampling has 6–8× lower variance (exactly zero for equal contributors) yet misses the pot by up to 7% in a run; reversing each permutation cuts RMSE 1.6× at no cost; Hoeffding sample counts are 4–5× larger than needed, and stratification finds the top-3 payees with about 4× fewer samples. Stylised, n≤10. Pure-Python, 9 tests.

Code and white paper

Which proper score should verifiers face with K outcomes?

For K-ary reports the Brier, spherical and log scores have exact regrets and exact worst cases (1−2pmin+‖p‖² for Brier, ‖p‖−pmin for spherical). Per unit of payment range the spherical score gives exactly √K times Brier’s incentive at a uniform truth, but both bounded scores nearly ignore a dropped rare class: at a 1% class the loss is 1.3×10−4 (Brier) and 1.0×10−4 (spherical) against 0.15 for log. Multiclass follow-up to tangent-log. Pure-Python, 6 tests.

Code and white paper

Can the multiclass log score be made payable?

Extending x ln x below a cutoff ε by its second-order Taylor polynomial gives a strictly proper K-class score that equals −ln ry whenever every rj≥ε and has payment range exactly 1−ln ε, the same for any K. Per unit of range it has 3× Brier’s rare-class incentive at a 5% class and 63× at 0.1%, the best cutoff is the rarest class’s mass, and a verifier that zeroes out a 1% class loses a closed-form 0.005 (Brier 1.3×10−4, log unbounded). Closes the gap left open in categorical-scores. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

What does it cost to pay for a ranking instead of probabilities?

A verifier who reports only the order of K classes can be paid with a score linear in the outcome indicator. It is strictly proper, and swapping two classes at adjacent ranks costs exactly (pi−pj)(wr−wr+1), linear in the gap. Per unit of payment range that beats a Brier-derived ranking whenever the gap is below 1/(K−1) (2.5× at gap 0.1, 250× at 0.001, K=5). Equal spacing maximises the smallest incentive, ranking everything costs K−1 times the mode, a top-k set costs the same as the mode, and the sample size to detect a swap is identical to Brier’s. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

Should severity reports be scored with the order in mind?

For ordered fault severities the ranked probability score is Brier on the cumulative distribution: strictly proper with exact regret Σ(Rk−Pk)², so moving mass ε a distance d costs exactly dε² where Brier charges 2ε² for every d. Pooling adjacent classes costs exactly half of Brier’s, and every threshold probability is within √regret of the truth. The price: per unit of payment range RPS gives Brier’s incentive only for a maximal-distance shift (1/(K−1) for adjacent ones). Extends categorical-scores. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

Can we elicit the mode of a mixture of honest and cheating drift?

When some workers cheat, drift is a mixture and the mean, which squared loss elicits, lands where almost no task lies (at a 30% cheater 6σ away, the mean’s window holds 0.15 of the mass versus 0.48 at the mode). The mode is not elicitable, but the centre of the width-2α window with the most mass is, with the bounded loss 1[|y−r|>α]. Regret is an exact window-mass difference; the best window is α=σ for normal drift and γ/√3 for Cauchy (no mean exists); an equal bimodal mixture has one α-mode iff α exceeds a closed-form root α*; and under 10–40% contamination the sample α-mode has ~0 bias while the mean is off by 5ε, at a 3.7× RMSE cost when clean. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

Can a verifier be paid for a tolerance interval, not a point?

The Winkler interval score is strictly proper for the pair of quantiles, with closed-form regret and an optimal expected score of exactly 4sφ(z)/α. Misreporting the width by the same factor costs more when narrow at 95% coverage but more when wide at 80%, so there is no universal rule that overconfidence is worse. Under Cauchy drift the scores have no mean, yet paired differences are bounded, so evaluate verifiers against a benchmark report.

Code and white paper

Should drift tolerances be per layer or on the total?

Giving each of L layers its own tolerance lets a prover hide the sum of them: L·c(L,α)σ versus zα√Lσ for one test on the total, 6.6× more at L=16 and 23× at L=128. The sum test’s power depends only on the total shift; the exact (Šidák) max test’s depends on how it is spread, the prover’s best split is even (log Φ is concave), and the max test catches a 2.7σ one-layer shift half the time but lets 16σ through spread over all 16 layers. A union of both at α/2 caps the hidden budget at the sum test’s (7.8σ) while keeping one-layer sensitivity. Gaussian, independent layers, known σ. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

How do you pay a verifier whose report decides the job?

If a report of “fault” gets the job rejected and the outcome is seen only on acceptance, scoring observed jobs is improper: verifiers shade under the threshold to get scored, and every job is accepted (1.1–2.8× optimal decision loss at thresholds 0.7–0.2). A reserve payment for rejection makes truth optimal iff the score’s entropy minimum τs is at least the threshold τd, and then it is unique, 1+τd²−2τdτs. Plain Brier (τs=½) therefore fails above τd=½; recentring the score by a term linear in the outcome fixes every threshold, cheapest at τs=τd with rent τ3/3. Exploration with inverse-propensity payment is also proper but multiplies payment variance by about 1/ε. Stylised, single verifier. Pure-Python, 10 tests.

Code and white paper

How should a tolerance interval be paid for?

The Winkler interval score is the sum of two pinball losses: proper for the equal-tailed quantile interval with exact regret (2/α)[PR(l,α/2)+PR(u,1−α/2)], finite even for Cauchy drift where the expected score does not exist, but its payment grows without bound in the miss distance. A width-plus-miss loss (u−l)+λ1[miss] is bounded by width+λ and elicits the density level set, the shortest interval for its coverage: 22–31% narrower than equal-tailed on lognormal(0,1) drift. The price is statistical: to detect a 20% understatement of a normal tolerance it needs 3–48× more tasks for α≥0.1 and about the same at α=0.01. Pure-Python, 9 tests.

Code and white paper

How well does Freivalds' check work in floating point?

Checking a claimed matrix product by A(Br) ≈ Cr needs a tolerance t, so the error bound becomes size-dependent: a rank-one corruption of Frobenius norm F is missed by a Gaussian probe with probability exactly erf(t/(√2F)), rank one is the worst case for fixed F, and m probes give erfm (4 probes for 1% at 3t). Rademacher probes miss a two-entry corruption with probability ½ at every size. Emulated float32 noise grows ≈n0.9; a hashed probe with free retries lets a cheater grind in 1/erf tries (125 at 100t). Stylised, additive corruption. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

Who trades decides how liquid a verification market should be

A Glosten–Milgrom market maker facing an informed share μ with accuracy q moves its posterior log-odds by exactly 2·atanh(μ(2q−1)) per net buy, so its price path is an LMSR with b* = 1/(2 atanh m) (verified to 2×10−16). A wrong b costs log loss only in a transient whose peak is scale-free in m and 1.8–2.5× worse when overconfident; the LMSR subsidy tends to b* ln 2, exactly the spread the GM maker charges. Pure-Python, 10 tests, stylised.

Code and white paper

How many honest runs does a slashing tolerance need?

A conformal tolerance (the k-th order statistic of n honest drift scores) has an exact, distribution-free false-slash rate (n+1−k)/(n+1) — but only 51–56% of calibration sets deliver a rate ≤ α. A PAC-safe tolerance exists iff n ≥ ln δ/ln(1−α) (459 runs at 1%/1%), and its margin is hiding room for a cheater: the threshold sits 1.26× above the true quantile at n=2000 on Pareto-3 drift. Gaussian plug-in tolerances over-slash skewed drift up to 17×; pooling calibration across mixed hardware slashes the noisy class 4.8× too often and lets the quiet class hide 2.9× more. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

What does a fee do to a prediction market’s price?

A proportional fee f on an LMSR verification market gives every trader an exact no-trade band [q/(1+f), (q+f)/(1+f)] of width f/(1+f), so an informed trader leaves the price at q/(1+f). At price ½ a signal of log-likelihood ratio λ moves the price iff f < tanh(λ/2) = 2a−1, above which the market is dead; fee revenue on a monotone path is exactly fb ln((1−p0)/(1−pT)). With ten 0.65-accurate traders, the break-even fee (≈0.11) raises Brier error from 0.115 to about 0.16 and revenue is hump-shaped in f. Naive traders, synthetic signals. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

How big should a random verifier committee be?

Drawing m verifiers from a pool of N with B Byzantine, majority capture is exactly hypergeometric: zero once m ≥ 2B+1 and up to 26× below the with-replacement binomial (N=100, B=30, m=41: 1.4×10−4 vs 3.6×10−3). For failure 2−40 the exact size is a steady ≈0.90 of ln(1/ε)/KL(½‖β) while Hoeffding over-sizes it up to 2.2×. With stake-weighted draws only the Byzantine stake share counts: 20 of 100 nodes at 4× stake capture a 41-member committee half the time. A threshold-t rule trades wrong acceptance (2.7×10−7 to 1.1×10−16) against stalls (2.7×10−7 to 3.3×10−2). Static adversary, exact computation. Pure-Python, 11 tests.

Code and white paper

Can a calibration test certify a verifier?

No. A hedger with no information at all keeps its expected calibration error below √(K+1)(1/(2K)+1/√T) against any outcome sequence, even one that sees its forecast distribution: ECE 0.016 at T=2000 while its Brier score is 0.254 against 0 for a verifier who knows the rule. A lazy constant forecaster is slashed; the hedger passes every calibration threshold tried, but a Brier-gap test against an informed benchmark catches it in 100/100 runs.

Code and white paper

When should a paid verifier stop checking?

A verifier who checks a claim one noisy check at a time and stops when it likes, paid a proper score, follows a symmetric threshold rule (confirmed against dynamic programming over all policies). Accuracy is pk = 1/(1+((1−a)/a)k) and expected checks are k(2pk−1)/(2a−1), exactly. Participation needs a score scale κ ≥ 4c/(2a−1)² under Brier (log needs about half), Brier’s threshold is ln(κ(2a−1)²/((1−a)c))/λ within one step, and adaptive stopping matches a fixed-sample verifier’s accuracy with 2–3× fewer checks. Binary state, known accuracy. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

Why should the first verifiers be sealed?

Verifiers who are paid for being right and see earlier verdicts herd: once two more revealed signals point one way than the other, everyone copies. With signal accuracy a the cascade is wrong with probability exactly (1−a)²/(a²+(1−a)²) (0.155 at a=0.7) and forms after 2/(a²+(1−a)²) revealed signals (3.4), so accuracy is capped at 0.845 however many verifiers join, versus ≈1 for an independent majority of 101. A sealed first batch of m ≥ 3 lifts the cap (0.875 at m=3, 0.949 at 11) and beats a majority of the same paid size. Recursion checked against fully Bayesian simulated agents. Stylised, symmetric signals. Pure-Python, 9 tests.

Code and white paper

How many verifiers does deterrence-by-audit need?

Stake sets the audit rate a = G/(G+S); the audits then form a queue with offered load R = λas. Erlang-C waiting matches simulation (P(wait) 0.409 vs 0.407), and square-root staffing c = R + 1.06√R is within 1.5 servers of the exact minimum for R ≥ 100, so the spare capacity needed falls from 60% at R=5 to 1.1% at 104. Stake and headcount trade off with first-order optimum G+S = √(ws G/(rd0)): total cost 23.6 at the optimum versus 76.8 with too little stake and 65 with too much. Heavy-tailed audit times make Allen–Cunneen pessimistic (0.97 vs 0.63); batches of simultaneous audits make it optimistic (0.82 vs 1.45 at batch size 4). Stylised costs, FIFO, static outages. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

When most verifiers miss a fault, who should be believed?

If a fault is flagged by fewer than half of the verifiers (0.45 detection, 0.05 false alarms), majority vote is wrong on faulty jobs with probability 0.84 at n=101 and 0.96 at n=301. The surprisingly-popular rule (verdict plus predicted verdict fraction) reduces for truthful Bayesian verifiers to an exact fraction threshold θ = v/(1−u+v) and errs 2.1×10−5 on faulty jobs at n=101, needing 47 votes for 10−3 total error against 36 for a Bayes rule that knows the detector. A wrong believed prior wrecks finite-n accuracy (0.51 error), a wrong believed detector quality breaks the limit, and Byzantines who vote clean and predict “everyone flags” break it at exactly 13.6%. Stylised, truthful reports assumed. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

What is a seat in a prediction market worth?

In a sequential LMSR verification market the verifier in position k earns in expectation b·I(y; sk | s<k), a conditional mutual information, so seat rents telescope to the maker’s expected loss (at most b ln 2); an explicit cost-function simulation agrees to three decimals. Rents fall with position, the successive ratio approaching e−C (Chernoff information) from below; order only redistributes a fixed total (a 0.9-accurate verifier gets 0.368 of 0.407 first, 0.303 last). With entry cost c, accuracy improves roughly as 1/b: 11 verifiers at b=0.25 (92%), 41 at b=5 (99.6%). Myopic traders, symmetric signals, monotonicity numerical. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

How should a model be cut across devices of unequal speed?

For a fixed pipeline order, greedy filling is an exact test of a target stage time (agreeing with an independent dynamic program, with and without memory caps), and every order satisfies W/V ≤ T* < W/V + m wmax/V. A speed-blind equal split costs exactly v̄/vmin times the lower bound (2.40× at log-speed spread 0.5, 8.25× at 1.0) while speed-aware cutting stays within 1.4% at 240 layers. What is left is the device order: at 14 layers and 6 devices the worst order is 1.34× the best, fast-first and slow-first sorts do no better than an arbitrary order (all about 1.16× optimal), and pairwise-swap search gets within 1.1%; the penalty fades to 1.03× at 224 layers. Memory that shrinks as speed grows inflates the bottleneck 1.7×. No communication cost, static speeds. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

What does it cost to skip the slowest workers?

Waiting for the fastest k of n workers has exact round time s + (Hn−Hn−k)/μ for exponential tails, and for Pareto tails the mean is finite iff n−k+1 > 1/α, so with α ≤ 1 waiting for everyone has infinite expected round time. For SGD on a quadratic the time to accuracy has a minimum k and an interior optimum (34× faster than waiting for all at zero fixed cost, 1.12× at large fixed cost). If speed correlates with data, the fastest-k average is biased by Σ(πi/k−1/n)θi; Horvitz–Thompson reweighting removes it but only pays when the bias is large.

Code and white paper

Does a bigger swarm learn more from shared rollouts?

Not without incentives. With diminishing returns and a peer-rollout discount θ, symmetric Nash play gives every agent exactly the learning level of a lone agent whatever the swarm size (total effort caps at (a/c−1)/θ), while the efficient level grows linearly in N: welfare per agent is 4.5× higher at N=256. At θ=1 a single agent generates everything. A Pigouvian matching subsidy covering θ(N−1)/(1+θ(N−1)) of cost implements the optimum exactly, and junk rollouts beat honesty iff c−ε > p(τ+F).

Code and white paper

What does it cost to make workers race?

If a round pays the first k of n finishers a prize R and workers buy speed at cost c per unit rate, the win probability’s slope at the symmetric point telescopes to (1−k/n)(Hn−Hn−k), so equilibrium speed is R(n−k)(Hn−Hn−k)/(nc) and the round time is exactly nc/((n−k)R). Paying every finisher buys no speed at all; for a fixed budget, speed alone wants winner-take-all (0.10 at k=1 versus 3.2 at k=16 for n=32), and only the statistical floor on k justifies more winners. Recruiting more workers barely helps: total speed bought saturates at kR/c. Exponential races, linear cost, symmetric risk-neutral workers; equilibrium checked on a grid. Pure-Python, 12 tests.

Code and white paper

Who drops out of a race when workers have unequal costs?

If only the first k of n finishers are paid, a slow worker entering at a vanishing rate wins with probability rate × E X(k) of the fast workers, which gives an exact exit rule: workers with cost ratio cs/cf ≥ nf/(nf−k) stay out entirely, and paying k ≥ nf never excludes anyone (checked by best-entry payoffs at thresholds 4/3, 2, 4). At cost ratio 4 with four fast workers, k ≤ 3 shuts the slow ones out and k=4..7 readmits them (share of prizes 0.21→0.46 against a fair 0.5). The note also proves the telescoping identity behind the symmetric race and shows that with convex speed cost, headcount does buy speed. Two cost types, exponential races, grid-checked equilibria.

Code and white paper

How should a router treat modules that are usually asleep?

If only awake modules report and each awake module’s wealth is multiplied by 1+η(ℓ̂−ℓi), the ledger is exactly budget balanced, sleeping wealth never moves (each regime keeps a private ledger), and a module’s regret against the market on its awake rounds is at most ln(1/πi)/η + ηni in its own awake time (the exponential variant pays ηT/8 and is not budget balanced). Admitting a module with wealth ε costs each incumbent ln(1/(1−ε))/η in its bound. With recurring regimes the ledger matches the per-round oracle (0.1004 vs 0.1000, regret about 2.7 whatever the number of specialists) while a forced-to-report Hedge sits at the generalist (0.30) and fixed share is worse (0.34–0.36). The bound is loose (measured regret 2.7 against a bound near 103); losses bounded, wake sets exogenous. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

How stale can a shared rollout be before it is worthless?

With Gaussian policies whose mean has moved by δ standard deviations, the importance weight has exact moments E w = 1 and E w² = eδ², so the effective-sample fraction is e−δ² (0.37 at δ=1) and a learner needing fraction ρ accepts a lag of √ln(1/ρ)/drift policy versions. Truncating weights has closed-form lost mass, bias and variance (matched by simulation); the best cap cuts the mean-shift estimator’s MSE 1.9× at δ=1, 12.8× at δ=2 and about 750× at δ=3, and finite-sample ESS is optimistic once weights are heavy-tailed. Equal-variance Gaussians, one statistic. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

How should a verifier's vector report be scored?

For a report of an expected drift r ∈ ℝd with noise covariance Σ, every quadratic Bregman score −(y−r)TA(y−r) is proper and charges a misreport D exactly DTAD. Against a trusted reference the per-task gap has exact mean DTAD and variance 4DTAΣAD for any noise law, and Cauchy–Schwarz shows A=Σ−1 has the best signal to noise for every deviation at once, needing 4z²/(DTΣ−1D) tasks. An isotropic score has efficiency at least 4κ/(1+κ)² (Kantorovich), attained by a deviation split between the extreme eigendirections: 25× more tasks at condition number 100, and power 0.29 against 0.80 at 48 tasks in simulation. Per-layer normalisation alone barely helps; with Σ estimated from m reference draws, efficiency is 0.61 at m=2d and 0.95 at m=100. Quadratic scores, trusted reference, finite covariance. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

Can a module game a ledger by choosing when to sleep?

Yes, if it declares after seeing its loss. The wealth ledger pays each awake module exactly its leave-one-out saving, ηWA(1−pi)Si, but a module that sleeps whenever its own loss exceeds θ earns ηpBθ(1−θ)/2 per unit wealth against an equal-skill honest rival (best 1/8 at θ=1/2) and takes the market from a 0.1 share in about 130 rounds, while the router’s realised loss stays at 0.5. Declared before the router serves, the same wealth is a real saving that falls from 0.125 to 0.011 as the module’s signal about its own loss gets noisier. A sleeping tax that stops the exploit must be at least ηpB/2, a fixed-share rate that halves an honest specialist asleep 90% of the time in 6 rounds, so commitment, not taxation, is the fix. Two modules, uniform losses, threshold strategies; mean-field predictions 3–8% slow. Pure-Python, 9 tests.

Code and white paper

How should a router pick k distinct experts?

Sparse mixture-of-experts routing as a capped Hedge market: expert prices are min(1, λ wi) with a single shadow price λ and an exact KL projection. Regret against the best fixed k-set stayed within k ln(N/k)/η + ηTk/2 in every run (41–58% of it, not proved here); plain normalisation prices an expert above 1 in 282 of 300 rounds and understates loss 3.2×; systematic sampling realises exactly k distinct experts with 8–14× lower loss variance. Oblivious losses only. Pure-Python, 6 tests.

Code and white paper

How many skipped training steps hide in the loss noise?

If a worker paid for T steps runs only (1−f)T, the verifier’s log-loss test (null sd σ′, level α) hides exactly the compute at which the loss curve, inverted, crosses the noise band: L((1−f*)T) = L(T)eσ′(zα+zP). For a power law with a loss floor this is closed form and grows as the reducible share r falls (6% at r=1 but 64% at r=0.05 for σ′=0.02). Run-to-run seed noise is a floor that no evaluation size removes: with 2% seed noise a 5% cap is unreachable for r ≥ 0.05, while without it 104 to 4×106 eval samples suffice. On exactly solvable quadratic GD the predicted detection probability matches simulation within 1.5 points, and the loss test is worth only about 4.4 random step audits at best (0.16 once training is floor-dominated). Stylised: one statistic, normal approximation, known curve family. Pure-Python, 14 tests.

Code and white paper

How much does an appeal ladder of juries buy, and what must appeals cost?

A dispute goes to 3 jurors; the loser may pay a fee (proportional to panel size) to appeal to 11, then 27. If the fee lies in the window V(1−q) ≤ j n < V q, only the wrongly ruled truthful side appeals and the final error is exactly the product of the tiers’ error rates; below the window both sides appeal and only the last tier counts, above it nobody appeals. With jurors 70% accurate and prize 100 the smallest deterring panel is 11 (23 at prize 1000, 41 at 104); the 3→11→27 ladder errs 2.4×10−4 at 5.8 expected juror seats, against 12.6% for a single 7-seat panel, while a 9-juror middle tier leaks 0.78 wrong-side appeals per dispute. If jurors share a common bias with probability ρ, error cannot fall below ρ(1−a) however many tiers are added. Independent jurors, myopic appeals, no juror incentives or bribery; exact results agree with 200,000-trial simulation.

fiat-shamir-grinding12 tests

Do free retries break hash-derived spot checks?

Hash-derived audit challenges under free retries: cheat profit exactly G − c/p, deterrence needs ln(G/c)·T/k opened steps vs ln2·T/k for a beacon (10×–60×), stake is irrelevant, and the proof-of-work optimum is x* = v/λ_p − c0.

Abstract Project page →

When an audit challenge is the hash of the prover's own commitment, a cheater simply re-rolls until the challenge misses its corrupted steps, so expected profit is exactly G−c/p (p = C(T−k,q)/C(T,q)) and the stake plays no role. Deterrence needs q ≈ ln(G/c)·T/k opened steps against ln2·T/k for a post-commitment beacon: 10×–60× more for G/c = 210…260. Proof-of-work on the challenge has a closed-form optimum x* = v/λp − c0. Real SHA-256 grinding matches the geometric law. Stylised.

verifier-complements8 tests

When do verifiers complement rather than substitute?

Verifiers as informational complements: decision value is zero below a closed-form committee size while mutual information is submodular; myopic hiring buys nothing and leave-one-out pay is a sawtooth that vanishes.

Abstract Project page →

Exact value of verifier committees for an accept/slash decision: value is zero below a closed-form minimum committee size (4 at π=0.05, q=0.7) even though mutual information is submodular, 24–34% of triples violate diminishing returns, myopic marginal-value hiring buys nothing (ratio 0 to the optimum) and leave-one-out pay is a parity sawtooth that falls 7× below average value at 40 verifiers. Stylised.

committee-sampling11 tests

How big should a random verifier committee be?

Verifier committees from a finite pool: exact hypergeometric capture (zero once m ≥ 2B+1, up to 26× below binomial), exact size ≈0.90 of ln(1/ε)/KL(½‖β) vs Hoeffding up to 2.2× too large, stake-weighted draws depend only on Byzantine stake share (20 of 100 nodes at 4× stake capture a 41-committee w.p. ½), and the threshold safety/liveness trade-off.

Abstract Project page →

Drawing m verifiers from a pool of N with B Byzantine, majority capture is exactly hypergeometric: zero once m ≥ 2B+1 and up to 26× below the with-replacement binomial (N=100, B=30, m=41: 1.4×10−4 vs 3.6×10−3). For failure 2−40 the exact size is a steady ≈0.90 of ln(1/ε)/KL(½‖β) while Hoeffding over-sizes it up to 2.2×. With stake-weighted draws only the Byzantine stake share counts: 20 of 100 nodes at 4× stake capture a 41-member committee half the time. A threshold-t rule trades wrong acceptance (2.7×10−7 to 1.1×10−16) against stalls (2.7×10−7 to 3.3×10−2). Static adversary, exact computation.

sybil-stake7 tests

Are reward pools identity-proof?

Identity splitting vs merging under stake-weighted pools: split-invariant iff the weight is linear in stake, per-head optimum √(Rn/c)−n, sharp deterrence fee Rn/((n+1)(n+2)), wagering split-neutral.

Abstract Project page →

Sybil splitting and whale merging under stake-weighted pools: only linear-in-stake weights are split-invariant, per-head pools are captured at k* = √(Rn/c) − n identities (exact match), a sharp per-identity deterrence fee, exponents above 1 reward merging, and weighted-score wagering is split-neutral. Stylised.

stake-screening9 tests

Can a bond tell reliable hardware from unreliable?

Can a bond tell reliable hardware from unreliable? Single crossing runs the wrong way: reliable rent (θ_H−θ_L)(c+(1+ρ)s_H)/(1−θ_H) is minimised at zero stake, a flat wage is optimal, and a deterrence stake scales rent by (c+(1+ρ)s)/c.

Abstract Project page →

Workers have hidden fault rates and accept a wage-and-stake contract. Single crossing runs the wrong way: the reliable worker is the one who would copy a high-stake contract, so its rent is exactly (θH−θL)(c+(1+ρ)sH)/(1−θH), minimised at zero stake, and with continuous types a flat wage with no stake is optimal (no random 2–4-contract menu beats it). A stake needed for deterrence is a tax: it scales reliable workers’ rent by (c+(1+ρ)s)/c and lowers the pool’s fault rate (0.169→0.089) at 9–55% of profit. Stylised.

milestone-schedules8 tests

How many milestones does an unenforced job need?

Milestone payments without enforcement: a split pre-payment needs only the pooled relationship value (C/(W_r+W_w) vs P/W_r, C/W_w), and front-loading makes the milestone count logarithmic, ⌈ln(1+(V−C)/W)/ln(V/C)⌉ (17 vs 100 at W=1).

Abstract Project page →

A requester and an anonymous worker split a job into milestones, each a stage of pre-payment, work and late payment, with a grim trigger that forfeits the remaining surplus and a relationship value W. A milestone is self-enforcing under some pre-payment split iff its cost is at most the pooled continuation value, so pay-after-delivery needs P/Wr equal milestones, pay-before C/Ww, and the best split C/(Wr+Ww) (110, 25 and 20 in the example), whoever holds the value. Because early defection also forfeits the remaining work, the largest milestone shrinks geometrically and the minimum count is ⌈ln(1+(V−C)/W)/ln(V/C)⌉: 17 instead of 100 at C=100, V=120, W=1, with the first milestone 1−(C−W)/V of the job. Cheap re-entry caps W and costs ln(1/e) milestones. Matched on 2000 random instances. Stylised: complete information, pro-rata value.

04

Detection & tolerances

Statistics for catching cheats under floating-point noise: tolerances, anytime-valid tests and robust aggregation.

reproducible-refereed-training10 tests

Reproducible operators and refereed training

Measured float32 reduction-order drift, RepOps-style canonical order, Merkle-committed training traces with a teacher-forced referee; per-step tolerance is a cumulative hidden-deviation budget.

Abstract Project page →

Measured float32 drift across reduction orders (relative drift is Cauchy-tailed, state-level drift is a few ulps), a Merkle-committed training trace with a teacher-forced referee, and the finding that a per-step tolerance is a cumulative hidden-deviation budget while bitwise-reproducible operators remove it.

conformal-tolerance7 tests

How many honest runs does a slashing tolerance need?

Calibrating slashing tolerances from honest runs: split-conformal false-slash law (n+1-k)/(n+1) is exact but only ~51–56% of calibration sets are ≤ α, PAC safety needs n ≥ ln δ/ln(1−α) (459 at 1%/1%), the margin is cheater hiding room (×1.26 at n=2000, Pareto-3), Gaussian plug-ins over-slash skewed drift up to 17×, pooled hardware calibration over-slashes the noisy class 4.8× and lets the quiet class hide 2.9×.

Abstract Project page →

A conformal tolerance (the k-th order statistic of n honest drift scores) has an exact, distribution-free false-slash rate (n+1−k)/(n+1) — but only 51–56% of calibration sets deliver a rate ≤ α. A PAC-safe tolerance exists iff n ≥ ln δ/ln(1−α) (459 runs at 1%/1%), and its margin is hiding room for a cheater: the threshold sits 1.26× above the true quantile at n=2000 on Pareto-3 drift. Gaussian plug-in tolerances over-slash skewed drift up to 17×; pooling calibration across mixed hardware slashes the noisy class 4.8× too often and lets the quiet class hide 2.9× more.

layer-tolerance8 tests

Should drift tolerances be per layer or on the total?

Per-layer vs total drift tolerances: a tolerance per layer admits L·c(L,α)σ vs z_α√L σ on the total (6.6× at L=16), the sum test ignores how a cheat is spread while the max test catches 2.7σ in one layer but lets 16σ through spread over all, and a union test caps the hidden budget at the sum test's.

Abstract Project page →

Giving each of L layers its own tolerance lets a prover hide the sum of them: L·c(L,α)σ versus zα√Lσ for one test on the total, 6.6× more at L=16 and 23× at L=128. The sum test’s power depends only on the total shift; the exact (Šidák) max test’s depends on how it is spread, the prover’s best split is even (log Φ is concave), and the max test catches a 2.7σ one-layer shift half the time but lets 16σ through spread over all 16 layers. A union of both at α/2 caps the hidden budget at the sum test’s (7.8σ) while keeping one-layer sensitivity. Gaussian, independent layers, known σ.

freivalds-float7 tests

How well does Freivalds' check work in floating point?

Freivalds' matrix-product check in floating point: rank-one corruption missed with probability exactly erf(t/(√2F)) (worst case for fixed norm), erf^m for m probes, Rademacher probes stuck at ½ for any size, measured float32 noise floor, and 1/erf grinding tries when the probe is hashed from the result.

Abstract Project page →

Checking a claimed matrix product by A(Br) ≈ Cr needs a tolerance t, so the error bound becomes size-dependent: a rank-one corruption of Frobenius norm F is missed by a Gaussian probe with probability exactly erf(t/(√2F)), rank one is the worst case for fixed F, and m probes give erfm (4 probes for 1% at 3t). Rademacher probes miss a two-entry corruption with probability ½ at every size. Emulated float32 noise grows ≈n0.9; a hashed probe with free retries lets a cheater grind in 1/erf tries (125 at 100t). Stylised, additive corruption.

compute-shirking14 tests

How many skipped training steps hide in the loss noise?

Detecting skipped training steps from the loss alone: hidden compute is the loss curve inverted at the noise band (f* = 1−(1+(e^q−1)/r)^{−1/β}), grows as reducible loss falls, seed noise sets a floor no eval size removes, simulation matches within 1.5 points, and the loss test is worth ≈4.4 step audits at best.

Abstract Project page →

If a worker paid for T steps runs only (1−f)T, the verifier’s log-loss test (null sd σ′, level α) hides exactly the compute at which the loss curve, inverted, crosses the noise band: L((1−f*)T) = L(T)eσ′(zα+zP). For a power law with a loss floor this is closed form and grows as the reducible share r falls (6% at r=1 but 64% at r=0.05 for σ′=0.02). Run-to-run seed noise is a floor that no evaluation size removes: with 2% seed noise a 5% cap is unreachable for r ≥ 0.05, while without it 104 to 4×106 eval samples suffice. On exactly solvable quadratic GD the predicted detection probability matches simulation within 1.5 points, and the loss test is worth only about 4.4 random step audits at best (0.16 once training is floor-dominated). Stylised: one statistic, normal approximation, known curve family.

inference-substitution10 tests

How much can a provider steal by serving a cheaper model?

Detecting a provider that serves a cheaper model on a fraction of queries: mixture e-process (valid under peeking), delay ∝ 1/(f p² χ²), so the cheater's best response is to leak rarely and steal ∝ √N not N; closed-form audit rate and cost-optimal check rate (hK/2Nc)^{2/3}.

Abstract Project page →

A decentralised inference provider substitutes a cheaper model on a random fraction p of queries; a verifier re-scores a fraction f under an anytime-valid mixture e-process. Detection delay scales as 1/(f p² χ²), so the profitable attack is a slow leak: undetected savings grow as √N rather than N (measured ×7.75 for ×64 queries). Closed-form audit rate to cap theft, cost-optimal check rate (hK/2Nc)2/3, and a substitute close enough to the claimed model that even checking every response cannot cap the theft. Seeded Monte Carlo. Stylised.

sequential-slashing6 tests

Can you slash while watching the data stream?

Anytime-valid slashing of miscalibrated verifiers: peeking z-test falsely slashes 37% of honest verifiers (nominal 5%), an e-process holds ≤α by Ville, detection delay ≈ ln(1/α)/KL (within 12%), q-free mixture costs ×1.36.

Abstract Project page →

Anytime-valid slashing of miscalibrated verifiers with e-processes: repeatedly re-running a z-test falsely slashes 37% of honest verifiers at nominal 5%, the likelihood-ratio e-process stays under α by Ville’s inequality, detection delay tracks ln(1/α)/KL within 12% (logarithmic in 1/α), and not knowing the cheating rate costs a factor 1.36. Stylised.

forecast-duel7 tests

Can two verifiers be compared while the data streams in?

Anytime-valid duels between two verifiers: the optimal betting e-process on the Brier difference grows at exactly KL(q‖(rA+rB)/2), a peeking z-test falsely declares a winner 19–38% of the time at nominal 5%, a bet mixture stays ≤3.8% and costs 15–41% more decisions.

Abstract Project page →

For fixed reports rA, rB and binary outcomes with frequency q, the Brier difference is a two-point gamble and A is better exactly when q is on A’s side of the midpoint π=(rA+rB)/2. Betting a fraction λ of wealth on it gives an anytime-valid e-process whose best bet grows at exactly KL(q‖π), so the expected decision time is ln(1/α)/KL. A z-test checked after every task falsely declares a winner in 19–38% of null runs at nominal 5%; a uniform mixture over bets stays at or below 3.8% and costs 15–41% extra tasks; a bet twice too large has negative growth. Fixed reports, i.i.d. outcomes. Stylised.

verifier-league11 tests

Which of n verifiers is best, decided at any time?

Anytime-valid best-of-n verifier identification: delay set by the rival whose report midpoint sits nearest q (the best opposite-side rival, not the runner-up), mixture within 1.35–1.60× of oracle, elimination 4–5× cheaper, peeking declares a false best in 59% of ties vs 1.6%.

Abstract Project page →

Under Brier loss the best verifier is the one whose report is closest to the outcome frequency q, and each pair has an anytime-valid betting e-process growing at KL(q‖midpoint). Certifying the leader means beating every rival, so the delay is ln(1/α) over the smallest such rate, which belongs to the rival whose midpoint with the leader is nearest q: the best rival on the opposite side of q, not the runner-up (rate 0.0026 against 0.0086 in a six-verifier league). A bet mixture certifies within 1.35–1.60× of the oracle prediction; successive elimination cuts verifier evaluations 4cuts evaluation cost 2–4× at n=8–12ndash;5× at n=8–12; a peeking z-test declares a false strict best in 59% of exact-tie runs against 1.6% for the e-process. Stylised: fixed reports, i.i.d. tasks.

robust-aggregation7 tests

How much can Byzantine verifiers move an aggregate?

Byzantine-robust aggregation of verifier reports: mean bias βB unbounded, median bias σΦ⁻¹(1/(2(1−β))) independent of B, trimmed-mean closed form for τ≥β verified by simulation.

Abstract Project page →

Mean, median and trimmed-mean aggregation of verifier reports under a Byzantine fraction β: mean bias βB is unbounded, median bias σΦ−1(1/(2(1−β))) is independent of B and diverges at β=½, trimmed-mean closed form for τ≥β matches simulation, and trimming below β fails. Stylised.

forgetting-audit7 tests

Can a verifier tell from old-task losses that a continual-learning job skipped or shortchanged tasks?

Auditing skipped or partial continual-learning training from old-task losses: exact loss law (ρ^{t−1}[(1−2m₁+m₂)(r/d)λᵏ+(r/d)ρ(ρᵏ−λᵏ)]), a skipped task is ≥ d/(d−r)× worse but only clearly so inside a lag window, detecting a skipper takes ~0.7/s² jobs at any lag, a 10% step shortfall needs ~9600.

Abstract Project page →

Extends the forgetting law to a trainer that skips each task with probability s or takes a step fraction a: the final-checkpoint loss on the task at position t is exactly ρt−1[(1−2m1+m2)(r/d)λk + (r/d)ρ(ρk−λk)], matching exact quadrature and simulation. A skipped task is at least d/(d−r) times worse than a trained one at every lag but clearly so only in a window (ratio ≥2 for lags ≤6.7 at d=16, r=2). Catching a skipping trainer is lag-free: about 17–20 jobs for 20% skipping at any audit lag, scaling as 0.7/s2 and falling with job length, while a 10% step shortfall needs about 9,600 jobs. Stylised: linear regression, Haar-random tasks, known initial error.

interference-twin10 tests

Is an interference-free or mean-noise-rise radar twin right when robots' radars interfere with each other?

Interference-free or mean-noise-rise radar twin vs intermittent mutual radar interference between robots: exact closed-form per-frame Pd, real Pd plateaus at 0.656 (no-hit probability), mean-rise twin 9% optimistic at Pd ≥ 0.9 yet badly pessimistic for hit-tolerant missions, geometry knowledge helps 9-of-10 missions (Brier 0.089 vs 0.101). Abstract Project page →

Mutual radar interference between robots, with heavy-tailed c/d2 interferer power hitting each frame intermittently. Per-frame detection probability has a closed form (matches Monte Carlo within 0.003); real Pd plateaus at the probability that no interferer hits the frame (0.656) rather than shrinking in range. A mean-noise-rise twin is 9% optimistic at Pd ≥ 0.9 (63.7 vs 58.4 m) but badly pessimistic for missions that tolerate hit frames (Brier 0.690 vs 0.003 for 3-of-10); for 9-of-10 missions knowing the interferer geometry helps (0.089 vs 0.101). Stylised: simulated interference, illustrative parameters, no radar data.

delayed-routing11 tests

What does late feedback cost a market router?

Hedge/LMSR routing with delayed feedback: regret ≤ ln N/η + ηT/8 + ηD/2 (mean delay inflates horizon by 1+4d̄), 12× regret from ignoring delay against a reactive adversary, delay-tuned rate too cautious on oblivious data, LMSR subsidy ~20× at mean delay 5.

balanced-routing10 tests

Is load balancing a congestion price?

Capacity-constrained expert routing as a congestion-priced market: softmax with dual prices, verifier-computable duality-gap certificate from prices alone, sign-update balancing has a ≈2.5/√B sampling floor plus a step-size limit cycle, closed-form two-expert price of balance, Hoeffding load audit.

Abstract Project page →

Capacity-constrained expert routing is a softmax with a per-expert price, the Lagrange multiplier of its capacity, and the dual is smooth and concave. Any price vector gives a computable upper bound and, after repair toward the uniform assignment, a feasible lower bound, so a verifier certifies near-optimality from prices alone (gap below 10−4 at the optimum, always above the true suboptimality). Sign-update balancing has a sampling floor of about 2.5/√B in max relative overload that no step size removes, plus a step-proportional limit cycle on a fixed batch (22.6% at γ=0.2, 1.2% at 0.01). Two-expert Gaussian price of balance is closed form with price shift equal to the median gap; a Hoeffding audit of ln(2N/δ)/(2ε2) tokens covered 400 of 400 trials. Synthetic scores only. Stylised.

kelly-markets11 tests

Is risk tolerance the learning rate of a wealth market?

Fractional-Kelly wealth markets as expert routers: risk-tolerance-weighted price, ln(1/s)/λ regret bound, growth-optimal λ*=(π−p)/(q−p), manipulation cost V·χ² vs LMSR b·KL (7.5× stiffer at p=0.99), and a switching-truth trade-off where λ≈0.1–0.2 beats full Kelly 3–7×.

Abstract Project page →

When agents bet a fraction λ of wealth Kelly-style, the clearing price is the λ·wealth-weighted mean belief, total wealth is conserved, and λ=1 is exactly the Bayes mixture. Market log-loss exceeds expert i’s by at most ln(1/si)/λi on any sequence (loose on i.i.d. data), the growth-optimal fraction is (π−p)/(q−p), and moving the price against calibrated others costs Vχ²(p0‖p): equal to LMSR b·KL at b=2V for small shifts but 7.5× stiffer at p=0.99. On a truth that switches regimes, full Kelly is wrong about half of every segment (regret about 1630 at T=4000) while λ of 0.1–0.2 cuts it 3–7×. Binary events, static experts. Stylised.

topk-routing6 tests

How should a router pick k distinct experts?

Top-k MoE routing as a capped Hedge market: price min(1, λ w_i) with exact KL projection, regret vs the best fixed k-set held under k ln(N/k)/η+ηTk/2 in every run (41–58% of it), plain normalisation prices experts above 1 (282/300 rounds, loss understated 3.2×), and systematic sampling gives exactly k distinct experts with 8–14× lower variance.

Abstract Project page →

Sparse mixture-of-experts routing as a capped Hedge market: expert prices are min(1, λ wi) with a single shadow price λ and an exact KL projection. Regret against the best fixed k-set stayed within k ln(N/k)/η + ηTk/2 in every run (41–58% of it, not proved here); plain normalisation prices an expert above 1 in 282 of 300 rounds and understates loss 3.2×; systematic sampling realises exactly k distinct experts with 8–14× lower loss variance. Oblivious losses only.

sleeping-ledger8 tests

How should a router treat modules that are usually asleep?

A self-financed wealth ledger for specialist modules that sleep: total wealth conserved exactly, sleeping wealth frozen (one private ledger per regime), regret ≤ ln(1/π_i)/η + η·n_i in the module's *own* awake time, entry of a module with wealth ε costs incumbents ln(1/(1−ε))/η; matches the regime oracle (0.1004 vs 0.1000) where forced-to-report Hedge sits at 0.30 and fixed share is worse.

Abstract Project page →

If only awake modules report and each awake module’s wealth is multiplied by 1+η(ℓ̂−ℓi), the ledger is exactly budget balanced, sleeping wealth never moves (each regime keeps a private ledger), and a module’s regret against the market on its awake rounds is at most ln(1/πi)/η + ηni in its own awake time (the exponential variant pays ηT/8 and is not budget balanced). Admitting a module with wealth ε costs each incumbent ln(1/(1−ε))/η in its bound. With recurring regimes the ledger matches the per-round oracle (0.1004 vs 0.1000, regret about 2.7 whatever the number of specialists) while a forced-to-report Hedge sits at the generalist (0.30) and fixed share is worse (0.34–0.36). The bound is loose (measured regret 2.7 against a bound near 103); losses bounded, wake sets exogenous.

sleeping-incentives9 tests

Can a module game a ledger by choosing when to sleep?

When may a module choose to sleep? The ledger pays exactly leave-one-out savings ηW_A(1−p_i)S_i; sleeping *after* seeing losses gains wealth ηp_Bθ(1−θ)/2 (best 1/8) and takes the market in ~130 rounds with the router's loss unchanged; committed *before* serving it is a real saving; the deterring tax ηp_B/2 is a fixed share that halves honest specialists in 6 rounds.

Abstract Project page →

Yes, if it declares after seeing its loss. The wealth ledger pays each awake module exactly its leave-one-out saving, ηWA(1−pi)Si, but a module that sleeps whenever its own loss exceeds θ earns ηpBθ(1−θ)/2 per unit wealth against an equal-skill honest rival (best 1/8 at θ=1/2) and takes the market from a 0.1 share in about 130 rounds, while the router’s realised loss stays at 0.5. Declared before the router serves, the same wealth is a real saving that falls from 0.125 to 0.011 as the module’s signal about its own loss gets noisier. A sleeping tax that stops the exploit must be at least ηpB/2, a fixed-share rate that halves an honest specialist asleep 90% of the time in 6 rounds, so commitment, not taxation, is the fix. Two modules, uniform losses, threshold strategies; mean-field predictions 3–8% slow.

decision-markets16 tests

What does it cost to route between models with conditional markets, and what does a stake do to the answer?

Conditional markets that route between models: inverse-propensity Brier is proper even when the router reads the report, exploration costs exactly 1+(K−1)e^{ω²/2τ²} in payment variance (probit: infinite for τ ≤ ω), and a stake gap distorts the reported gap by a closed-form fixed point with second-order harm.

Abstract Project page →

Markets that forecast each model’s loss if chosen only ever see the chosen arm. An inverse-propensity Brier payment is exactly proper even when the router reads the report (without the weight a trader shades its forecast, or hides), and its price is exact: E[1/π] = 1+(K−1)eω2/2τ2, so payment variance blows up as the router cools (a probit router has infinite variance for τ ≤ ω; Monte Carlo at τ=0.3 sees 29 against the exact 195). Exploration regret is at most 0.2785τ. Equal owner stakes cancel in the decision, a stake gap shifts the reported gap by a closed-form fixed point, and the loss it causes is second order, ∝(ΔB/k)2. Gaussian, one-shot, stylised.

module-entry6 tests

What share of the mass should a new module get?

Admitting new modules to a Hedge/LMSR router: regret certificates obey a Kraft identity Σ e^{−c_i}=1, so uniform entry 1/(n+1) is the unique minimax rule; prior-optimal shares P_j/S_j cost H(P); the price of entry is exactly ln(1/π)/η independent of the quality gap.

Abstract Project page →

When a modular system adds an expert to a Hedge/LMSR router, the regret certificate to every expert is ci/η + ηT/8 with ci = ln(1/πi) + Σj>i ln(1/(1−πj)), and for any share sequence Σi e−ci = 1 (a Kraft identity). So uniform entry π = 1/(n+1) is the unique minimax rule (every ci = ln N, against 4.1–9.7 for constant shares at 4+12 modules), and against a prior on which module will be best the optimal shares are Pj/Sj with expected coefficient equal to the entropy of the prior. The price of entry is exactly ln(1/π)/η for a better arrival and ln(1/(1−π))/η for a worse one, independent of the quality gap; a recency prior cuts simulated regret from 3.11 to 2.70 nats. Known arrival rounds, fixed η. Pure-Python, 6 tests.

06

Prediction-market design

Liquidity, fees, privacy and manipulation in the LMSR markets that aggregate verifier beliefs.

anytime-liquidity12 tests

What does not knowing the horizon cost a market maker?

LMSR with time-varying liquidity as anytime Hedge: b_t = c*√t costs exactly √2 over the horizon-aware bound, doubling is 1.70× worse, and self-tuning liquidity makes the subsidy equal the accumulated mixability gap (1.3 vs 102 on easy data).

Abstract Project page →

An LMSR with liquidity b routes like Hedge with rate 1/b, but the tuned b needs the horizon T. A bt = c√t schedule with c* = 1/(2√ln N) pays exactly √2 over the horizon-aware bound (1.36 rising to 1.41 measured); the doubling trick is 1.70× worse than the continuous schedule against a price-reactive adversary; and self-tuning liquidity bt = Δt−1/ln N makes the subsidy equal the accumulated mixability gap (1.3 against 102 on easy data) with regret at most 2Δ. Regret analysis only. Stylised.

private-markets6 tests

The subsidy cost of privacy in prediction markets

Differentially private LMSR via the binary-tree mechanism: path-wise loss bound, and the accuracy/subsidy cost of privacy.

Abstract Project page →

Differentially private LMSR via the binary-tree mechanism: error scales as 1/(bε), tree noise beats per-release noise ~15×, and privacy noise is exploitable so market-maker loss far exceeds b ln 2. Stylised.

market-manipulation9 tests

Who pays for the information in a manipulated market?

Manipulating an LMSR verification market: manipulator loss b·KL(q‖τ) equals the extra informed rent, and manipulation raises accuracy only in a liquidity band (thin: costs 1−2q; deep: neutral).

Abstract Project page →

An uninformed manipulator pushing an LMSR verification market from q to τ loses exactly b·KL(q‖τ), which equals to the digit the extra rent it hands to informed traders; the accuracy change is μ[e1(1−q) − e0q − (1−2q)], positive only in a liquidity band (0.107, 0.413 in the baseline): below it nobody enters and manipulation costs 1−2q accuracy, above b = Nc/(H(q)−ln(1/(1−ε))) entry is certain and manipulation is neutral. Matches an executable LMSR Monte Carlo. Stylised.

market-sandwich13 tests

What does a slippage limit give away in a prediction market?

Sandwiching an LMSR verification market: attacker profit is exactly the victim's slippage tolerance times its fair cost, needs capital ≈ εb/(1−p), dies to a fee ≈ v(1−p)/(2b); pro-rata batching keeps 99% of the extraction, random ordering cuts it 3×.

Abstract Project page →

A searcher who buys before and sells after a victim's LMSR trade extracts exactly the victim's slippage tolerance times its fair cost (εC0, error 1.4×10−14 over 216 instances), with a closed-form front-run of about εb/(1−p) shares, so return on capital falls as 1/b. A proportional fee of about v(1−p)/(2b) makes it unprofitable at any tolerance; the victim's optimal tolerance grows only like √log of the stakes; pro-rata batching keeps 0.989–0.999 of the extraction and uniformly random ordering cuts it exactly 3×. Stylised.

order-flow-liquidity10 tests

Who trades decides how liquid a verification market should be

Glosten–Milgrom vs LMSR for a verification market: informed share fixes b* = 1/(2 atanh m) (verified to 2e-16), peak misspecification regret is scale-free and overconfident b costs 1.5–2.4× more, LMSR subsidy → b* ln 2 is the spread GM charges.

Abstract Project page →

A Glosten–Milgrom market maker facing an informed share μ with accuracy q moves its posterior log-odds by exactly 2·atanh(μ(2q−1)) per net buy, so its price path is an LMSR with b* = 1/(2 atanh m) (verified to 2×10−16). A wrong b costs log loss only in a transient whose peak is scale-free in m and 1.8–2.5× worse when overconfident; the LMSR subsidy tends to b* ln 2, exactly the spread the GM maker charges. Stylised.

lmsr-fees8 tests

What does a fee do to a prediction market’s price?

Proportional fees on an LMSR verification market: exact no-trade band [q/(1+f),(q+f)/(1+f)], price lag q/(1+f), dead-market cliff f ≥ 2a−1 (threshold 2 atanh f at ½), exact fee revenue f·b·ln((1−p₀)/(1−p_T)), and a break-even fee that costs +38% Brier error.

Abstract Project page →

A proportional fee f on an LMSR verification market gives every trader an exact no-trade band [q/(1+f), (q+f)/(1+f)] of width f/(1+f), so an informed trader leaves the price at q/(1+f). At price ½ a signal of log-likelihood ratio λ moves the price iff f < tanh(λ/2) = 2a−1, above which the market is dead; fee revenue on a monotone path is exactly fb ln((1−p0)/(1−pT)). With ten 0.65-accurate traders, the break-even fee (≈0.11) raises Brier error from 0.115 to about 0.16 and revenue is hump-shaped in f. Naive traders, synthetic signals.

position-rent8 tests

What is a seat in a prediction market worth?

Sequential LMSR seat rents are conditional mutual information: they telescope to the maker's expected loss (≤ b ln 2), fall with position at the Chernoff rate, order only redistributes a fixed total, and entry costs make error fall only ~1/b in the subsidy.

Abstract Project page →

In a sequential LMSR verification market the verifier in position k earns in expectation b·I(y; sk | s<k), a conditional mutual information, so seat rents telescope to the maker’s expected loss (at most b ln 2); an explicit cost-function simulation agrees to three decimals. Rents fall with position, the successive ratio approaching e−C (Chernoff information) from below; order only redistributes a fixed total (a 0.9-accurate verifier gets 0.368 of 0.407 first, 0.303 last). With entry cost c, accuracy improves roughly as 1/b: 11 verifiers at b=0.25 (92%), 41 at b=5 (99.6%). Myopic traders, symmetric signals, monotonicity numerical.

market-subspace-descent11 tests

How fast does a prediction market converge when traders only understand part of it?

Convergence of cost-function markets with partially informed traders as randomized subspace descent: maker loss telescopes to ½(e₀'Ae₀−e_T'Ae_T), closed-form slowdown from correlated securities (31→356 rounds at c=0.95, d=5), A-conjugate bundles restore 1−1/d exactly, noisy-belief step size is an SGD step (running mean beats best constant step), LMSR simulation checks the local rates.

Abstract Project page →

Traders who each move prices within a subspace of securities make a cost-function market a randomized subspace descent. The market maker’s expected loss telescopes to ½(e0′Ae0 − eT′AeT) whoever trades, so accuracy is bought once. Correlated securities slow single-security traders in closed form (5 securities: 31 rounds to reach 10−3 of the error uncorrelated, 356 at correlation 0.95), while offering A-conjugate bundles restores the exact rate 1−1/d at any correlation. With noisy beliefs the fraction κ a trader moves acts as an SGD step size: floor dκσ2/(2−κ), and a per-security running-mean step beats the best constant step (error 0.26 vs 0.47 at 100 rounds; full steps stay at 5). A simulated 4-outcome LMSR matches the local rate predictions to within 0.01 for two of three bundle designs and is faster than predicted for the third, for a reason not isolated. Quadratic-cost theory with i.i.d. trader arrival and Gaussian belief noise.

cfmm-markets10 tests

What does a constant-product pool concede to informed traders?

Constant-product AMMs as cost-function prediction markets: worst-case loss C0 never attained, informed-trader profit exactly C0(1−n·GM(π)) (ratio to LMSR → ln n, crossover at n=e), polynomial price tails (p=0.999 costs 3.4× LMSR), exact regret identity, no forgiveness gain under regime switches.

Abstract Project page →

A Uniswap-style pool with invariant ∏ri = C0n is a cost-function prediction market: its worst-case loss is C0 and is never attained, and a trader who moves the price to belief π earns exactly C0(1 − n·GM(π)) with GM the geometric mean, against C0(1 − H(π)/ln n) for LMSR at equal worst-case loss. Near uniform beliefs the ratio is exactly ln n, so the pool is cheaper than LMSR for two outcomes and dearer from three. Its price tails are polynomial, (C0/gap)n, so pushing a binary price to 0.999 costs 3.4× LMSR. As an expert router it satisfies an exact regret identity (settlement term ≤ C0 plus Bregman terms), but under regime switches it shows no advantage over Hedge (negative result). Symmetric pools, no fees. Pure-Python, 10 tests.

07

Paying contributors

Buying compute, data and model improvements: holdout markets, Shapley payments, contests and races.

holdout-market4 tests

Paying for improvements, not for overfitting

Paying for model improvements against a hidden holdout: telescoping budget, a payment-feedback overfitting attack (paid 0.15 while true loss worsens 0.37), and the Ladder fix with its measured cost.

Abstract Project page →

A model-improvement market paying holdout-loss decreases: the budget telescopes, but naive payment feedback lets a data-less adversary be paid while the published model's true loss worsens; a Ladder-style threshold removes the attack at a measured cost to honest small contributors. Stylised.

data-valuation-replication9 tests

What does submitting copies earn under Shapley payments?

Shapley and leave-one-out payments under replication: Shapley pays every extra copy even when worthless, saturating at stand-alone value ((n+2)/2× honest), naive evaluators hand over the pot, LOO pays copies 0 but distributes 1/(n+1), dedup underpays lookalikes by 45%.

Abstract Project page →

Paying contributors of data or gradients by Shapley value rewards replication even when copies add zero information: in a Bayesian mean-estimation game the replicator's payment rises with every copy to its stand-alone value, exactly (n+2)/2 times the honest payment against n unit-precision others (5.5× at n=9). If the evaluator treats copies as independent the replicator's pot share tends to 100%; leave-one-out pays true copies exactly zero but distributes only 1/(n+1) of the pot; collapsing duplicates fixes it but underpays independent look-alikes by 45%. Exact computation checked against permutation brute force. Stylised.

shapley-sampling9 tests

How should Shapley payments be sampled and audited?

Auditing sampled Shapley payments: exact estimator variances in a saturating game, permutation sampling is exactly efficient but stratified sampling has 6–8× lower variance (zero for equal contributors) at up to 7% budget error, antithetic reversal gives 1.6× lower RMSE, Hoeffding sample counts are 4–5× conservative.

Abstract Project page →

In a saturating contribution game v(S)=1−exp(−Σwi) every estimator variance is exact. Permutation sampling always pays out exactly v(N) but is noisy; size-stratified sampling has 6–8× lower variance (exactly zero for equal contributors) yet misses the pot by up to 7% in a run; reversing each permutation cuts RMSE 1.6× at no cost; Hoeffding sample counts are 4–5× larger than needed, and stratification finds the top-3 payees with about 4× fewer samples. Stylised, n≤10.

contest-precision11 tests

How precise should a training-contest leaderboard be?

Winner-take-all training contests scored on a noisy holdout: effort V a_n √m/s with a_2 = a_3 = 1/(2√π) exactly, a precision ceiling V/σ² ≤ λ_max(n) beyond which no pure equilibrium exists (below the zero-rent limit), and the resulting optimal holdout size.

Abstract Project page →

In a winner-take-all contest ranked on a noisy holdout of m samples, equilibrium effort is V·an√m/s with a2=a3=1/(2√π) exactly, but the formula stops being an equilibrium once V/σ² passes a ceiling (12.35, 7.78, 6.11, 5.60, 5.80 for n=2, 3, 5, 10, 20) that sits below the zero-rent limit and falls to half of it at n=20. The organiser's optimal holdout is min(mcap, (wVan/2sκ)²): when evaluation is cheap the ceiling, not cost, binds. Quadrature checked against Monte Carlo and brute-force best replies. Stylised.

compute-procurement9 tests

What does it cost to buy decentralised compute?

Buying k units of decentralised compute by reverse auction: exact VCG payment k(k+1)/(n+1) is exactly 2× winners' cost, optimal reserve is exactly v/2, first-price equilibrium matches by revenue equivalence.

Abstract Project page →

Reverse auction for k compute units from n devices with private costs: the truthful threshold auction pays exactly k(k+1)/(n+1), twice the winners’ true cost for every n and k (also with a reserve), the buyer-optimal reserve is exactly v/2 (worth up to +1.03 utility in thin markets, nothing once v≥2), and the pay-as-bid equilibrium has closed form and matches revenue (1.3334 vs 1.3333). Stylised.

speed-race12 tests

What does it cost to make workers race?

Paying the first k of n finishers makes speed a contest: π'(1)=(1−k/n)(H_n−H_{n−k}), equilibrium speed R(n−k)(H_n−H_{n−k})/(nc), exact round time nc/((n−k)R); paying all finishers buys no speed, a budget favours winner-take-all until an accuracy floor k_min binds, and recruiting more workers barely speeds the round.

Abstract Project page →

If a round pays the first k of n finishers a prize R and workers buy speed at cost c per unit rate, the win probability’s slope at the symmetric point telescopes to (1−k/n)(Hn−Hn−k), so equilibrium speed is R(n−k)(Hn−Hn−k)/(nc) and the round time is exactly nc/((n−k)R). Paying every finisher buys no speed at all; for a fixed budget, speed alone wants winner-take-all (0.10 at k=1 versus 3.2 at k=16 for n=32), and only the statistical floor on k justifies more winners. Recruiting more workers barely helps: total speed bought saturates at kR/c. Exponential races, linear cost, symmetric risk-neutral workers; equilibrium checked on a grid.

race-heterogeneity13 tests

Who drops out of a race when workers have unequal costs?

Paying the first k of n finishers when costs differ: proof of the π'(1) telescoping identity, exact exit rule (slow workers idle iff c_s/c_f ≥ n_f/(n_f−k), never for k ≥ n_f), cost ratio 4 excludes slow workers for k ≤ 3 of 4 fast, convex costs make headcount buy speed.

Abstract Project page →

If only the first k of n finishers are paid, a slow worker entering at a vanishing rate wins with probability rate × E X(k) of the fast workers, which gives an exact exit rule: workers with cost ratio cs/cf ≥ nf/(nf−k) stay out entirely, and paying k ≥ nf never excludes anyone (checked by best-entry payoffs at thresholds 4/3, 2, 4). At cost ratio 4 with four fast workers, k ≤ 3 shuts the slow ones out and k=4..7 readmits them (share of prizes 0.21→0.46 against a fair 0.5). The note also proves the telescoping identity behind the symmetric race and shows that with convex speed cost, headcount does buy speed. Two cost types, exponential races, grid-checked equilibria.

private-data-market8 tests

How much accuracy can a market buy from contributors who value their privacy?

Buying private data with a telescoping log-score market: payment equals information, best Gaussian-mechanism noise in closed form, participation iff κa<1 so precision is capped at λ/(cΔ²) for any number of contributors, and early arrivals over-collect (1–22% welfare loss).

Abstract Project page →

A market pays each contributor the log-score gain of a public Gaussian belief for releasing a statistic plus Gaussian-mechanism noise, so the expected payment is exactly the information released, ½λln(1+τ/a). The best noise is a closed-form quadratic root, and participation is possible if and only if κa < 1 with κ = cΔ2/λ: precision is capped at λ/(cΔ2) however many contributors arrive, approached geometrically at rate 2σ2/(2σ2+κ), and total payout is at most ½λln(1/(κa0)). Early arrivals add too little noise (1.5–5×; 1–22% welfare loss against a planner), and admitting small data holders first lifts final precision from 28.0 to 34.2. Checked against grid search and 106-run Monte Carlo. Stylised.

Decentralised training systems

Gossip, local SGD, pipelines, checkpoints and shared rollouts on unreliable, heterogeneous workers.

gossip-consensus7 tests

What can one stubborn node do to gossip training?

Pairwise gossip for decentralised training: exact contraction (n−2)/(2(n−1))≈½ per matching round (~20 rounds at any n), noise floor (n−1)(n−2)s²/n, one stubborn node captures consensus at rate 1−1/(n(n−1)), trust-region clipping caps drift at τ/(n(n−1)) per step.

Abstract Project page →

Pairwise gossip averaging as a stand-in for all-reduce: disagreement contracts by exactly (n−2)/(2(n−1)) ≈ ½ per matching round (about 20 rounds at any n), the noise floor is (n−1)(n−2)s²/n (matched to 0.3%), a single stubborn node captures the honest mean at exact rate 1−1/(n(n−1)), and a trust-region clip turns capture into linear creep of at most τ/(n(n−1)) per step. local-sgd-bias8 tests

What does infrequent averaging do to the answer?
