Negative result: fixed deletion does not lower RMSE, and MSER-5 truncation leaves a larger bias (−0.77), covers 61% against 72% for no truncation, and passes a violating system 28% of the time against 18%. Stylised (Gaussian AR(1), M/M/1, simulated “real” system).

nlos-twin8 tests

How wrong is a twin's localisation error when real ranges have non-line-of-sight bias?

A twin with Gaussian range noise vs real non-line-of-sight bias: exact rms law GDOP·√(σ²+p(2−p)m²) (4.5–7.3× the twin's error, zero mean), a predictable bias for a blocked side, anchor counts 4 → 28–46 for a 1 m / 95% corridor, and a trimming fix that costs 24% when NLOS is absent.

Abstract Project page →

A twin draws anchor ranges as true distance plus Gaussian noise; real sites also have long-biased NLOS ranges. On a ring of anchors the rms position error is exactly GDOP·√(σ2+p(2−p)m2) (1.105 vs law 1.095 m at p=0.1, n=6), 4.5× and 7.3× the twin's at p=0.1 and 0.3, with zero mean. A blocked side is a bias the linear formula predicts to about 0.02 m per coordinate (0.924 vs 0.930 m) while the twin predicts none. Sized on the twin, a 1 m / 95% corridor needs 4 anchors; the NLOS site needs about 28 (p=0.1) or 46 (p=0.2), and the 4-anchor ring leaves the corridor 34.7% of the time instead of 5%. Dropping the largest-residual anchor cuts rms error 0.947→0.414 m at p=0.1 but costs 24% with no NLOS. Stylised: 2-D ring, iid exponential NLOS, simulated site, no sensor data.

closedloop-twin8 tests

Can a twin identified from logs of the deployed controller tell you whether a different controller is stable?

A twin identified from logs of the deployed controller: held-out error is 1.00σ² at every dither level while the predicted pole under a new gain has sd (σ/√n)√((k−k')²/τ²+1/v) (0.037→0.82), no dither gives a confident wrong twin (b̂=−0.22 vs +1), point-rule false stability certification 3–48% vs 0.1–4.7% for the OLS bound.

Abstract Project page →

A twin fitted to closed-loop logs predicts the pole under a new gain k′ with sd (σ/√n)√((k−k′)2/τ2+1/v), set by the dither τ: held-out one-step error is 1.00–1.005σ2 at every τ, while the predicted pole's sd goes 0.037 to 0.82 (matching the formula to a few percent). With no dither the minimum-norm fit gets b̂=−0.22 (true +1) and certifies a real-unstable gain in 100% of fits. Point-rule false certification is 3–48%; the OLS upper bound cuts it to 0.1–4.7% but rarely certifies a good gain at low dither (5–9%). A predicted-pole sd of 0.05 needs τ=1.23 / 0.40 / 0.16 at n=200 / 1000 / 5000. Stylised: scalar linear plant, simulated data.

input-twin7 tests

How much of a digital twin's error is that it was fitted to finite real data, however long it is simulated?

A twin fitted to finite real data: exact delta-method error √(1+(2−ρ)²)/((1−ρ)√n) of its steady-state wait, data needed grows as (1−ρ)⁻² (22 100 per stream for 10% at ρ=0.9), exact instability probability, false SLA certification 36–46% fixed by bootstrap/posterior bounds (delta bound under-covers).

Abstract Project page →

A twin fitted to n real interarrival and service times has a steady-state wait that is one fixed number, so its error is input error that more simulation cannot remove. The relative sd is √(1+(2−ρ)2)/((1−ρ)√n) (0.255 vs 0.257 simulated), so a 10% sd needs 1300 / 22 100 observations per stream at ρ=0.5 / 0.9. The fitted twin is unstable with exact probability P[F(2n,2n) ≥ 1/ρ] (0.370 at ρ=0.9, n=20). Used as truth, the point twin certifies a 10%-violated SLA in 36–46% of fits; the delta-method bound under-covers at high load (0.87–0.89), while bootstrap and posterior bounds reach 0.94 and cut false certification to 2–5% at a large power cost. Stylised: M/M/1, simulated data.

budget-twin8 tests

For a fixed budget, how much should a fitted digital twin spend on real data and how much on simulation length?

Real data or more simulation for a fitted twin: relative variance a(ρ)/n + b(ρ)/m (matches simulation), one real pair ≈ 2 simulated jobs at any load, optimal real-data share 0.57–0.97 by cost ratio, and a simulation-only interval whose real coverage falls 0.79→0.17 as the run lengthens while the input-aware one stays 0.92–0.95.

Abstract Project page →

A twin fitted to n real observations and simulated for m jobs has relative variance a(ρ)/n + b(ρ)/m about the real wait (Whitt’s M/M/1 constant matched to simulation: 30.4 vs 29.0). One real interarrival–service pair carries the information of about two simulated jobs at any load (ratio 2.23 → 2.00), so the optimal real-data share of a budget is interior: 0.97 / 0.81 / 0.57 as a simulated job costs 0.001 / 0.05 / 0.5 of a real observation. In a full pipeline the optimal split has 2.5× lower RMSE than 20% real data. A simulation-only confidence interval is for the twin, not the system: its coverage of the real wait falls from 0.79 to 0.17 as the run grows from 200 to 50 000 jobs, while adding the input variance gives 0.92–0.95 for runs of 1000 or more. Stylised: M/M/1, simulated data, first-order variances.

stop-twin8 tests

When should a twin run that counts rare failures stop?

When to stop a twin run counting rare failures: sequential Wald stopping halts on zero failures (90% of runs at p=10⁻³, coverage 9.6%), inverse sampling to m failures gives exactly unbiased (m−1)/(N−1) with relative sd ≈1/√(m−2) and an exact interval (95.0–95.5%), while a fixed run planned for the wrong p delivers 63–200% half-width.

Abstract Project page →

Running a safety twin “until the interval is narrow” stops on zero failures, because p̂=0 has Wald half-width 0: with a target of p/5, 90% of runs stop at the first check for p=10−3 (99% at 10−4), the interval covers p in 9.6% of runs and the reported rate is 10× too low. Running until m failures (inverse sampling) makes (m−1)/(N−1) exactly unbiased while m/N is about m/(m−1) too high, gives relative sd ≈1/√(m−2) whatever p is (m=102 for 10%; measured 0.101), and an exact interval covers 95.0–95.5%. A fixed run planned for p=10−3 delivers a 20% relative half-width there but 63% at 10−4. A one-failure minimum alone restores Wald coverage in this configuration, because the target already forces ~96 failures. Stylised (iid Bernoulli failures, faithful twin, no run cap).

terrain-twin5 tests

What stopping distance can a twin with independent terrain cells certify?

Stopping distance certified by a twin with independent per-cell friction: exact incomplete-gamma law (matches braking simulation), 100 twin cells certify 1.17× the mean distance but real terrain with 1–10 patches exceeds it 44%–18% (claimed 0.1%), finer cells are worse, the mean is nearly right, and the measured patch count repairs it.

Abstract Project page →

Braking on Gamma-distributed patch friction has an exact incomplete-gamma law. A twin drawing 100 independent cells across the stopping distance certifies 1.17× the mean-friction distance at level 10−3; on real terrain with 1, 3 or 10 patches across it the exceedance is 0.44, 0.33 and 0.18, and finer twin cells make it worse. The mean stopping distance is nearly right (1.00–1.32×) while the tail is not. Matching the measured patch count restores the level; overstating it 2× gives 16× the claimed risk. Stylised.

beam-twin11 tests

What approach speed can a lidar twin that returns every beam certify?

Approach speed certified by a lidar twin with independent beam dropout vs real whole-scan fades: exact scan-product miss law, real miss ~100× the level at the twin's speed, speed off 10–30% (probabilities off by orders of magnitude), sign reverses when several returns are needed, repaired by a few hundred calibration scans.

Abstract Project page →

Scanning-lidar detection of a thin obstacle has an exact random-phase beam-count law and a product-over-scans miss probability (matched to a beam-pattern Monte Carlo). A twin calibrated on the mean return rate but with independent beams has no whole-scan fades; the real miss probability cannot fall below sn for n scans. At level 10−3 the twin certifies 13.3 and 12.9 m/s against the real 12.0 and 10.9 (fade rates 0.3, 0.5), with real miss probability 0.09–0.125, about 100× the level; the gap vanishes for early-visible obstacles and reverses sign when several returns are required. The probabilities are off by orders of magnitude but the speed by only 10–30%, because miss probability is a cliff in speed. A few hundred calibration scans repair it. Stylised.

tilt-twin6 tests

How do you estimate a one-in-a-million failure from a twin you can only run a thousand times?

Importance sampling of a rare twin failure: exact mean-shift variance, 10⁸→535 runs for 10% error at p=1e-6, a narrow shift target (2× the optimum is 1.7·10⁵× worse, 0% coverage) and effective sample size as the only warning.

Abstract Project page →

Shifting the twin's disturbances and reweighting failures is unbiased for any shift, with an exact variance enθ²Q((b+nθ)/√n) (5.53 vs 5.51 simulated). At the optimal shift, 10% error at p=10−6 takes 535 runs instead of 108. But the shift is a narrow target: half the optimum costs 23× the variance, twice the optimum 1.7×105×, and a shift tuned for one design is 1.6–17.6× worse at thresholds 0.8–1.5× away. The usual 95% interval covers 94.9% at the optimum but 2.8% at twice it, and only the effective sample size warns. Stylised: Gaussian additive disturbances, constant shift, no field data.

doppler-twin8 tests

Which ego-velocity estimator should a radar twin choose when the real scene has moving targets?

Radar ego-velocity from Doppler returns: a static-world twin picks least squares, but with moving targets its variance is exactly 1+ετ² times the claim (95% interval covers 48.7% at ε=0.1, τ=10) and the median wins on a band of ε (0.006–0.97 at τ=10; never at τ=1).

Abstract Project page →

Radar ego-velocity from n Doppler returns. In a static-world twin least squares beats the median by exactly π/2, so the twin picks the mean; in a scene where a fraction ε of returns come from moving targets (extra offset sd τσ) the mean’s variance is exactly 1 + ετ2 times the twin’s claim and the median’s exact variance is a one-dimensional integral, both matched to simulation. The twin’s choice is wrong on a band of ε (τ=10: 0.006–0.97; τ=3: 0.086–0.83; τ=1: never); at ε=0.1, τ=10 the mean has 5.8× the median’s variance and the twin’s 95% interval covers 48.7% of the time. 2-D least squares scales the same way. A residual-kurtosis test needs about 50 returns to detect it at ε=0.1, τ=10, and hundreds at ε=0.02, τ=3. Stylised: zero-mean Gaussian contamination, no RANSAC, no radar data.

alias-twin10 tests

A radar twin with no Doppler folding certifies an ego-velocity estimator at every speed: what does the folding sensor do to it, and when can it be unfolded?

A radar twin with no Doppler folding: the twin-tuned ego-speed estimator breaks at v_u−2σ with an exact closed-form bias (saturating at one fold off), and a wrapped-cost search unfolds it iff azimuths are diverse, with a confusion probability Φ(−√E₁/2σ) matching Monte Carlo.

Abstract Project page →

Real radar radial speeds wrap modulo 2vu (vu=10 m/s); the twin’s do not. The twin-tuned least-squares ego-speed estimator has RMSE 0.022 m/s in the twin and on the real sensor up to 9.5 m/s, then 0.18 (9.8), 1.9 (10) and 14.9 m/s (12). Its large-n bias is exact in closed form (−14.94 at 12 m/s, simulated −14.92) and saturates at −D, D=2vuΣc/Σc2, once every target is one fold off. A wrapped-cost grid search restores the twin’s accuracy to 60 m/s with no mode errors, provided the azimuths are diverse: the nearest wrong speed has residual energy 4vu2(n−(Σc)2/Σc2), independent of speed, and Φ(−√E/2σ) matches Monte Carlo (0.061 vs 0.054 at ±8°); at ±5° the search picks the wrong fold in 120 of 300 scenes. Stylised: stationary scene, known azimuths and vu, Gaussian noise, no multi-PRF.

validate-twin8 tests

How many real trials before “the twin passed validation” means anything for a rare failure?

Validating a twin's rare-failure rate against real trials: an exact difference test "passes" a 3×-wrong twin 81% of the time at 500 trials, rejecting a 2× error needs ~11 real failures (any q), and an equivalence test needs ~20/58/178 failures for margins 2/1.5/1.25 (~20/q trials).

Abstract Project page →

A twin states a failure probability q; the real rate is c q. An exact two-sided binomial difference test “passes” a twin that is 3× wrong with probability 0.81 at 500 trials (q = 10−3), and rejecting a 2× error with 80% power needs about 11 real failures, independent of q (normal approximation 9.9). Passing barely moves the odds that a twin is off by 2× (0.325 prior, 0.31 after passing at 0.3 expected failures). An equivalence test (TOST) caps false validation at 5% but needs about 20, 58 and 178 real failures for margins 2, 1.5 and 1.25, so certifying a rare-failure twin within 2× takes about 20/q real trials. Stylised: one Bernoulli failure, known q, no scenario shift, illustrative prior.

intent-twin6 tests

How safe is a robot's goal inference when its commit threshold was tuned against a simulated human?

Goal inference tuned against a simulated human: exact real error 1/(1+r^h) of a commit threshold, 3.9×–165× over target for a too-rational twin, 2–4.5× slower for a too-irrational one, population floor P(p<½), and calibration from n real cues misses the target 14–42% of the time.

Abstract Project page →

A robot commits to one of two goals when the evidence lead reaches h (a sequential test on binary motion cues); against a human of cue accuracy p the wrong-goal probability is exactly 1/(1+rh), r=p/(1−p), matched to simulation. A threshold set for error 10−3 in a twin with ps=0.9 gives real error 3.9× / 33× / 165× the target at p=0.8 / 0.7 / 0.6, while a too-irrational twin (ps=0.6) is safe but 2.0–4.5× slower. A heterogeneous population (sd 0.08–0.10) doubles the error of the mean-human threshold, and humans with p<½ put a floor under any threshold. Calibrating ps from n real cues misses the target with probability 0.38 / 0.42 / 0.33 / 0.30 / 0.14 at n=10 / 20 / 50 / 200 / 1000; a lower-confidence-bound design cuts that to ≤4% at the cost of time. Stylised: two goals, i.i.d. binary cues, simulated humans.

sync-twin10 tests

How much does a twin's perfectly synchronised sensor clock over-promise a fused estimate?

Sensor clock offset and jitter a twin does not simulate: exact added variance 2σ²[1−(1+s²/ℓ²)^{−½}e^{−δ²/2(ℓ²+s²)}], a synchronised-clock fusion design is 1+ag/(b(a+b))× its claim (+44% at 0.3ℓ) and worse than one sensor beyond 0.225ℓ, better delayed sensors hurt more, clock randomisation fixes it.

Abstract Project page →

Two sensors observe a smooth signal (length scale ℓ); the second has a clock offset δ and jitter s, which the twin does not simulate. The added variance is exactly g = 2σ2[1−(1+s2/ℓ2)−1/2e−δ2/2(ℓ2+s2)] ≈ σ2(δ2+s2)/ℓ2 (matched to simulation within 0.5%), so inverse-variance fusion designed in the twin has real MSE 1 + ag/(b(a+b)) times its claim: +44% at a 0.3ℓ offset, +118% at 0.5ℓ, and worse than the reference sensor alone beyond 0.225ℓ. The more accurate the delayed sensor, the more it hurts. Randomising the twin’s clock at the right variance recovers the optimal weight; no randomisation costs up to 29%, a range 4× too wide only 1–4%. Stylised: very smooth signal, static weights, offset known, no real logs.

eiv-twin5 tests

What does a twin get wrong when its gain is fitted from a noisy logged input, and does more data fix it?

A twin gain fitted from a noisy logged input is attenuated by exactly the reliability ratio λ (0.800 vs 0.802 simulated), more data makes the twin's own 95% interval worse (covers the true gain 53%→0% for n=20→200) with no residual warning, a feedforward controller overshoots by exactly 1/λ, and known-noise or instrument repairs cost variance and fail at small n.

Abstract Project page →

Regressing the plant output on a logged input that carries sensor noise attenuates the fitted gain by the reliability ratio λ = σu2/(σu2+σv2) exactly (0.800 vs 0.802 simulated at λ=0.8). It is bias, not variance, so more data makes it worse: the twin's own 95% interval covers the true gain 53% / 15% / 0% at n=20 / 50 / 200 while covering the attenuated value 94–97%, and the twin's fit residuals are exactly uncorrelated with its regressor, so nothing warns. A feedforward controller built on it overshoots the real plant by exactly 1/λ (1.25× at λ=0.8, 2× at 0.5). A known-noise correction or a second independent measurement as instrument removes the bias (RMSE 0.20 to 0.02–0.05 at n=200–1000), but a 20% misjudged noise variance leaves a ±5% bias and at n=20 with λ=0.5 the repairs are far worse than the biased fit. Stylised: scalar Gaussian plant, simulated “real” system.

deadband-twin8 tests

What does a twin with no actuator deadband promise a proportional loop, and what does the real one do?

An actuator deadband the twin lacks: real loop rests at exactly d/k while the twin goes to 0, tolerance ε needs k ≥ d/ε, a fitted linear gain is 2Q(d/s) (excitation-dependent, small-signal gain 0), and bisection compensation leaves exact (d−d̂)/k or a (d̂−d)/(2−k) chatter (8 probes: 0.784 → 0.0005).

Abstract Project page →

With a deadband d the real servo loop rests at exactly |x| = d/k (0.500 at d=0.2, k=0.4) while the twin converges to zero, so the twin certifies tolerances the real loop never meets and needs k ≥ d/ε, which fails beyond k = 1. A linear twin fitted from Gaussian excitation of std s recovers 2Q(d/s) (Stein’s lemma; 0.0457 vs 0.0455 at s=0.5), an excitation-dependent gain, while the small-signal gain is 0. Bisection needs about 8 real probes to cut the stall 0.784 → 0.0005, with exact residuals (d−d̂)/k under-compensated and a period-2 chatter (d̂−d)/(2−k) over-compensated. Stylised: scalar integrator, noiseless, k ≤ 1.

deadband-noise-twin5 tests

Does measurement noise, or dither, hide an actuator deadband the twin lacks?

Follow-up to deadband-twin: measurement noise flips the linear twin's error from 27× optimistic (s=0.01) to conservative (0.37× at s=0.05), dither helps only without noise, and mild under-compensation beats the exact width under noise (single-seed simulations).

Abstract Project page →

At K=0.5, d=0.1 the linear twin’s exact stationary rms is s√(K/(2−K)); the real deadband loop is 27× worse at s=0.01 (0.1591 vs 0.0058) but 0.37× at s=0.05 (0.0107 vs 0.0289), because noise dithers the actuator, so a validation in the high-noise regime would call the deadband harmless. Deliberate dither removes the noise-free stall (rms 0.2000 to 0.0001 at a=d) but only hurts at s=0.05 (0.0103 to 0.0226), and under noise mild under-compensation of the width beats the exact width (0.0053 vs 0.0116 at s=0.02). Follow-up to the deadband twin. Stylised: scalar integrator, single-seed simulations without confidence intervals.

slew-twin7 tests

How large a manoeuvre can a twin without an actuator rate limit be trusted for?

A twin without an actuator rate limit is exact only for x₀ ≤ r/k; beyond it the real loop overshoots (0.90 of x₀ at x₀/r=10⁴) and settles in O(amplitude) steps, with an empirical overshoot threshold 2n(2n−1) for k=1/n.

Abstract Project page →

The real loop x⁺ = x + a⁺, with the command rate-limited to r per step, is scale-invariant: it depends only on ρ = x0/r, while the first-order twin does not. The twin is exact iff x0 ≤ r/k (difference 0 at 0.999×, 0.1–0.6% of x0 at 1.01×). Beyond that the real loop overshoots the target (0.23 of x0 at ρ=100, 0.90 at 104, k=0.3) and settles in O(ρ) steps (29418 at ρ=105 vs the twin’s 13). For k=1/n the overshoot threshold is empirically ρ*=2n(2n−1) (not proved); avoiding overshoot needs a rate limit 12–38× lower than keeping the twin exact. Stylised: scalar plant, no noise or delay.

backlash-twin8 tests

Does a twin with a rigid drivetrain miss the hunting cycle caused by gear backlash?

A rigid-drivetrain twin says the PI loop converges but gear backlash makes the real loop hunt at 1.3–2.9× the gap (exactly ∝ h); describing-function prediction 7–10% high, and bistable starts can hide it.

Abstract Project page →

On a discrete PI loop the rigid twin has spectral radius 0.71–0.89 and converges, yet the real loop with a gap of half-width h settles on a limit cycle of motor amplitude 1.30–2.94h that scales exactly with h (1.302317 for h=0.01, 1, 100). The backlash describing function is an excitation-dependent gain (0.21 at A/h=1.2, 0.99 at 30) with a phase lag, and harmonic balance predicts the cycle but overestimates its amplitude by 6.7–10.1%. Negative result: the loop is bistable in some settings (hunting 1.165h from small starts, converging from large steps), so a large-step validation can pass a configuration that hunts. Follow-up to the deadband twin. Stylised: scalar loop, symmetric known gap, noiseless.

friction-twin8 tests

How wrong is the stopping distance of a twin that models friction as purely viscous?

A viscous-only twin never stops (6.5–17.7 s to reach 1e-3…1e-9 vs 1.95 s real) and its fitted gain b + c·E[v]/E[v²] depends on the logged speed range; fitted on [1,3] it overestimates stopping distance ×1.8–17 below and underestimates above v*=7.3, no single viscous gain beats 0.87 worst error over [0.05,3], affine fit recovers exactly.

Abstract Project page →

With Coulomb friction c the real coast-down stops in finite time with exact distance (m/b)[v0−(c/b)ln(1+b v0/c)] (RK4 agreement 9×10−9), while the viscous twin only decays exponentially (6.5 s to reach 10−3 vs 1.95 s real). The least-squares gain b+cE[v]/E[v2] depends on the logged speed range (1.23 on [1,3], 3.44 on [0.05,0.3]); fitted on [1,3] the twin overestimates stopping distance ×1.8 at v0=1 and ×17 at 0.05, is exact at 7.34 and underestimates above. Negative result: no single viscous gain does better than 0.87 worst relative error over [0.05,3], while an affine fit recovers (b,c) exactly. Stylised: one mass, noiseless logs.

stiction-twin8 tests

Does a twin with correct sliding friction still miss stick-slip hunting from static friction?

A twin with the right sliding friction says the PID loop converges, and with no stiction it does; a breakaway excess Fs−Fc makes the real loop stick-slip hunt at ≈0.5–0.9 ΔF/kp (independent of Fc), and short runs can mistake a long stick for convergence.

Abstract Project page →

Unit mass under PID, frictionless twin stable (error below 1e-58). With Fs=Fc (sliding friction identified correctly) the real loop converges in all 15 cases tried, so that twin validates. With a stiction excess ΔF=Fs−Fc it hunts in stick-slip at 0.54–0.93 ΔF/kp in four of five gain settings, independent of Fc (0 to 20) and of the start, falling with damping; one setting (kd=4, ki=5) converges. Scaling is bit-exact for power-of-two scales but the cycle is unique only to about three digits. Negative result: a 1000 s run can show a motionless “converged” error for large Fc/ki while a 20 000 s run still hunts; the amplitude constant has no closed form here. Follow-up to the backlash twin. Stylised: unit mass, Coulomb plus static friction, noiseless.

lag-twin8 tests

How much bandwidth can a controller tuned in a twin with an instantaneous actuator really have?

A twin with an instantaneous actuator is stable at any gain; the real loop with lag τ is stable iff τ<kd/kp=2ζ/ωn, hunts at the twin's own ωn, decays no faster than 1/(3τ) for any gains, and the real-optimal bandwidth is ≈0.26–0.46 of the limit.

Abstract Project page →

Unit mass under PD control with a first-order actuator lag τ the twin omits. The twin’s loop is stable for every gain; the real loop is stable iff τ<τ*=kd/kp=2ζ/ωn (Routh, agreeing with the roots in 168 of 168 cases), hunts at exactly the twin’s own ωn, and grows at ωn2/(2(1+4ζ2)) per unit excess lag (formula, numeric slope and simulation agree). “Faster is better” fails: at τ=0.05, ζ=0.7 the real decay rate peaks at 4.8 (ωn≈8) and is zero at ωn=28 where the twin promises 19.6; the poles sum to −1/τ, so no gains decay faster than 1/(3τ). Mild lag is nearly invisible in a step test (twin RMS error ≈0.04 ε). Companion to the slew, deadband and backlash twins. Stylised: linear, one lag, noiseless.

flex-twin9 tests

How high a bandwidth does a rigid-body twin let you push when the real joint is flexible?

A rigid-body twin certifies every PD bandwidth; with load-side sensing the real two-mass loop is unstable above ε_c ≈ δ/ζ of the flexible-mode frequency (exactly independent of mass ratio, unstable at any gain with no modal damping), step-response validation misses it, and the certified bandwidth inherits modal-damping error one-for-one.

Abstract Project page →

A twin with one rigid inertia says the PD loop is stable at every bandwidth. With load-side sensing the real two-mass loop is unstable above εc = w/ws, the smallest root of a cubic in modal damping δ and twin damping ratio ζ: exactly independent of the mass ratio, ≈ δ/ζ for small δ (0.0143, 0.0714, 0.286 for δ = 0.01, 0.05, 0.2 at ζ = 0.7), and unstable at every gain with no modal damping. Motor-side (collocated) sensing was stable at all 7 320 grid points, so the twin is right about one sensor placement and wrong about the other. Twin and real step responses differ by under 1% at 0.9 εc, so ordinary validation gives no warning; a twin that overstates δ by a factor f certifies εc high by the same factor, and a design at fraction m of the certified bandwidth tolerates f ≈ 1/m. Stylised: one flexible mode, linear, PD only, continuous-time, noiseless.

coupling-twin9 tests

Does a twin that models each axis alone certify gains that actuator coupling destabilises?

A per-axis twin of a two-axis loop certifies gains that actuator coupling destabilises: stable-gain limit 2/(1+√p) not 2 (a 10% margin fails at c=1/9), twin-deadbeat rate is √|p| not 0, and a fitted diagonal gain 1+cρ depends on log correlation while the full fit's variance grows as 1/(1−ρ²).

Abstract Project page →

For a two-axis loop x’ = x − kGx with cross-gain c, the stable-gain limit is 2/(1+√p) (p=c12c21≥0) or 2/(1+|p|) (p<0) instead of the twin’s 2, so a twin-certified 10% margin (k=1.8) fails at c=1/9, and no positive gain is stable once √p≥1. The twin-deadbeat gain has real rate √|p|, not 0 (6–270 steps to 10−6 for c=0.1–0.95 vs 1). A diagonal gain fitted from logs is 1+cρ for input correlation ρ (Monte Carlo matches to four digits), giving real rate c(1+ρ)/(1+cρ) (0.300 at ρ=0, 0.461 at ρ=1); the unbiased full fit has variance ∝ 1/(1−ρ2) (verified within 5%), so near-collinear logs make coupling unidentifiable while the per-axis fit returns a confident wrong gain. Follow-up to the control twin. Stylised: linear constant coupling, two axes, noiseless plant.

windup-twin7 tests

A twin with an unlimited actuator says a PI step response ignores step size: what does the real loop with a command limit do?

A twin with an unlimited actuator is exact for a PI step only while kp·x0 ≤ U; beyond it the integrator winds up to x0²/(2U), overshoot rises from 21% to 97% and settling from 4.9 to 944, loads d ≥ U are never rejected, and the twin-tuned faster gains settle slower (clamping recovers most).

Abstract Project page →

Integrator plant under PI control, real actuator limited to |u|≤U with constant load d; the twin has neither. The twin is exact iff kpx0≤U (zero deviation up to x0=0.714), so gentle step tests certify it. Beyond that the integrator winds up to exactly x02/(2U): overshoot rises from the twin’s 21% to 74%, 93%, 97% and the settling time from 4.9 to 17, 165, 944 (x0/U=5, 20, 50); a load d≥U is never rejected and settling blows up as d→U. “Faster is better” fails: the twin’s settling time falls 32× over ωn=0.25–8 while the real one is best near ωn=1 and rises to 77; conditional integration recovers most of it. Companion to the lag and slew twins. Stylised: one integrator, static limit, noiseless.

impact-twin10 tests

A fixed-step twin of a bouncing ball: how wrong are its restitution and time to rest, and does calibrating on the first bounce fix it?

A fixed-step twin of a bouncing ball: the true rest time (v1/g)(1+e)/(1−e) is hypersensitive to e (2/(1−e²)), the twin's apparent restitution and settling time are off by O(dt) with scheme-dependent sign (−20% to +4% at dt=10⁻², e=0.9), and calibrating e on the first bounce is not a reliable fix.

Abstract Project page →

Truth is closed form: infinitely many impacts in the finite Zeno time T=(v1/g)(1+e)/(1−e), with d ln T/de=2/(1−e2) (10.5 at e=0.9, 100 at 0.99). A semi-implicit-Euler twin with a penetration test has an apparent restitution biased by the step with scheme-dependent sign (true 0.9: 0.886, 0.895, 0.879 at dt=10−2) and its time to come to rest is off by −19.6%, +4.0%, −30.8% (e=0.9; up to 47% at e=0.95), first-order in dt and 0.1–0.3% at 10−4. The restitution bias explains most of the clamp error (predicted −14.9%, measured −19.6%), but fitting e on the first rebound is not a reliable repair: it helps the clamp twin at dt=10−2 (−19.6% to −4.8%), does nothing at finer steps and makes the mirror twin worse (+4.0% to +53%). Twin impact counts (238–688) are mostly floor chatter against 43–87 resolvable bounces. Stylised: one dimension, constant restitution, rigid contact, closed-form real system; the crude interpolated-contact variant is the worst here.

jitter-twin8 tests

Does a twin fitted to the sensor-delay histogram certify gains that bursty delay makes unstable?

A twin fitted to the sensor-delay histogram is blind to its persistence: i.i.d. jitter at the mean delay barely moves the mean-square gain limit (1.00 for {0,2}), but with the marginal fixed, lag-1 autocorrelation 0.9 cuts it to 0.67 (0.9 certified by the twin is unstable from ρ=0.435) and inflates variance 2.4×; almost-sure stability (≈1.84) hides it.

Abstract Project page →

Scalar loop x[n+1]=x[n]−k x[n−dn]+w[n] with random delay; the twin has the same marginal delay law (constant mean: stable iff k<2 sin(π/(2(2d+1)))). Independent jitter moves the mean-square limit little and in either direction (1.000 for {0,2}, 0.952 for {0,1,2}, 0.668 vs the twin’s 0.618 for {0,1,2,3,4}); for {0,2} with P(d=2)=p it fits k(k+1)=1/p. Persistence, invisible in the histogram, is the large effect: at fixed marginal the limit falls 1.000→0.875→0.672→0.624 at lag-1 autocorrelation ρ=0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99 (towards the worst-case constant delay’s 0.618); a twin-certified k=0.9 is unstable from ρ=0.435, and below the limit the variance at k=0.6 inflates from 2.56 to 6.26 (ρ=0.9) and 15.2 (ρ=0.99). Almost-sure stability (simulated limit ≈1.84) is insensitive to ρ, so which stability the safety claim needs decides whether persistence matters. Companion to the latency twin. Stylised: scalar plant, sticky-redraw delay, Monte-Carlo almost-sure limits (one seed).

gravity-twin5 tests

Does a twin with no gravity certify PD gains that sag, or cannot hold a pose at all?

A gravity-free twin certifies PD with zero error; the real pendulum sags to the root of kp(θ*−θ)=g sin θ (0.18 rad at kp=4, falling only as ~1/kp), cannot hold upright unless kp>g (basin 0.12 rad at 1.02g), and a 10%-off gravity feedforward leaves a sag linear in the error.

Abstract Project page →

A pendulum under PD control u=kp(θ*−θ)−kdω; the twin omits gravity and promises zero error at every gain. The real hold sags to the root of kp(θ*−θ)=g sinθ nearest the target (RK4 agrees to six digits; 0.182 rad at kp=4, θ*=1), falling only as ≈1/kp. Holding upright is stable iff kp>g: below it the arm settles 0.2–1.9 rad away, and just above it the basin is tiny (0.116 rad at 1.02g, 0.519 at 1.05g, none below 3 rad from 1.1g; numerical scan). A gravity feedforward with calibration error leaves a sag linear in (g(g−gff)minus;gff) (±0.0185 rad at ±10%). Companion to the lag and flex twins. Stylised: one rigid joint, noiseless, no friction.

sample-twin8 tests

A continuous-time twin certifies PD at every gain: which gains survive a zero-order-hold sampled loop?

A continuous-time twin certifies PD at every gain; the real zero-order-hold loop is stable iff kp·T/2 < kd < 2/T (ωn·T < min(4ζ, 1/ζ)), overshoot is 5× the twin's at ωn·T = 1.2, raising ωn past ωn·T ≈ 1 slows settling, and deadbeat (2 samples) is the real speed limit.

Abstract Project page →

Double integrator under PD control computed at period T and held. The twin (T→0) is stable for every gain; the exact step matrix gives the real stable region kpT/2 < kd < 2/T, i.e. ωnT < min(4ζ, 1/ζ), matched to bisection and an independent RK4 held-input run (ζ=0.7 fails at ωnT=1.4286). The twin is accurate for ωnT ≲ 0.2 but at 1.2 the real overshoot is 0.234 against its 0.046, and at fixed T raising ωn past ωnT≈1 slows settling (0.4 → 5.2) then diverges. Deadbeat gains (kpT2=1, kdT=3/2) settle in 2 samples, the real speed limit. Stylised: noiseless, no computation delay.

drag-twin10 tests

A linear-drag twin of a quadratic-drag vehicle: what does it get wrong about braking, terminal speed and the safe speed under a stopping limit?

A linear-drag twin of a quadratic-drag vehicle: coast-down time and terminal speed are off by fit-speed ratios, least-squares fit gives k = 3c·vmax/4, and the safe speed under a stopping limit is mis-stated by −21% to +41% with sign set by the fit speed.

Abstract Project page →

Real drag cv|v|, twin kv with k matched at one speed. Coast-down time to fall to v0/10 is 9/(cv0) for the truth and independent of v0 in the twin (0.05×, 0.51×, 1.02× the truth at v0=1, 10, 20 for a fit at 5); terminal speed is off by vterm/vfit; a least-squares fit over [0, vmax] has k=3cvmax/4, exact only at 0.75vmax. The safe speed under a 10 m stopping limit is mis-stated by −20.8%, −8.9%, +7.0%, +41.1% for fits at 1, 5, 10, 20 m/s, so the error changes sign with the fit speed, and trace-fitted k falls from 0.382 to 0.223 as the coast-down lengthens because the slow tail dominates. Stylised: one dimension, pure quadratic drag, closed-form noiseless truth.

slip-twin10 tests

A kinematic-bicycle twin ignores tyre slip: how wrong is its turning radius, and does calibrating that reveal where a twin-tuned steering loop goes unstable?

A kinematic-bicycle twin of a car ignores tyre slip: steady-turn radius is off by exactly 1 + Kv²/L (twin 4–63% too small, half at the characteristic speed), calibrating K fixes that but both twins certify steering gains stable at every speed while 11 of 30 real gain pairs lose stability below 60 m/s.

Abstract Project page →

Real car: linear single-track model with tyre slip; twin: ψ′=vδ/L. Steering with the twin’s angle gives radius R(1+Kv2/L) for understeer gradient K, matched by simulation (R=100 m: 104.6, 118.5, 174.0, 266.4 m at 5, 10, 20, 30 m/s; twin 4–63% too small, exactly half at the characteristic speed 23.26 m/s; oversteer car up to 136% too large at 20 m/s). Fitting K removes that error exactly, yet both the kinematic and the calibrated twin certify δ=−kpy−kdψ as stable at every speed and gain, while 11 of a 30-point gain grid lose stability on the real car below 60 m/s (kp=0.4, kd=0.5: 14.0 m/s; confirmed in the time domain, 1.1×10−9 m at 8 m/s vs 4.6×107 m at 20 m/s). An oversteer car with feedback loses stability at 23.7 m/s, below its open-loop critical speed 26.33 m/s. Stylised: linear tyres, constant speed, no actuator lag or delay; the closed-loop limit is not derived in closed form.

grid-twin11 tests

A grid twin over-states every route by a heading-dependent factor: does a finer grid fix it, and can it rank two routes the wrong way round?

A grid twin over-states every route by a heading-dependent factor that cell size does not shrink (8-connected: mean 8(√2−1)/π = 1.0548, worst 1.0824 at 22.5°), calibrating the mean leaves −5.2% to +2.6%, and the twin ranks two routes (lengths 1 and 1.03) the wrong way round 19% of the time; rotating the map flips a fixed pair for 31% of orientations.

Abstract Project page →

Real route: a straight line of length L; twin: shortest path on a k-connected lattice. The grid/Euclid ratio depends on heading and connectivity, not cell size: 8-connected it is cosφ+(√2−1)sinφ, mean 8(√2−1)/π=1.0548 and worst 1.0824 at 22.5° (4-connected mean 1.2732, worst 1.4142; 16-connected 1.0144, 1.0275), matched by Dijkstra; refining the cell from 8 m to 0.1 m leaves a 100 m route at 22.5° at 1.0824. Calibrating by the mean leaves −5.2% to +2.6% (8-connected). For two routes of Euclidean length 1 and 1.03 at random headings the twin ranks the longer one shorter with probability 0.194 (0 at ratio ≥ 1.0824), and for a fixed pair 22.5° apart rotating the map flips the ranking for 31% of orientations. Stylised: free space only, no obstacles, length as a proxy for time or energy.

shutter-twin8 tests

A global-shutter twin of a rolling-shutter camera ignores target motion: how biased is a twin-trained orientation estimate, and what does the same frame reveal?

A global-shutter twin of a rolling-shutter camera ignores target motion: a moving rectangle is sheared and stretched by exact closed forms, a twin-trained orientation estimate is biased by half the edge tilt (1.79° at 1000 px/s), and one frame of a known-size target identifies pose and velocity (0.027° and 16 px/s at 0.25 px noise). Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Row r is exposed at t=rτ/H, so a moving rectangle is imaged sheared and stretched; closed-form edge normals match a row-by-row simulation. At 1000 px/s horizontal speed the vertical edges tilt 3.58° and the horizontal ones 0, so averaging the two edge families (what a global-shutter twin certifies) is biased 1.79°; 1000 px/s vertical speed makes the target 6.7% taller. One frame of a known-size rectangle identifies orientation and both velocities in closed form: with 0.25 px edge noise orientation error falls from 0.24–0.97° to 0.027° and speeds are recovered to 16 and 4.8 px/s, but vertical speed is very sensitive to the assumed size (a 5% height error moves it by about 800 px/s). Stylised: straight edges, constant velocity, known size, no real footage.

sweep-twin12 tests

A snapshot twin of a spinning lidar ignores that the platform moves during the sweep: how biased is the map, what does one scan reveal, and what do yaw and acceleration do?

A snapshot-scan twin of a spinning lidar ignores motion during the sweep: length biased by exactly vτ/2 (0.5 m at 10 m/s), parallel walls converge by vτ/2π·(1/d₁+1/d₂), one scan gives speed to 0.13 m/s, yaw scales bearings by −κβ/(1+κ), acceleration biases odometry by a·t_f without accumulating.

Abstract Project page →

Real sensor: 2-D lidar at 10 Hz firing each beam at a different time while the platform moves; twin: all beams at t = 0. At 10 m/s the front and back walls are placed 0.25 and 0.75 m short, so apparent room length is biased by exactly vτ/2 = 0.50 m while the width is exact, and deskewing with the true motion removes it. Parallel walls appear to converge by ≈ vτ/(2π)(1/d1+1/d2) (1.94° measured vs 2.05° first order), so a wall-angle estimator certified on the snapshot twin inherits a heading bias; inverting that angle recovers speed from a single scan to 0.13 m/s at 1 cm range noise (first-order bias −1.8%). Yaw scales bearings by exactly −κβ/(1+κ), and acceleration biases scan-to-scan odometry by exactly a tf in velocity, bounded and non-accumulating. Stylised: 2-D rectangular room, constant velocity or acceleration along one axis, known platform motion.

gnss-twin9 tests

A satellite-positioning twin with white range noise certifies an error radius the real receiver does not meet: how wrong is it once multipath is correlated, and does averaging fix it?

A white-noise satellite-positioning twin vs a receiver with correlated multipath: exact HDOP √(4/n) and bias map 2b/n, averaging loses the 1/√T gain (95% radius covers 33% at T=10, 5% at T=100), and a residual integrity test tuned on the twin false-alarms 21% at equal multipath. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Real receiver: 2-D position and clock from n pseudoranges with multipath; twin: white noise σ only. For an evenly spread constellation HDOP is exactly √(4/n) (simulated to 0.3%) and collapses to 4.25 over a 90° arc; one biased satellite of size b moves the fix by exactly 2b/n toward that satellite, which no amount of averaging removes. With AR(1) multipath (ρ = 0.99) the twin predicts a 1/√T gain but the simulated error only falls from 1.58 to 0.80 m over 500 epochs (exact 0.80), and a 95% radius calibrated on single epochs covers 33% of fixes at T = 10 and 5% at T = 100 (exact 31% and 5%). A residual integrity test tuned to 1% false alarms on the twin alarms 21% of the time when multipath equals the noise (exact closed form), and the statistic rises by only b²(1−3/n) while the position bias is 2b/n. Stylised: 2-D, linearised, evenly spread or arc constellations, stationary AR(1) multipath.

inertia-twin8 tests

A point-mass twin of a rolling body ignores rotational inertia: how wrong are acceleration, slip and coast distance, and what does one calibration fix?

Point-mass twin of a rolling body ignores rotational inertia: acceleration overstated by exactly 1+k, slip threshold k tanα/(1+k) invisible, coast distance 40–100% off, one calibration cannot fix a mixed fleet.

Abstract Project page →

A frictionless point mass overstates down-ramp acceleration by exactly 1+k (k=I/mr2: 1.4, 1.5, 2.0 for sphere, disc, hoop), so a 2 m descent takes 0.90 s instead of 1.07–1.28 s; a stick/slip simulation matches the closed forms to 3×10−4 m/s2. The slip threshold μ* = k tanα/(1+k) is invisible to the twin, and a launch speed picked in the twin to coast 1 m carries a rolling body 40–100% farther. A gain fitted on one shape removes its own error but leaves −16% to +20% fall-time error on the others (pooled fit +6.7% to −10.7%), and the twin cannot rank the shapes. Stylised: planar incline, Coulomb friction, no rolling resistance or drag, no hardware data.

lens-twin9 tests

A pinhole twin of a radially distorted camera mis-ranges the near field: how far off does a twin-trained braking policy stop, and does focal calibration fix it?

A pinhole twin of a radially distorted camera mis-ranges the floor by exactly 1/(1+k₁h²/R²) (+8.1% at 1 m for k₁=−0.3), a twin-trained braking policy stops 9 cm short of 1 m, focal calibration trades the near-field error for a far-field one, and one grid image identifies k₁.

Abstract Project page →

With Brown distortion xd=x(1+k1r2) and a camera at height h, the pinhole twin reads floor range off by exactly 1/(1+k1h2/R2): for k1=−0.3, h=0.5 m that is +15.4% at 0.75 m, +8.1% at 1 m and +0.5% at 4 m. A policy trained to stop at 1.0 m stops at 0.909 m (16.4 cm short at 0.75 m; the first-order formula understates this at large ρ). Least-squares focal calibration (s=1+3k1ρmax2/5) moves the error rather than removing it: near-field 8.1% → 3.2% but a new 4.4% far-field under-read, and a 4 m stop lands 17 cm long. One image of a known grid identifies k1 (RMS 0.001 at 0.002 normalised-pixel noise). Stylised: one distortion term, axis-column floor points, known grid pose, no real lens.

blur-twin9 tests

An instantaneous-exposure twin of a finite-exposure camera certifies detection at every speed: what is the real speed limit, and what does a blur-matched filter buy back?

An instantaneous-exposure twin of a finite-exposure camera certifies detection at every speed; a moving bar is an exact trapezoid (peak C·min(1, w/d)), a twin-tuned peak detector has a hard speed limit wC/(σz), and a blur-matched box filter raises it quadratically (5–55×).

Abstract Project page →

A bar of width w moving d = vT px during the exposure is imaged as an exact trapezoid (peak C·min(1, w/d), energy Cw conserved), matching a 2000-sub-exposure simulation to its quantisation. A single-pixel peak detector that the twin certifies at Pd = 1 everywhere loses power as soon as d > w (at w = 6, C/σ = 10: Pd 1.00 → 0.28 at d = 24), with speed limit d* = wC/(σz) (13.7 px). A box filter of length d collects all of Cw at noise cost √d, output Cw/(σ√d)·(1−w/4d), so the limit grows quadratically in SNR: 5–55× faster over 12 settings, but it needs the speed, and a filter tuned on the twin (length w) still drops to Pd 0.26 at d = 60. Stylised: 1-D, known location, constant velocity, white Gaussian noise, no real footage.

compass-twin11 tests

A twin with an ideal magnetometer returns the true heading: how large is the hard-iron and soft-iron error, what does it do to a compass-held path, and how much of a turn does a swing calibration need?

A twin with an ideal magnetometer hides hard/soft-iron heading error: exact peaks asin(β/B) and asin(|1−r|/(1+r)), a compass-held square misses by exactly 2Lβ/B, and swing calibration error grows ×12 at a 90° arc. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

A hard-iron offset β (relative to the field B) gives a peak heading error of exactly asin(β/B) (11.5° at 0.20, 53.1° at 0.80); soft-iron axis scaling r gives asin(|1−r|/(1+r)) (6.4° at r = 0.8), unchanged by removing the offset. A compass-held 100 m square misses its start by 2Lβ/B (2, 6, 20, 60 m at 0.01–0.3) for every offset direction tried, while the ideal twin closes to 10−14 m; a straight leg stays within 1 m cross-track for only 10–50 m at β/B = 0.02–0.10. A circle-fit swing calibration over a full turn has offset error ≈ 2σ/√n (0.0040 at n = 100), growing ×1.8 at 180°, ×12 at 90° and ×45 at 60° of turn (median heading residual 0.18° → 2.2° → 10.7°). Stylised: level 2-D sensor, simulated data, no gyro fusion, no ellipse fit; the 2Lβ/B closure law is verified numerically, not proved beyond first order.

gyro-twin8 tests

A gyro twin calibrated on white noise hides the bias random walk: how wrong are its heading error, re-alignment interval and dead-reckoning budget, and does a single-point Allan fit help?

A gyro twin calibrated on white noise hides the bias random walk: heading variance ratio exactly 1+(t/t*)² (2.33 at 100 s, 134 at 1000 s), the twin's re-alignment interval is 24× too long (10 000 s vs 416 s), a single-point Allan fit is right at one horizon only, and dead-reckoning range is over-stated 1.25–1.74×. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Real rate = white noise N plus a random-walking bias K; the twin keeps only N. Heading variance is N2t + K2t3/3, so the real/twin ratio is exactly 1 + (t/t*)2 with t* = √3N/K = 86.6 s (2.33 at 100 s, 134 at 1000 s), confirmed by Monte Carlo and a simulated Allan deviation (within 3% for short averaging times, noisy at 1000 s). Re-aligning to keep 2σ heading within 1° is needed every 416 s; the twin allows 10 000 s (24×), where the real error exceeds 1° with probability 0.986. An Allan fit at 1–10 s changes nothing; a fit at τ0 = 100 s is exact only there (variance ratio 2.3 at 1 s, 0.18 at 300 s) and one at 1000 s is 5.6× too conservative. For 2σ cross-track error within 1 m the twin reports 1.74× (1 m/s) and 1.25× (5 m/s) too much usable distance. Stylised: linear-Gaussian, one axis, parameters chosen by me, no aiding, no real IMU data.

roundtrip-twin9 tests

A zero-wind twin of a UAV out-and-back leg: does a tailwind repay the headwind, and what does a twin calibrated on one leg say about the return?

Zero-wind twin of a UAV out-and-back leg: wind does not cancel (real/twin energy 1/(1−(w/v)²)), the best airspeed moves to v²=w²+√(w⁴+1), and a one-leg-calibrated twin is off by exactly ±w/v with the sign of the leg flown.

Abstract Project page →

Real round-trip energy is (v4+1)/(v2−w2), so wind does not cancel: real/twin is exactly 1/(1−(w/v)2), 1.33× at w/v=0.5 and 5.3× at 0.9, the same for either sign, with no return at |w|≥v. The twin-optimal airspeed is 1 for every wind while the real optimum solves v2=w2+√(w4+1), so flying the twin's optimum costs 1.5%, 9.8%, 52% extra at w=0.4, 0.6, 0.8. A twin calibrated on one leg and assumed to see the same wind back is off by exactly +w/v (headwind leg) or −w/v (tailwind leg): ±33% at w=0.5, v=1.5, with a sign set by which leg was flown. Stylised: steady along-track wind, constant airspeed, two-term power law.

thermal-twin8 tests

A constant-gain twin of a motor holding a load certifies every load: what does thermal derating do to the real hold?

A constant-gain twin of a motor holding a load certifies every load: magnet derating makes holding a positive thermal feedback with a fold at λ=4/27 (real temperature 1.33–2.25× the twin's near it, no hold above it, runaway in ≈4π/(9√ε) thermal time constants), short tests cannot see it, the twin overstates holdable torque 1.1–1.6×, and refitting a constant gain does not remove the fold.

Abstract Project page →

Holding a torque dissipates Ri2; heating lowers the torque constant, so the hold current rises and heats more. In scaled variables φ′=λ/(1−φ)2−φ the hold exists iff λ≤4/27 (fold at φ=1/3) while the twin says φ=λ at every load: the real temperature rise is 1.33× and 1.76× the twin’s at λ=0.10 and 0.14 (current 1.15×, 1.33×) and 2.25× at the fold; above it there is no hold and the torque constant collapses in finite time, ≈4π/(9√ε) thermal time constants near the fold (ratio 0.925 at ε=0.002, 0.994 at 10−5). Tests shorter than the thermal time constant cannot see it (0.1 time constants at λ=0.14: +1.4% current). Under a winding temperature limit the twin overstates holdable torque by 1/(1−φm) (1.11× at φm=0.1, 1.64× at 0.4); refitting a constant gain on a hot low-load run still under-predicts (−0.06 to −0.10) and keeps no fold; winding-resistance rise lowers the fold (0.148 to 0.113 at β/α=1). Companion to the windup and gravity twins. Stylised: one thermal node, linear derating, constant load.

range-twin8 tests

What does a twin whose sensor reads at any distance get wrong about a loop with a range-limited lidar or radar?

A twin whose sensor reads at any distance vs a range-limited one: exact step-count law (49 vs 4021 steps from 1000R), PI overshoot neither bound nor lower bound (4.1× at 1000R), exact scale invariance, and the gain fitted from logs of a given extent.

Abstract Project page →

A twin with unlimited sensor range predicts geometric convergence; a real sensor reading clip(x, −R, R) caps the approach speed at kR. The exact step-count law matches simulation in 108/108 cases; for k=0.25 the twin says 49 steps from 1000R and the real loop takes 4021 (82×), an error linear in x0/R with slope 1/k. For a PI loop the twin's overshoot is neither a bound nor a lower bound: smaller at 2–5R, 4.1× larger at 1000R; conditional integration repairs overshoot but not settling time. Logs within range fit the gain exactly and cannot reveal R; from logs uniform on [−L, L] the fitted gain factor is 1.5q−0.5q3, q=R/L. Stylised: scalar noiseless loop, hard symmetric clip.

replicate-twin9 tests

One long twin run or many replications when every run starts in the wrong state?

One long twin run or many replications under a start-up transient: exact AR(1) MSE and t-interval coverage (single run minimises MSE; replication costs 1.07×–2.2×; 92% coverage at MSE-optimal deletion for short replications), batch means not worse, preliminary M/M/1 coverage 6–84%.

Abstract Project page →

Splitting a fixed budget of N twin draws into r replications, each started at an offset and with d draws deleted, gives iid replication means, but the warm-up bias does not shrink with r. For an AR(1) the MSE and the exact coverage of the Student-t interval are closed-form (0.921 vs 0.921 simulated at r=50): a single run minimises MSE, replication costs at most 1.07× at φ=0.9 but 2.2× at φ=0.99, and the nominal-95% interval covers 92% at the MSE-optimal deletion once replications are short (no deletion reaches 94% at 40 draws each). Single-run batch means were not worse in this model. Preliminary M/M/1 simulation: 30 short replications cover 5.8% of the time, and no setting tried reaches 95%. Stylised: Gaussian AR(1), one start offset, simulated “real” system.

warmstart-twin10 tests

How biased is a short digital-twin run that starts from a default state?

Cold-start bias of short twin runs: exact AR(1) bias/variance/warm-up deletion, M/M/1 empty-start bias constant ρ/(1−ρ)³, negligible at valid-interval lengths but −5.6 of 9 at 50 jobs; MSER-5 did not help.

Abstract Project page →

A twin reset to an empty queue and averaged over n steps is biased toward that start. For AR(1) output the bias, variance and best warm-up deletion are exact (bias/sd 1.88 to 0.12 for n=20 to 2500 at φ=0.9). For the M/M/1 wait the summed empty-start bias is ρ/(1−ρ)3 (verified numerically against an exact series and coupled simulation), so it equals one standard deviation only at 23 jobs at ρ=0.9: at run lengths that give a valid interval it costs 1–3 coverage points. Short runs are different: 50 jobs from an empty start read 5.6 below the true mean wait of 9; starting at the mean reduces bias but not reliably RMSE; a noisy real-state start is unbiased with 3.6× the sd; MSER-5 truncation made bias and coverage worse here. Stylised (AR(1) and M/M/1, simulated “real” system).

twin-screen6 tests

How many designs should a digital twin shortlist for real-plant verification?

Shortlisting K designs in a twin and verifying the top m on the real plant under a fixed trial budget: twin-only value exactly ρc_K, best m falls from 8 to 2 as ρ rises 0.6→0.95 (K=50, B=20), and a useless twin still gains 0.12 from budget concentration alone. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

A twin ranks K=50 designs and a fixed budget of 20 noisy real trials verifies only the top m. The twin alone is worth exactly ρcK (cK=2.249), and the best shortlist shrinks as the twin improves (m=8 at ρ=0.6, 2 at 0.95), reaching 1.87 and 2.17 sd against 1.20 for real-only testing and an oracle 2.25. A useless twin still gains 0.12 by concentrating the budget on fewer designs, so that part is not the twin's. Stylised Gaussian model, even budget split, Monte Carlo.

twin-shrinkage7 tests

How far should a real-plant estimate be pulled toward its digital twin?

Pulling a real-plant parameter estimate toward its twin (James–Stein): exact risk d−(d−2)²E[1/(d−2+2K)], never worse in total for d≥3, perfect twin risk 2 at any d, worth n+σ²/τ² real samples at large d, but one mismatched parameter takes ≈d/4 noise variances (25.5 at d=100) unless shrinkage is blockwise (1.65 at blocks of 5, d=30).

Abstract Project page →

Shrinking a real estimate of d plant parameters toward the twin's prediction (James–Stein) has an exact risk d−(d−2)2E[1/(d−2+2K)], K~Poisson(λ/2): it never raises total error for d≥3, a perfect twin gives risk 2 at any d (saving 33% at d=3, 80% at d=10), and a twin as noisy as the data (λ/d=1) still saves 14–49% while using it alone saves nothing. At large d the twin is worth n+σ2/τ2 real samples (exact values 0.72–0.998 of that at d=5–100). The guarantee is aggregate only: one badly mismatched parameter among d takes about d/4 noise variances of damage (measured 2.9 at d=10, 25.5 at d=100 against 1), and blocks of 5 cap that at 1.65 (d=30) while keeping 72% of the perfect-twin saving. Stylised: Gaussian noise, orthogonal design, no robot data.

mount-twin6 tests

What does a twin that assumes the radar is aligned with the body get wrong about dead reckoning, and can loop-closure validation see it?

A radar twin assuming the sensor is body-aligned: planar dead reckoning is exactly the true path rotated by the mount yaw (error 2 sin(e/2)·|displacement|, bounded, zero after loops, so loop-closure validation is blind), closed-form rotation fit with std σ/√Σ|p|², but a pitched mount drifts vertically laps·2πR sin e.

Abstract Project page →

With a planar mount-yaw error e, radar ego-velocity dead reckoning is exactly the true path rotated by e: error 2 sin(e/2)·|displacement|, bounded by the path diameter and zero after any closed loop, so loop and out-and-back validations pass while a straight 157 m run is off by 27 m at 10°. A closed-form rotation fit recovers e with standard deviation σ/√Σ|pi|2 (matched by simulation, 95% coverage). Stylised: the result is planar; a pitched mount drifts vertically by exactly laps·2πR sin e despite perfect x-y closure.

twin-control-variate9 tests

How many real rollouts does a biased digital twin save when certifying a policy?

Certifying a policy with a biased digital twin: exact twin/plant cost correlation, optimal twin-to-real rollout split and speed-up (matched by simulation), bias first order but correlation second order in model error so the replayable-disturbance fraction caps the twin's value, and twin-only intervals cover ~0%.

Abstract Project page →

A twin evaluated alone is biased however many rollouts you run (nominal 95% intervals cover the truth 0–0.4% of the time at a 12% bias, 20% gain error); used as a control variate it removes variance without bias. In scalar LQ the rollout cost is a Gaussian quadratic form, so the twin/plant correlation ρ = λ tr(GG′)/√(tr G2 tr G′2) is exact, the optimal twin-to-real ratio is ρ/√((1−ρ2)w) and the speed-up 1/(√(1−ρ2)+ρ√w)2, matched by simulation to a few percent. Twin gain error is first order in the bias (5% error → 2.7%) but second order in 1−ρ, so the twin’s value is capped by the fraction λ of the real disturbance it can replay: a 5% certificate costs 168 real-only, 28 with λ = 0.95 and 163 with λ = 0.3. Twin-only beats real-only only below σ2/bias2 real rollouts (35 at 10% error). Stylised.

radar-detection-twin8 tests

What does a Gaussian-clutter radar twin promise about detection, not just false alarms?

What a Gaussian-clutter radar twin promises about detection: exact Pfa/Pd laws for CA- and OS-CFAR in textured clutter, OS inflated like CA, an SNR shortfall (6.3 dB at ν=2) larger than the threshold repair, and no CA/OS ranking reversal.

Abstract Project page →

With CA- and OS-CFAR thresholds set in a Gaussian twin and deployed in gamma-textured clutter, the exact false-alarm and detection laws (including a new one-dimensional OS-CFAR law) match simulation to ~1%. OS-CFAR is inflated much like CA (design 1e-4, ν=2: 30× vs 35×). Repairing the threshold costs 3.7–4.6 dB, yet the SNR needed for Pd = 0.9 at Pfa = 1e-4 is 6.3 dB above the twin’s promise at ν=2 (2.8 dB at ν=5, 0.8 dB at ν=20), and at the twin’s own threshold and promised SNR real Pd is 0.84 while Pfa is 30× design. Texture does not reverse the CA-beats-OS ranking (a negative result). Stylised: iid gamma texture, constant-SNR target, no interferers, no real radar data.

twin-multifidelity11 tests

How do you estimate a controller's real-world cost with a biased digital twin?

Estimating a controller's real cost with a biased digital twin as a control variate: cost correlation in closed form (0.985 → 0.472 as the twin's gain error grows while its bias grows 300×), exactly λ² under partial disturbance replay, optimal twin/real ratio √(c_rρ²/(c_t(1−ρ²))) and break-even twin price, simulated variance ratio 0.228 vs 0.225 predicted.

Abstract Project page →

A twin-only cost estimate is biased by the twin’s error, a real-only one is noisy; as a control variate the twin keeps the estimate unbiased and is worth its correlation with real rollouts, not its accuracy. Under common disturbances the cost correlation has a closed form and decays as (1+c4)/(1−c4)2(kδ)2 in the twin’s gain error (0.985, 0.941, 0.782, 0.472 for gains 1.15, 1.3, 1.6, 2.0 while the twin-only bias grows 0.004 to 1.34); replaying only a fraction λ of the real disturbance multiplies it by exactly λ2. The optimal twin-to-real rollout ratio is √(crρ2/(ct(1−ρ2))), the twin pays only below price (1−√(1−ρ2))2/ρ2, and a simulated estimator cut variance to 0.228 of real-only against 0.225 predicted. Twin-only wins at tiny budgets or tiny bias; the control variate is best elsewhere. Stylised.

twin-monitor13 tests

How fast can a deployed digital twin be caught going stale, and when is it invisible?

Anytime-valid monitoring of a deployed twin: e-process on closed-loop residuals (2.3% vs 51.6% false alarms under peeking), rate = twin-transfer score gap, an invisible blind line Δa = kΔb that needs dither v, and when dithering pays.

Abstract Project page →

An e-process on the twin's closed-loop prediction residuals is valid however often it is checked (2.3% false alarms versus 51.6% for a repeatedly refit χ2 test at nominal 5%). Its detection rate is exactly the twin-transfer score gap, affine in the exploration variance v; a mixture-delay formula matches simulated medians within 10–20% (leading order L/rate is 40–55% too fast). Twins on the line Δa = kΔb are invisible under the deployed policy (rate exactly 0) and detectable at rate Δb2v/2σ2 with dither; most of them cost almost nothing (regret 6·10−4) so dither does not pay, but the one that thinks the actuator is nearly dead (regret 0.23) is worth a v≈0.006 dither that cuts expected cost 12×. Stylised.

compressed-outer10 tests

How far can DiLoCo reports be compressed?

Compressing DiLoCo reports: unbiased compression multiplies the contraction (c = 1+ω/M, stable iff αsc<2, participation is ω = 1/p−1), dithered quantisation only adds Δ²/12 and keeps stability, and at fixed bandwidth quantisation has an interior optimum near 1.3 bits per coordinate (~4× below 8-bit reports) while sparsification favours few full reports.

Abstract Project page →

Unbiased compression of each worker’s pseudo-gradient (noise proportional to the signal, ω) has exact stationary variance αVw(1+ω)/(Ms(2−αsc)), c = 1+ω/M: it caps the outer step at 2/(sc) and the contraction at 1−1/c (keeping 10% of coordinates with 8 workers: 0.53, 22 rounds to 10−6 against 1), and random participation is the special case ω = 1/p−1. Dithered quantisation only adds Δ2/12 to the variance and leaves stability alone. At fixed bandwidth, sparsifying favours few full reports, while quantising has an interior optimum near 1.3 bits per coordinate with many workers, about 4× below 8-bit reports (the textbook high-resolution law understates the noise 2.9× at 1 bit). Matched to simulation within 3%. Stylised.

sparse-outer-sync12 tests

What does it cost to send only a fraction of the outer update, and does error feedback help?

Sending a fraction p of the outer update: unbiased rescaling costs 1/p in noise floor, error feedback costs only 1+αs(1/p−1) at small steps but caps contraction at √(1−p); exact closed form, stability limits, horizon losses.

Abstract Project page →

Each worker transmits a random fraction p of its pseudo-gradient. Rescaling the subset (unbiased) inflates the stationary noise floor by exactly 1/p. Adding a per-worker error-feedback memory gives an exact closed form from a four-dimensional second-moment recursion and costs only 1 + αs(1/p − 1) at small steps, for any number of workers, because the virtual iterate follows uncompressed SGD. The price is speed: the mean dynamics have determinant 1 − p, so the contraction cannot beat √(1 − p) per round; over a 400-round horizon error feedback reaches 0.39, 0.24 and 0.17 of the unbiased loss at p = 0.25, 0.1, 0.03, and the advantage disappears when the horizon is shorter than about 1/p. Stylised: diagonal quadratics, Bernoulli masks, no top-k.

outer-delay13 tests

Can a DiLoCo-style run hide its synchronisation by applying the outer update rounds late?

Overlapping the DiLoCo sync by applying the outer step τ rounds late does not pay: stable iff αs < 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)), best rate 1−2 sin(π/(4τ+2))/κ_H (exactly κ_H/(κ_H+1) at τ=1), momentum is useless once τ≥1 (69 → 1388 rounds at κ_H=100), hidden-sync gain ≤ (τ+1) sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≤ 1 (search: 1.5–4.9× slower than blocking averaging), fixed if the fresh pseudo-gradient has weight >½.

Abstract Project page →

Applying the outer step τ rounds late gives a mode the recursion xt+1 = xt − αs xt−τ, stable iff αs < 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≈ π/(2τ+1). The best step sits at that edge, so the rate is 1 − 2 sin(π/(4τ+2))/κH (exactly κH/(κH+1) at τ=1), and outer momentum stops helping the moment τ ≥ 1 (69 rounds at τ=0 become 1388 at κH=100). Even with the sync fully hidden the gain over blocking averaging is at most (τ+1) sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≤ 1, and an exact search over (H, τ) finds overlapped training 1.5–4.9× slower than blocking averaging and 2.3–31× slower than blocking with tuned momentum. Giving the fresh pseudo-gradient weight above ½ removes the penalty entirely (stable for every τ; at weight 0.75 and τ=1 the stale term acts as negative momentum, 2× faster than no delay). Stylised: noiseless quadratic, shared Hessian, one common delay.

gust-twin12 tests

A twin whose wind gusts are matched to the logged variance each step: how wrong is the position variance of a PD-held vehicle, and does matching the spectrum instead fix it?

A twin whose wind gusts are iid per step with the logged variance: real position variance is s²(a+k_d)/(k_d k_p(a²+a k_d+k_p)), the twin's is 141× smaller at a=1, dt=0.01 and scales as dt, its 1e-3 margin is exceeded 78% of the time, and a spectrum-matched white twin is always conservative.

Abstract Project page →

Real gust: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck with rate a and variance s2; exact real variance s2(a+kd)/(kdkp(a2+akd+kp)). A twin drawing iid gusts per step has variance s2dt/(2kdkp): 141× too small at a=1, dt=0.01 (270× at a=0.05), a standard deviation scaling as √dt, and a 10−3 margin that the real system exceeds 78% of the time. A spectrum-matched white twin is always conservative, real/twin = a(a+kd)/(a2+akd+kp) < 1 (0.71 at a=1). Fitting the OU rate from logged wind recovers the real variance (within 1% at 105 samples). Stylised: linear loop, Gaussian gusts, no wind data.

multipath-twin16 tests

A free-space radar twin ignores ground-bounce lobing: how wrong is it, and can a two-ray twin with a slightly wrong target height be worse?

Free-space radar twin vs two-ray ground-bounce lobing: detection fraction exactly 2/3 at the free-space range edge, real detects 44% beyond it, a two-ray twin with height error δh disagrees ≈4h_rδh/(λr) and is worse than free space at short range, a height-jitter ensemble scores Brier 0.119 vs 0.197 deterministic. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Two-ray detection 16 sin4u, u=2πhrht/(λr): lobe-mean gain exactly 6 and a detected phase fraction 1−(2/π)asin((c/16)1/4), exactly 2/3 at the free-space range edge. The real system misses 20% of ranges inside the free-space range and detects 44% of those beyond it. A deterministic two-ray twin with height error δh disagrees ≈4hrδh/(λr) (0.200 at 0.5 m, matching simulation) and is worse than free space at short range; a height-jitter ensemble scores Brier 0.119 against 0.197 deterministic and 0.533 free space. Stylised: perfect reflection, flat earth, hard threshold, no radar data.

glint-twin17 tests

A point-target radar twin of two unresolved scatterers: it has the right median, so what does it get wrong, and does averaging looks converge where it says?

Point-target radar twin of two unresolved scatterers under ideal monopulse: real mean is exactly the strong scatterer and median exactly the power centroid, outside-span probability arccos(r)/π, a variance-matched Gaussian twin is 27× too optimistic at a 3σ gate (r=0.9), averaging looks floors at bias 2r²/(1+r²) where the twin predicts √(var/N), and the median beats the mean for r≥0.477. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Ideal monopulse on two unresolved scatterers (strong 1, weak r, random phase) gives Y=(1−r2)/(1+r2+2rcosφ): the mean is exactly the strong scatterer and the median exactly the power centroid, variance 2r2/(1−r2), and the estimate lies outside the target span with probability arccos(r)/π. A variance-matched Gaussian centroid twin gets the median right and the mean wrong by 2r2/(1+r2), is 27× too optimistic at a 3σ gate at r=0.9, and predicts √(var/N) for averaged looks where the real mean floors at that bias (0.90 vs 0.09 at N=1024); the median converges and beats the mean on variance for r≥0.477. Stylised: noise-free ideal monopulse, two scatterers, no radar data.

shot-twin7 tests

A constant-variance Gaussian camera twin of Poisson photon counting: which dark/bright decision rule does it teach, and what does that cost on the real sensor?

Constant-variance Gaussian camera twin of Poisson photon counting: the real Bayes threshold is the logarithmic mean, the twin's the arithmetic mean (7.28 vs 8.00 for 4 vs 12), a detector tuned in it has 1.25–1.83× the optimal error and 23× at λ0=200 (λ1=2λ0), and a square-root twin recovers the optimum in 8 of 9 pairs. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

For Poisson counts the Bayes dark/bright threshold is the logarithmic mean (λ1−λ0)/ln(λ1/λ0); a Gaussian twin with one matched variance puts it at the arithmetic mean (7.28 vs 8.00 for 4 vs 12), and a square-root twin lands in between at (A+G)/2. A detector tuned in the arithmetic twin has 1.25× the optimal real error at (4,12), 1.83× at (10,30) and 1.74× at (50,100), and with λ1=2λ0 the penalty grows to 23× at λ0=200, while the twin’s own predicted error stays within 1.8× of the optimum; the square-root rule recovers the optimal integer rule in 8 of 9 pairs. Stylised: ideal Poisson counts, no read noise, no camera data.

sidelobe-twin17 tests

A radar twin whose targets occupy a single range cell: how far around a strong target does the real matched filter ghost, and does tapering fix it?

Single-cell radar twin vs a real matched filter: exact Rician ghost false alarms (0.020 at 20 dB, 1.0 at 30 dB for rect vs the twin's 1e-6), ghost zone radius growing √10 per 10 dB, taper gain exactly sidelobe difference + ENBW loss, and a 60 dB Hamming zone 6× Hann's despite the lower peak sidelobe. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

A lone strong target through a matched filter alarms at neighbouring cells with an exact Rician probability where the point-response twin says Pfa0=10−6: at the rect peak sidelobe (−13.3 dB) it is 0.020 at 20 dB SNR and 1.0 at 30 dB, and the ghost zone radius grows √10 per 10 dB (3 to 331 cells for 20–60 dB). Tapers raise the ghost-free SNR by exactly the sidelobe-level difference plus the ENBW loss (20.0 dB Hann, 30.8 dB Hamming) at 1.5–1.6× mainlobe width, but ordering by peak sidelobe misleads at very strong targets: Hamming’s 1/x far sidelobes give a 42-cell zone against Hann’s 7 at 60 dB. A weak target beside a 40 dB one is ‘detected’ with Pd=1.0 where the empty cell alarms with probability 1.0. Stylised: white output noise, no CFAR or clutter, no radar data.

interleave-twin10 tests

A link twin with independent packet loss says to send repeats back to back: what does burstiness do to repetition coding for shared maps, and what does spacing buy?

Independent-loss link twin vs a bursty loss chain for repeated map updates: exact residual p·q_g^(r−1), the twin's 5 back-to-back copies leave 81–311× the claimed loss at λ=0.5–0.8, spacing needs 6–36 slots for two copies, and with ≤8 copies the best design is 12–154 slots of latency vs the twin's 4.

Abstract Project page →

An update is sent as r copies g slots apart and is lost only if all are. Against a two-state loss chain with the same marginal rate p = 0.2 and lag-1 correlation λ, the exact residual is p(p + λg(1−p))r−1 against the twin’s pr. The twin’s 5 back-to-back copies for 10−3 give a real residual of 0.026 at λ = 0.5 and 0.10 at 0.8 (81× and 311× the claim); two copies need spacing of 6 to 36 slots to come within 10% of the twin. With at most 8 copies the minimum-latency design is 12 to 154 slots (λ = 0.5 to 0.95) against the twin’s 4, and with at most 4 copies no spacing reaches 10−3. A counter-case: with no copy budget and a long deadline, back-to-back copies still beat a few spaced ones. Stylised: simulated link, known stationary parameters, no radio traces.

fog-twin15 tests

A lidar twin without atmospheric loss overstates range in fog: by how much, how sensitive is it to a mis-set extinction, and what does it do to a driving policy?

Clear-air lidar twin vs fog: detection range W(αr0)/α overstated by exactly e^{αr}, range error is W/(1+W)<1 times the extinction error, a policy sized on median fog is violated 50% of the time (5%-quantile range: 5%, 43.5% slower), and one extinction calibrated on a bright target fails for dark ones in patchy fog. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Detection range solves reαr = r0, i.e. r = W(αr0)/α; the clear-air twin overstates it by exactly eαr (×2.32 at 200 m visibility) and a relative extinction error moves range by the elasticity W/(1+W) < 1. With lognormal episode-to-episode fog a policy sized on the median fog is violated 50% of the time (mean fog 34%), the 5%-quantile range gives exactly 5% at a 43.5% speed cost, and in patchy fog one extinction calibrated on a bright target underestimates dark targets by up to 29% (calibrated on a dark one, bright targets are overestimated 61–168%). Stylised: hard threshold, Beer–Lambert medium, no lidar data.

rain-twin9 tests

Is a clear-air or mean-rain-rate radar twin right when rain comes in cells?

Clear-air or mean-rain-rate radar twin vs intermittent storm-cell attenuation: Jensen gap 1.52× in the rain-rate power law, Lambert-W mean-rate range reached by only 39% of real fields, mean-matching barely helps, a rain ensemble scores Brier 0.038 vs 0.101 clear air. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Radar detection range under intermittent rain attenuation. The power law in rain rate has a Jensen gap (1.52× the mean-rate attenuation), so a mean-rate twin (closed-form Lambert W range, 18.84 km) is reached by only 39% of real storm fields; matching the mean attenuation barely helps (Brier 0.054 vs 0.055). A rain ensemble scores 0.038 vs 0.101 for clear air, and long cells flip the mean-rate twin from optimistic to pessimistic. Stylised: simulated rain, illustrative coefficients, no radar data.

runlength-twin11 tests

How long must a real test run be when its length was sized in a twin with the wrong plant pole?

Real test-run length sized in a wrong-pole twin: exact autocorrelated-cost variance, 3.8× too short (coverage 0.69 vs 0.95) or 2.1× too long depending on the real closed-loop pole, and a pilot-run repair that under-sizes half the time.

Abstract Project page →

A gain designed in a twin whose pole is m× the real one is validated on hardware for a run length chosen in the twin. The variance of the time-averaged cost of a Gaussian AR(1) loop is exact and depends on the closed-loop pole through (1+ρ)/(1−ρ), ρ=ac2, so the twin-sized run is 3.8× too short at m=2, r=0.1 (3,177 vs 12,110 steps; real coverage of a ±5% claim 0.69 vs 0.95 nominal, simulated 0.68) and 2.1× too long at m=1.5, r=5; an oscillating (negative-pole) loop averages as slowly as a sluggish one. Sizing from a real pilot’s lag-one autocorrelation is close to median-unbiased but under-sizes about half the time. Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian, fixed known gain, normal-approximation interval.

aliasing-twin9 tests

What does a radar twin with unlimited unambiguous velocity over-certify?

What a radar twin with unlimited unambiguous velocity over-certifies: exact wrapped-Gaussian bias (−V at μ=V) and MSE with a bias² floor so averaging widens the gap (7.9× → 2.1×10³ at μ=0.8V, n=1→10⁴), safe speed ≈V+sΦ⁻¹(tol/2V), and prior-unwrapping failure 2Φ(−V/√(s²+s_p²)) needing prior error ≤ 0.26V.

Abstract Project page →

A pulsed Doppler radar reports radial velocity modulo 2V; a twin that renders velocity as a real number never aliases. The real bias of a wrapped return is an exact Gaussian tail series (−V at speed V, −2V beyond) and the real MSE has a bias2 floor, so averaging widens the gap to the twin's claim s2/n: at V=10, s=1 and speed 8 the real/claimed MSE is 7.9× for one return and 2.1×103 for 104. Speeds with |bias| ≤ 0.1 reach only 87%, 74% and 48% of V for noise 0.5, 1, 2. Unwrapping against a prior has exact failure probability 2Φ(−V/√(s2+sp2)) and stays within 10% of the twin's claim only for prior error ≤ 0.26V. Stylised: one radial channel, Gaussian noise, simulated radar.

twin-ladder6 tests

Which rungs of a ladder of digital twins are worth running?

Which rungs of a multi-fidelity twin ladder to run: exact nested-estimator variance, a cheaper rung pays iff ρ₂/ρ₁ > 2√r/(1+r) (step correlation, 0.943 for halved cost), using all rungs can be worse than none (1.41× real-only at q=0.9) while the best subset gets 0.83, and a timestep-ladder plant shows 0.156 of real-only variance (0.204 single twin) collapsing to the cheapest twin when disturbance replay is only 90%.

Abstract Project page →

For twins of decreasing cost and fidelity used as nested control variates the variance is exact, σ2Σ(ρi2−ρi+12)/mi, and a cheaper rung pays below a twin already in use iff ρ2/ρ1 > 2√r/(1+r) (0.943 for halved cost, 0.575 for a 10× drop), the single-twin threshold applied to the step correlation. Using every rung is not best (q=0.99, r=0.5, six rungs: 0.284 of real-only variance vs 0.196 for the best two; q=0.9 makes all rungs 1.41× worse than real-only while the best subset gets 0.83), and 10 of 336 paying grid points are infeasible. On a saturated PD mass-spring timestep ladder the best ladder reaches 0.156 of real-only variance (0.204 for the best single twin), collapsing to the cheapest twin at 90%/70% disturbance replay (0.52/0.89 simulated); a coarser rung diverged in 2 of 20,000 contexts. Stylised: one plant, known correlations, step-count costs.

watchdog-twin12 tests

A heartbeat twin that drops packets independently: how often does the real bursty link trip a missed-beat watchdog, and what timeout is safe?

I.i.d.-loss heartbeat twin vs a bursty Gilbert link: a 5-missed-beat watchdog false-trips every 3.4e6 ticks in the twin but every 235–990 on the real link, worst at burst length ≈ m (mean time to trip ≈ e·m/p), and a 1e6-tick target needs m = 16–154 instead of the twin's 5. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

At 5% mean loss a watchdog that e-stops after m = 5 missed heartbeats false-trips once in 3.4×106 ticks (18.7 h at 50 Hz) in the i.i.d.-loss twin but every 235–990 ticks (5–20 s) on a two-state bursty link with mean burst 2–50, from an exact recursion checked against enumeration and Monte Carlo. The error is not monotone in burst length: it is worst at L ≈ m, where the mean time to trip is only ≈ em/p. For a 106-tick target the twin picks m = 5 (0.10 s to detect a dead link) while the real link needs 16–154 (0.3–3.1 s) growing linearly in L, and with L unknown no affordable timeout guarantees it. Stylised: Gilbert channel, plain miss counter, no link traces.

gate-twin14 tests

A twin whose sensor never produces outliers: does an innovation gate help or hurt the real estimator, and what does it do after a jump?

Gaussian-sensor twin vs a real sensor with outliers under an innovation gate: the twin says the gate costs 8.5% MSE, the real sensor gains 3.0× from it, the worst outlier scale for a gated filter is finite (κ≈4) while ungated error grows as κ², and a gate locks out recovery from a jump for ≈76·D² steps. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

With a Gaussian-sensor twin an innovation gate (z = 2.58) costs 8.5% of the update MSE, since every gated measurement is good data; with 5% real outliers at 10× the noise scale the same gate cuts the MSE 1.74 → 0.58 (3.0×) while still passing 28% of the outliers. The ungated error grows like κ2 in the outlier scale, the gated error is bounded and worst at a finite κ* ≈ 4, and a better-tuned gate width gains only 0–6%. After a jump D in a random-walk state the gate rejects the correct measurements and re-convergence takes ≈ 76D2 steps (30,512 at D = 20) against 30 with no gate. Exact post-update MSE checked by quadrature and Monte Carlo. Stylised: scalar update, simulated outliers, simplified covariance rule in the jump experiment.

groundeffect-twin12 tests

A twin without ground effect: where does a landing altitude loop go wrong?
