With a 0.05 ms timestep and 0.1 ms contact time constant the simulated minimum force is 0.89 to 1.02 times the bound over 39 cases (median 1.00); with the earlier settings no force up to 60 N holds a part at 400 or 800 m/s2, a contact-lag artefact. Stylised: rigid box pads, one friction coefficient, no arm dynamics or trajectory.

robofab-solrefmap5 tests

How fine must the MuJoCo contact settings be for a moving grasp?

How fine must MuJoCo contact settings be for a moving grasp? On all seven toy-gripper parts, solref 0.2 ms and below reproduce the jaw-force bound (0.98–1.04×) at 100–800 m/s²; 0.5 ms fails at 400 and above, and the adequate value falls with acceleration (stylised, upward load only).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-graspfast. On all seven printed parts of a toy gripper, a jaw assembly accelerating upward at 100, 400 and 800 m/s2 needs a simulated minimum force of 0.98–1.04 times the bound at contact time constants of 0.2 ms and below (63 cases). At 0.5 ms the bound is matched at 100 m/s2 but no force up to 60 N holds any part at 400 or 800. A scan on one part shows the largest adequate time constant falls with acceleration and is not a single threshold on their product. Stylised: upward load only, rigid box pads, one friction value, no arm.

robofab-solreftimestep6 tests

Is it the contact time constant or the timestep that breaks a moving grasp?

Is it solref or the timestep that breaks a moving MuJoCo grasp? On a 24-cell grid only 6 cells hold; a coarse step always fails, a finer step does not rescue a marginal solref, and solref 0.1 ms holds at steps of 0.1 ms and below (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-solrefmap. On the cover part of a toy gripper accelerating upward at 400 and 800 m/s2, a MuJoCo jaw-force test holds in only 6 of 24 cells of a grid of contact time constant (0.5, 0.3, 0.2 ms) and timestep (0.4 to 0.05 ms). A coarse timestep always fails, probably because MuJoCo raises the effective constant to twice the timestep. A finer timestep does not rescue a marginal constant (at 800 m/s2 and 0.2 ms only a 0.1 ms step holds, finer ones fail for an unexplained reason), while a 0.1 ms constant holds at every step of 0.1 ms and below. Stylised: one part, upward acceleration only, rigid box pads, no arm.

robofab-solrefsafe8 tests

Is MuJoCo's refsafe clamp what breaks a moving grasp at a coarse timestep?

Does MuJoCo's refsafe clamp break a moving grasp at a coarse timestep? Switching it off changes 7 of 32 grid cells' outcomes (11 hold on, 10 off), 10 runs go unstable, and the non-monotone timestep behaviour survives (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-solreftimestep, which only read the documentation on the refsafe flag. The same jaw-force test (cover part, 400 and 800 m/s2) is run over contact time constants of 0.5 to 0.1 ms and timesteps of 0.4 to 0.05 ms with the flag on and off. 11 of 32 cells hold with it on and 10 of 32 with it off, and the two settings disagree in 7 cells. With it off, 10 runs end in a solver instability, so the clamp protects some cells and costs others, and the non-monotone timestep behaviour survives with it off. Stylised: one part, upward acceleration only, rigid box pads, no arm.

robofab-graspoffset6 tests

Does an off-centre centre of mass need a harder grasp?

Does an off-centre centre of mass need a harder grasp? Ball-pad elliptic-cone bound matches MuJoCo within 1.1% (5× force at 20 mm offset); flat-pad MuJoCo lies between an equal-split and a best-split corner-contact bound (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-liftload, whose torque bracket was inconclusive. A 20 mm cube is pinched with its centre of mass shifted 0 to 20 mm in the pad plane. For ball pads (one point contact, an assumed torsional friction coefficient of 2 mm) the elliptic-cone bound matches MuJoCo within 1.1% and the needed force rises 5× (0.097 to 0.50 N). For flat pads the twist is resisted at the corner contacts: MuJoCo lies between an equal-split upper bound and a best-split lower bound at all eight offsets, and needs 0.39× the ball-pad force at 10 mm. The result is insensitive to the rotation tolerance (1, 3, 10°). Stylised: rigid pads, assumed friction, static hold only.

robofab-liftload7 tests

Does the friction-grasp bound survive lift acceleration and an off-centre centre of mass?

Does the friction-grasp bound survive lift acceleration and an off-centre centre of mass? Scaled bound matches MuJoCo within 6% over 66 cases; the torque bracket for an off-centre bar is inconclusive and depends on the rotation tolerance (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-grasp. With a constant lift or sideways acceleration applied as an effective gravity, the simulated minimum jaw force for the six free parts of the toy gripper stays within 6% of the scaled bound m √((g+az)2+at2)/(2μ) over 66 cases, at most 0.21 N. These parts are symmetric, so they test no torque. For a 10×10 mm bar held at one end the torque bracket is inconclusive: with a 5° rotation tolerance MuJoCo holds with less force than the lower bound in 11 of 12 cases, and with 1° the longer bars do not hold at 20 N. Stylised: constant load, boxes, assumed density and friction, thresholds chosen by me.

robofab-sliprate7 tests

Is the off-centre bar result in robofab-liftload a grasp effect or solver creep?

Is the off-centre bar result in robofab-liftload a grasp effect or solver creep? The bar creeps at about 3.7 deg/s from 0.3 to 3 N in MuJoCo, with a rate set by contact settings, so the earlier verdict reflects the simulator (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-liftload that replaces its pass/fail threshold with the bar’s rotation rate. A 10×10×40 mm bar held at one end creeps at about 3.7 deg/s from 0.3 to 3 N and still 2.2 deg/s at 20 N, so no force stops it. The rate scales with the contact time constant and drops tenfold when impratio goes from 1 to 10; torsional friction lowers it 2.5–3×. Free drops occur only at 0.1 N. The earlier verdict reflects simulator settings, not the grasp. Stylised: one engine, boxes, assumed density and friction.

robofab-slipcrit5 tests

Does a rate-based "holds" criterion make a MuJoCo grasp verdict independent of solver settings?

Does a rate-based "holds" criterion make a MuJoCo grasp verdict independent of solver settings? No: the minimum holding force still varies 33x to 400x or more across contact settings, like a 1 degree tolerance (negative, stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-sliprate. Judging a bar held at one end by its extrapolated creep over a 3 s hold (under 2 mm) instead of a rotation tolerance does not help: across eight MuJoCo contact settings the minimum holding force varies by 33× to 400× or more, about as much as under a 1° tolerance. Only a loose 5° tolerance is stable, and only for bars up to 40 mm. Negative and preliminary: the settings, not the criterion, drive the verdict. Stylised, one engine, no physical grip.

robofab-slipthresh6 tests

Is any rate threshold settings-robust for a MuJoCo grasp "holds" verdict?

Is any rate threshold settings-robust for a MuJoCo "holds" verdict? Spread falls with the allowed tip speed and is 1.6 only at a loose 20 mm/s (0.5 s, 10 mm); 242.7 to 400 at 2 mm/s or less (stylised, preliminary).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-slipcrit that sweeps the rate criterion’s task time (0.5–10 s) and tip bound (1–10 mm) over four bars and eight MuJoCo contact settings. The worst-case spread of the minimum holding force falls with the allowed tip speed: 242.7–400× at 2 mm/s or less, 89.4× at 3.3–5 mm/s, 20× at 10 mm/s and 1.6× only at 20 mm/s (0.5 s, 10 mm), a loose threshold; 10 s holds fail at every bound. Robustness comes from a loose threshold, not a better criterion. Stylised and preliminary: one engine, boxes, assumed density and friction.

robofab-slipmu8 tests

Does the loose 20 mm/s “holds” threshold stay settings-robust at other friction and under lift?

Does the loose 20 mm/s "holds" threshold stay settings-robust at other friction and under lift? It is the only threshold under 5x spread in all six conditions (1.6 to 4.5), every other is at least 20x (stylised, preliminary).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-slipthresh, repeating its 16-threshold sweep at friction 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8, with and without a 5 m/s2 lift acceleration. The loose 20 mm/s threshold (10 mm in 0.5 s) is the only one with a worst-case spread of the minimum holding force under 5× in all six conditions: 1.6× in four, 2.7× at mu 0.5 with lift and 4.5× at mu 0.3 with lift. Every other threshold is at least 20×. Robustness comes from looseness, and it weakens at low friction under load. Stylised, one engine, no physical grip.

robofab-barimpratio8 tests

Does a stiffer friction cone make the held-bar result in robofab-liftload threshold-free?

Does a stiffer friction cone make the held-bar result threshold-free? Creep falls about as 1/impratio (3.66 to 0.004 deg/s); from impratio 10 the 1 and 5 degree forces agree within 26%, and MuJoCo needs 0.67 to 1.17 times the old torque bracket's lower bound (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A follow-up to robofab-sliprate, which traced the bar’s creep to MuJoCo’s contact settings. Raising the impratio option from 1 to 1000 cuts the creep of a 10×10×40 mm bar held at one end from 3.66 to 0.004 deg/s, roughly as 1/impratio. From impratio 10 the minimum holding forces for 1° and 5° tolerances agree within 26% in all 12 cases, so the answer no longer depends on the threshold. The simulated force is below the uniform-pressure torque bracket in 10 of 12 cases (0.67–1.17× its lower bound) and 1.15–1.67× a point-contact bound built on the five contacts per pad MuJoCo reports. One engine, one bar section, no torsional friction. Stylised and preliminary.

12

Ambient AI assistant

An always-on, audio-first assistant: when it should speak, and how fast and cheaply the pipeline runs on a device. Simulation first, no real recordings.

ambient-pipeline7 tests

How much latency and memory does an open-model voice pipeline cost on a CPU, and what reply time does it leave?

CPU voice pipeline (Silero VAD, Whisper tiny.en, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Piper) on synthetic speech: per-stage latency/RTF/memory and a reply-latency budget of 0.9–1.5 s at 200–800 ms endpoint hangover, ~0.7 s of it compute. Server CPU, not a phone.

Abstract Project page →

A streaming Silero VAD, Whisper tiny.en (int8), Qwen2.5-0.5B (4-bit) and Piper chain on four CPU cores, on six synthetic sentences. VAD costs 0.15 ms per 32 ms frame, ASR 306 ms per segment (RTF 0.11), the first LLM sentence 267 ms, the first TTS chunk 88 ms, and the models add about 740 MB. End of speech to first audio is 0.94–1.55 s at 200–800 ms endpoint hangover, of which about 0.7 s is compute; a 200 ms hangover already cut one utterance in two, and a 0.5 s target is impossible once the hangover alone exceeds it. Stylised: synthetic clean speech, one server CPU not a phone, batch ASR, LLM answer quality not evaluated.

ambient-interject9 tests

When should an always-on assistant speak, and does a policy tuned in a simulator keep its annoyance budget in a real room?

When an always-on assistant should speak: wake, keyword, threshold and learned policies at equal annoyance, and what breaks when the simulator's room differs from the real one

Abstract Project page →

Simulated 10 s listening windows (needs at 3%, an intent score with d′ = 2, wake-phrase and keyword signals) compare interruption policies at equal annoyance. A wake word is precise (0.69) but catches 15% of needs; adding a keyword reaches 53% recall at 28.7 false interruptions per hour (0.72 for the wake word). At a budget of 1 false per hour a score threshold reaches recall 0.26 and a logistic policy that also uses the keyword and wake flag 0.33; recall at that budget climbs from 0.17 to 0.82 as d′ goes from 1 to 4. Tuned to 1 false per hour, policies keep the budget when only the need side shifts (weaker detector, rarer needs) but run at 3.6–3.9 per hour when the no-need background shifts (noisier score, more wake false alarms); 16 labelled hours restore it for the noisier score, and no threshold can for a wake detector that alone causes 3.5 false per hour. Stylised: independent windows, Gaussian scores, chosen costs, no real conversations.

ambient-memory9 tests

Under a storage limit, which transcripts should an on-device assistant keep, and what survives?

What an on-device assistant should keep from a week of simulated transcripts: BM25 retrieval, extractive summaries and byte-limited retention policies (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Seven simulated days of 1500 utterances each with 6 planted facts per day. BM25 finds every fact (hit@5 = 1.00) when the key words are rare, which is the easy case. With the store limited to 10% of the week, dropping oldest or random utterances keeps 0.11 and 0.10 of the facts; keeping the highest mean-IDF utterances keeps 0.93, because the facts are rare-word lines by construction. An importance-ranked extractive summary at 5% of a day holds 85% of its facts, against 3% for the first lines. Index build 0.04 s, query 1.9 ms on one container CPU. Stylised: synthetic words, lexical queries, no paraphrase, no speech errors. Produced with AI assistance.

ambient-android

Which parts of an always-on Android listening service can be tested without a phone?

Testable Kotlin core of an always-on listening service (re-framing, energy VAD, utterance segmenter, headset-drop policy; 7 tests pass under a shim) plus an unbuilt Android foreground-service sketch; no SDK, no device numbers

Abstract Project page →

A plain-Kotlin core (frame re-chunking, an energy-gate voice detector with hangover and pre-roll, an utterance segmenter that never emits silence, and a headset route policy that pauses rather than falling back to the phone mic) with 7 unit tests, which pass when compiled with Kotlin 2.0.21 and run through a test shim. The Android foreground-service shell is unbuilt: no SDK was usable, so no latency, battery or accuracy numbers exist. Synthetic square-wave frames only. Produced with AI assistance.

ambient-glance10 tests

When is a glance better than speech for an always-on assistant?

When a glanceable display beats speech for an always-on assistant: a stylised utility model over noise, company, free eyes and message length, with sensitivity and twin-gap checks

Abstract Project page →

A stylised expected-utility model chooses between speech, a glanceable display and silence by noise, other talkers, free eyes and message length; a Monte Carlo check agrees with the closed form to 0.001. A glance wins in about half of 84 grid contexts, and the look rate, the number a simulator is least able to supply, drives the twin gap (up to 0.036 utility per message). Every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

ambient-urgency9 tests

Does urgency, and a chime-plus-glance mode, change how an always-on assistant should deliver a message?

Urgency classes and a chime-plus-glance mode added to the glance-vs-speech utility model for an always-on assistant: a stylised model with sensitivity and twin-gap checks

Abstract Project page →

A stylised expected-utility model adds three urgency classes (deadlines of 120, 20 and 6 s) and a chime-plus-glance mode to the speech, glance and silence choice. Chime-plus-glance is the best mode in 62% of normal and high-urgency contexts and raises mean utility per message from 0.351 to 0.417 (partly by construction, since high-urgency messages carry twice the weight); a Monte Carlo check agrees with the closed form to 0.002. The look and reaction rates drive the twin gap (up to 0.018 utility per message). Every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

ambient-rechime9 tests

When is a second or third earbud tone worth it before a glance?

How many repeated earbud tones before a glance are worth their annoyance, by urgency, tone gap and masking, in the ambient-urgency utility model (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

A stylised extension of the urgency model lets the assistant repeat a tone up to four times, 3 s apart, each noticed independently and cancelled once the wearer looks. Choosing the number of tones per context raises mean utility per message from 0.387 (plain glance or one tone) to 0.409; two tones give most of it, and the gain is nil for low urgency and 0.062 for high urgency (partly built in by the weights). Always repeating is barely better than one tone. A Monte Carlo check agrees with the closed form to 0.002. Tones are assumed independent and annoyance flat per tone, and every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

ambient-misread8 tests

How accurate must an always-on assistant's urgency label be before acting on it beats ignoring it?

How accurate an urgency label must be before an always-on assistant should act on it: naive, Bayesian and label-ignoring policies in the ambient-urgency utility model (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

In the stylised urgency model, perfect urgency knowledge is worth 0.034 utility per message. Acting naively on a noisy label stops being worse than ignoring it at about 70% accuracy with uniform errors (about 53% if errors only hit neighbouring classes), and at 70% it loses in 18 of 48 contexts. A Bayesian reading of the label never loses to ignoring it when the prior and confusion matrix are known, but a prior that over-weights high urgency drops it below ignoring the label. Every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

ambient-confest6 tests

How many audited messages does an always-on assistant need before it can trust a noisy urgency label?

How many audited messages an assistant needs to estimate a noisy urgency label's confusion matrix and prior well enough to act on it: about 50 at moderate accuracy, with smoothing helping at tiny audit sets (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Extending the stylised urgency-label model, the assistant estimates the label’s class mix and confusion matrix from n audited messages and then acts by Bayes’ rule. With maximum-likelihood estimates, n = 10 is worse than ignoring the label (mean utility 0.363 against 0.382 at 70% label accuracy); n = 50 recovers 76% of the gain of knowing the true parameters and n = 200 recovers 92%. Add-one smoothing cuts the spread at tiny n but costs a little at high accuracy. Stylised: round-number utilities, uniform label errors, noise-free audit labels.

ambient-noisyaudit7 tests

What does a noisy auditor do to an assistant that learns its urgency label’s reliability from audits?

What a noisy human auditor does to an assistant that learns its urgency label's reliability from audits: taking audit labels as truth biases the estimate and loses 8% to 69% of the label's gain at a 0.9 to 0.7 auditor, and correcting for a known auditor accuracy recovers it (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Extending the stylised urgency-label model, the audit labels are themselves wrong. Taking them as truth biases the estimated label accuracy (0.57 instead of 0.70 with a 0.8-accuracy auditor) and does not improve with more audits: the policy loses 47% of the label’s gain over ignoring it at label accuracy 0.7, and 31% at 0.9. A 0.9 auditor costs only 8–14%. Maximum likelihood over the unseen true class, given the auditor’s accuracy, recovers the true-parameter value, but it needs that accuracy known (not identifiable from one auditor) and is no better at 50 audits with a poor auditor. Stylised; both label and auditor are made-up uniform-error matrices.

ambient-goldaudit7 tests

How many gold-labelled audits replace noisy ones when the auditor’s accuracy is unknown?

How many gold-labelled audits replace noisy ones when the auditor's accuracy is unknown: 25 gold audits match 1000 noisy ones read as truth, and a joint EM using 10 gold plus 200 noisy audits nearly reaches the true-parameter policy (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Extending the stylised noisy-audit model, 200 or 1000 audits from a 0.8-accuracy auditor read as truth give mean utility 0.387–0.388 (label accuracy 0.7) and do not improve with n, while 25 gold audits already match them and 10 do not. Pooling noisy with gold audits as truth is worse than gold alone. Fitting the mix, the label matrix and the auditor’s matrix jointly by EM, with 10 gold and 200 noisy audits, reaches 0.4054 against 0.4066 for the true parameters at label accuracy 0.9 (gold alone: 0.3955). The advantage vanishes by 200 gold audits. Stylised: uniform-error matrices, one auditor accuracy, EM started at the true value, round-number utilities.

ambient-auditbudget5 tests

How should a fixed audit budget be split between gold-labelled and noisy audits?

How to split a fixed audit budget between gold and noisy audits when gold costs 3 to 30 times more: all-noisy is worst or near-worst in all 12 cells, 25% on gold with a joint EM fit is within 0.0009 of the best, and all-gold loses when gold is expensive (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Extending the stylised gold-audit model with a price: a gold audit costs 3, 10 or 30 noisy audits, with budgets of 200 and 1000. Spending everything on noisy audits read as truth is the worst or near-worst split in all 12 cells (0.387–0.388 at label accuracy 0.7). There is no single best share, but 25% of the budget on gold, fitted jointly with the noisy audits by EM, is within 0.0009 of the best in every cell and 50% within 0.0016. When gold is expensive, all-gold is worse (0.3843 at B = 200, cost 30). Stylised: uniform-error matrices, one auditor accuracy, round-number utilities.

ambient-dsaudit6 tests

Can an assistant learn its urgency label’s reliability from two noisy auditors, and what does a wrongly assumed auditor accuracy cost?

Can the assistant learn its urgency label's reliability from two noisy auditors with no accuracy known (Dawid-Skene), and what does a wrong assumed auditor accuracy cost: over-trusting the auditor loses 31% of a 0.9 label's gain, and Dawid-Skene reaches within 0.0005 of the oracle at n = 1000 (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Extending the noisy-audit model, a wrongly assumed accuracy for a 0.8-accuracy auditor costs 31% of a 0.9 label’s gain if the auditor is trusted fully, 17% if assumed 0.9 and 6% if assumed 0.6 (about 39–47% at either extreme for a 0.7 label). With two independent auditors on every message, Dawid–Skene EM learns all three confusion matrices with none supplied: it recovers the true-parameter value exactly in the population limit and at n = 1000 is within 0.0005 of the oracle given the same number of labels, 0.0009 to 0.0128 above taking one auditor as truth. At n = 50 with two 0.7 auditors it still falls below ignoring the label in 18% of audit sets. Stylised: uniform errors, independent auditors, round-number utilities; nothing measured on people.

ambient-dscorr4 tests

What does Dawid–Skene do when the two auditors share their errors?

What does Dawid-Skene do when the two auditors share their errors: it over-trusts them (auditor accuracy read as 0.909 for a true 0.8 at half shared) and loses part of its edge over trusting one auditor, falling to equal it when the second auditor is a copy, never below it (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Extending the two-auditor model, the second auditor copies the first with probability ρ (each stays 0.8 accurate). Dawid–Skene reads their agreement as correctness: the accuracy it assigns auditor 1 rises from 0.80 to 0.91 at ρ = 0.5 and 1.00 at ρ = 1. At label accuracy 0.9 its policy utility falls from 0.4066 (ρ = 0) to 0.4026 and 0.3992, where it equals taking one auditor as truth, and never goes below that in this model; an oracle told auditor 1’s accuracy is unaffected. Stylised: one shared-error model, uniform errors, round-number utilities; nothing measured on people.

ambient-dshard7 tests

What if the two auditors only share errors on hard messages, and can a hardness-aware EM fix Dawid–Skene?

What if the auditors only share errors on hard messages: Dawid-Skene's cost is much smaller than with copying (policy utility 0.4060 vs 0.4066 at 30% hard messages), reaching the naive estimator only in an extreme cell, and a hardness-aware EM recovers the classifier but cannot identify the hard share (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

A fraction h of messages is hard for both auditors (accuracy 0.5 or chance) and the rest easy, with each auditor still 0.8 accurate overall. Dawid–Skene again over-trusts the auditors (0.84 for a true 0.8 at h = 0.3, hard accuracy 0.5), but the utility cost is far smaller than with copying: at label accuracy 0.9 its policy utility is 0.4060 against 0.4066 for the true parameters. Only in the extreme cell (30% of messages at chance, the rest perfectly easy) does it fall to the naive estimator’s 0.3992, and it never goes below it. A hardness-aware EM with an informed start recovers the classifier’s matrix and the policy utility at the population level, but the hard share itself is not identified: different starts fit the same joint distribution with P(hard) from 0.24 to 0.35. Stylised, simulated results only.

ambient-third5 tests

Does a third auditor identify the hard-message share, and does it help plain Dawid–Skene?

Does a third auditor identify the hard-message share: yes at the population level (P(hard) 0.300 from informed starts), only loosely at n=1000 (sd 0.07), and in the extreme cell plain Dawid-Skene with three auditors falls below the naive estimator (0.3912 vs 0.3992) while the hardness-aware EM does not (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Extending the hard-message model to three auditors (each 0.8 accurate overall, a fraction h of messages hard for all). A hardness-aware EM now recovers the hard share at the population level (P(hard) 0.300 from four informed starts, where two auditors left 0.24–0.35), but only loosely from samples (sd 0.07 at n = 1000) and a poor start still lands on a degenerate fit. Plain Dawid–Skene gets worse with more auditors: in the extreme cell (30% of messages at chance) it reads them as 0.85 accurate and its policy utility falls to 0.3912 at label accuracy 0.9, below the naive estimator’s 0.3992; the hardness-aware EM stays at the true-parameter 0.4066. Stylised: one shared-hardness model, uniform errors, round-number utilities; nothing measured on people.

ambient-multistart8 tests

Does a likelihood-ranked multi-start make the hardness-aware EM robust to a poor start?

Does a likelihood-ranked multi-start make hardness-aware Dawid-Skene robust to a poor start: at the population level yes (P(hard) 0.300, vs 0.500 and a lower likelihood from a poor single start), at finite n it matches one informed start, and where hardness is absent the hard share is not identified (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Fitting the three-auditor hardness-aware Dawid–Skene model from 8 grid starts (none near the truth) and keeping the highest-likelihood fit recovers the hard share at the population level (P(hard) 0.300), where a single poor start stays at 0.500 with a lower likelihood. At finite n it matches one informed start (P(hard) 0.290 vs 0.290 at n = 1000, hard accuracy 1/3) and avoids the poor start’s utility loss (0.3913 vs 0.3843). With no hardness at all the hard share is not identified, and fitted shares of 0.3–0.4 appear anyway. Stylised.

ambient-startcount5 tests

How many starts does the likelihood-ranked multi-start need, and are grid starts better than random ones?

How many starts does a likelihood-ranked multi-start need, and are grid starts better than random ones: one start is nearly enough with strong hardness or n = 1000, 4 starts reach the best optimum in most cells, more help only in the weak-hardness and null cells, and policy utility barely moves (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Fitting the three-auditor hardness-aware Dawid–Skene model from 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 nested grid starts versus the same number of random starts, keeping the highest-likelihood fit. When hardness is present and either strong or nWith strong hardness or n = 1000 one start nearly always reaches the best optimum and 4 starts reach it in every such cell;nbsp;=With strong hardness or n = 1000 one start nearly always reaches the best optimum and 4 starts reach it in every such cell;nbsp;1000, one start usually reaches the best optimum (72With strong hardness or n = 1000 one start nearly always reaches the best optimum and 4 starts reach it in every such cell;ndash;100%) and 4 starts reach it in 82With strong hardness or n = 1000 one start nearly always reaches the best optimum and 4 starts reach it in every such cell;ndash;100% of draws; with mild hardness at n = 200 and under the null, more starts keep improving the likelihood (grid hit rate 72% at K = 1 to 97% at K = 16) but mean policy utility moves by at most about 0.0002. Grid versus random is mixed. Stylised: one dependence model, 40 draws per cell, optimum judged against the best of 32 fits.

ambient-hlrt4 tests

Can a likelihood-ratio test tell “no hard messages” from “some”, and is the chi-square cutoff usable?

Can a likelihood-ratio test tell no hard messages from some: chi-square cutoffs reject 35-72% of null data sets, a parametric bootstrap holds its level and detects h = 0.3 at n = 1000 but not h = 0.1 (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Testing h = 0 in the three-auditor hardness-aware Dawid–Skene model. Under the null the likelihood-ratio statistic has median about 5 and 95th percentile about 13, so the chi-square cutoffs 3.84 and 5.99 reject 62–72% and 35–49% of null data sets. A parametric bootstrap (39 refits) rejects 7/60 and 0/60 under the null and detects h = 0.3 reliably at n = 1000 (100%) but only 37% at n = 200 with hard accuracy 0.5; h = 0.1 is undetectable. Stylised, 60 draws per cell.

ambient-hlrtlevel4 tests

Does the bootstrap likelihood-ratio test of “no hard messages” hold its level?

Does the bootstrap likelihood-ratio test of no hard messages hold its level: 200 null draws per n give rejection 0.040-0.055 at nominal 0.05, all intervals containing 0.05 (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A larger null-only check of the parametric-bootstrap test from ambient-hlrt (B = 39): 200 data sets with no hard messages at each of n = 100, 200 and 500. Rejection at nominal 5% is 11/200, 9/200 and 8/200 (exact 95% intervals all contain 0.05) and at 10% is 20, 16 and 19 of 200; mean p is about 0.5. The earlier 7/60 at n = 200 looks like noise. Stylised: one dependence model, level only, intervals about ±0.03.

ambient-hlrtmis5 tests

Does the bootstrap test of “no hard messages” stay valid when the auditors differ in accuracy?

Does the no-hard-messages bootstrap test keep its level when the three auditors differ in accuracy: 100 h = 0 draws per cell give rejection 0.00-0.10 at nominal 0.05, no inflation seen (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Data with no hard messages but three auditors of unequal accuracy (equal, 0.9/0.8/0.7, 0.95/0.8/0.65; mean 0.8), tested against a null that forces one shared auditor matrix. With 100 draws per cell at n = 200 and 500, rejection at nominal 5% is 6–10/100 at 200 and 0–6/100 at 500; five of six exact intervals contain 0.05 and the sixth (0/100) is conservative. No inflation is seen, but intervals are about ±0.05 wide. Stylised: accuracy heterogeneity only, level only.

ambient-bandit6 tests

Can an always-on assistant learn when to speak from accept/dismiss feedback alone, and what does it cost in dismissals?

Can an always-on assistant learn when to speak from accept/dismiss feedback alone: greedy, epsilon-greedy and Thompson online policies vs an offline oracle, mostly negative (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

A simulated assistant learns an interruption policy online (greedy, ε-greedy or Thompson-sampled logistic model) from the user’s reaction only when it speaks. With an uninformed prior none of the three learns a useful policy in 100 h; with a prior that the intent score is informative, greedy reaches 90% of an offline oracle’s rate after a median 22.5 h and about 185 dismissals, and Thompson sampling takes 32.5 h. It still earns 10.4 against the oracle’s 12.7 per hour, and after a drop in classifier quality it does far worse than frozen offline weights (0.3 vs 4.4 per hour). Stylised: independent windows, instant noise-free feedback, picked costs.

ambient-ips5 tests

Does inverse-propensity weighting fix an always-on assistant learning from its own accept/dismiss feedback?

Does inverse-propensity weighting fix an assistant learning from its own accept/dismiss feedback: mostly negative, exploration cost dominates (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-bandit: the assistant speaks with a known probability (ε-greedy) and refits its model with each labelled window weighted by 1/propensity. Mostly negative: exploration itself costs more utility than the learning gains at every ε tried, weights up to 500 make the weighted fit unstable at small ε (a standard deviation across seeds of tens of utility units per hour), and the weighting did not rescue the uninformed-prior or the drift scenarios. Only at ε = 0.02 with an informed prior is the weighted model slightly closer to the oracle (12.2 vs 11.4 per hour at 100 h, oracle 12.7). Stylised: every distribution is chosen by me.

ambient-fullinfo4 tests

Does selection bias actually hurt an always-on assistant that learns only from windows where it spoke?

Does selection bias hurt an assistant learning only from windows where it spoke: yes, a lot in this world; a full-information fit reaches the oracle, weighting recovers part (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-ips: on the same logged history, a model fitted only on windows where the assistant spoke is compared with an inverse-propensity-weighted fit and with a full-information fit that sees every window’s label. The full-information fit reaches the oracle (12.72 against 12.71 utility per hour); the biased fit loses 1.3 to 2.1 per hour with an informed prior and fails with an uninformed one, so the bias is large, contrary to a guess in ambient-ips. Weighting recovers part of the loss only at ε = 0.02 with an informed prior. The comparison also mixes bias with data volume (no label-matched control). Stylised, simulated only.

ambient-labelmatch4 tests

Is the gap in an assistant that learns only from windows where it spoke caused by selection bias or by too few labels?

Is the self-selected-feedback gap bias or label volume: mostly bias (a random sample of equal size nearly reaches the oracle); clipped weights help only with an informed prior (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-fullinfo. A control that fits on a uniformly random sample of windows, of the same size as the biased fit’s label set, gets 12.2–12.5 utility per hour against an oracle of 12.71, while the biased fit gets 10.6–11.4 with an informed prior and fails with an uninformed one: in this world the gap is mostly selection bias. Capping the inverse-propensity weights at 10 or 50 beats raw weights and the biased fit with the informed prior, but is worse than the biased fit with the uninformed prior; self-normalised weights are noisy. The control uses labels a real assistant never sees, so it locates the loss rather than recovering it. Stylised: chosen distributions, independent windows, noise-free feedback, simulated only.

ambient-dr5 tests

Does a doubly robust estimator fix learning from an assistant’s own self-selected feedback?

Does a doubly robust estimator beat IPS on an assistant's self-selected feedback: no, a stylised negative result; its pseudo-labels carry 1/ε residuals and are worse than the biased fit except with an informed prior.

Abstract Project page →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-labelmatch. Doubly robust pseudo-labels (an outcome model plus an inverse-propensity correction on the windows where the assistant spoke) are fitted on every window and compared with biased, IPS, clipped and self-normalised fits on the same logged history. A negative result: with an uninformed prior all three variants are far worse than the biased fit (utility per hour below −15 against 12.71 for the oracle) and have huge variance, and with an informed prior they are level with or above the biased fit at they match the biased fit at ε = 0.005 and 0.02 butepsilon; = 0.005 and 0.02 but are not better than clipped IPS. Simulated windows chosen by me; nothing is claimed about real users.

ambient-drclip6 tests

Does capping the inverse-propensity correction rescue doubly robust learning from an assistant’s own feedback?

Does capping the inverse-propensity correction rescue doubly robust learning from an assistant's own feedback: with an informed prior yes (the collapse at ε = 0.002 goes from 0.26 to about 12 utility/h), with an uninformed prior no; stylised, simulated only.

Abstract Project page →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-dr, which left clipping untested. Capping the correction weight at 1, 5, 20 or 100 (instead of 1/ε up to 500) removes the collapse with an informed prior: at ε = 0.002 the unclipped fit scores 0.26 utility per hour and the capped ones 11.7–12.2, against 10.6 for the biased fit and 12.71 for the oracle. With an uninformed prior it does not help: capped fits that use the clipped-IPS outcome model stay between −17 and −50, and those that use the prior as outcome model score 4–8 at best, still below the random-subset control (about 12). Simulated windows chosen by me; one cap grid, 20 seeds, nothing claimed about real users.

ambient-crossfit5 tests

Does cross-fitting the outcome model help capped doubly robust learning from an assistant’s own feedback?

Does fitting the doubly robust outcome model out-of-sample (2-fold cross-fitting) help the capped correction: no, a negative result; differences are within seed noise or worse, and the unclipped collapse at ε = 0.002 persists (1.53 vs 0.26 utility/h); stylised, simulated only.

Abstract Project page →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-drclip. The outcome model behind the doubly robust pseudo-labels is fitted on the other half of the windows (2-fold cross-fitting) instead of on the same data, with the inverse-propensity correction capped at 5, 20, 100 or not at all. Negative result: with an informed prior the cross-fitted and in-sample fits are within about 0.1 utility/h of each other wherever the cap is finite, and the unclipped collapse at ε = 0.002 remains (1.53 vs 0.26 utility/h, against 12.71 for the oracle). With an uninformed prior the gaps are large but have no consistent sign (cross-fitting is better in some cells, worse in others) and both variants stay far below the biased fit. Simulated windows with costs chosen by me; no claim about a real user or device.

ambient-capcv5 tests

Can the doubly robust cap be chosen by validation on an assistant’s own logs?

Can the capped doubly robust cap be chosen by 4-fold IPS validation on the log: with an informed prior it matches the best fixed cap within seed noise, with an uninformed prior it does not rescue learning; stylised, simulated only.

Abstract Project page →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-crossfit. The cap on the inverse-propensity correction is chosen from {2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, ∞} by 4-fold validation, scoring each candidate with an uncapped inverse-propensity estimate of its utility. With an informed prior the chosen cap matches the best fixed cap to within seed noise (12.23 against 12.19 utility/h at ε = 0.005; 11.45 against 11.84 at 0.002, with a wider spread). With an uninformed prior it does not rescue learning (between −21 and −1 utility/h with seed standard deviations of 24–51, against about 12 for a randomly sampled log), and the validation score is noisy enough that chosen caps scatter across the grid. Stylised, simulated only; 20 seeds, no significance tests.

ambient-drvalid7 tests

Does a doubly robust validation score choose the doubly robust cap better than an IPS score?

A doubly robust validation score does not pick the DR cap better than IPS with the same 4 folds (equal with an informed prior, mixed with the uninformed one); 8 random folds with the DR score is best in all three uninformed cells but still far below the label-matched control (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A stylised, mostly negative follow-up to ambient-capcv. Replacing the inverse-propensity validation score with a doubly robust one, on the same 4 folds, changes nothing with an informed prior and gives mixed results with the uninformed one (seed standard deviations of 20–51 utility/h). A doubly robust score on 8 random folds is the best selector in all three uninformed cells, but remains far below a label-matched control (about 12 utility/h against −11 to 6); score, fold count and fold type changed together, so the cause is untested. Simulated, independent windows only; preliminary.

ambient-drablate7 tests

Which of score, fold count and fold type made cap selection better in ambient-drvalid?

Ablating the three changes in ambient-drvalid (score, fold count, fold type): in the uninformed cells random folds help more than the DR score (IPS on 8 random folds is as good as DR on 8), no factor wins everywhere, and every selector stays far below the label-matched control (stylised, negative).

Abstract Project page →

A stylised, mostly negative ablation of ambient-drvalid: all 8 combinations of validation score (IPS or doubly robust), folds (4 or 8) and fold type (contiguous or random) choosing the doubly robust cap, 20 seeds. With an informed prior all eight are within 0.2 utility/h. With the uninformed prior, random folds are the most consistent help: at ε = 0.02 the 4-fold IPS selector gives −1.4 (std 24) against 5.6 (std 7.3) with random folds, and IPS on 8 random folds (6.3) matches DR on 8 random folds (5.9). At ε = 0.005 the DR score is worse than IPS on contiguous folds (−26.9 vs −17.7) and no selector is clearly best; seed standard deviations are 5–55. Every selector stays far below the label-matched control (about 12). Simulated, independent windows, no significance tests.

ambient-drrepeat8 tests

Do repeated random fold assignments stabilise validation-based cap selection?

Repeated random fold assignments for cap selection in the ambient-assistant world (follow-up to ambient-drablate): averaging 5 assignments helps the IPS-score selector at ε = 0.02 (3.5 → 5.3 utility/h) and nothing else beyond noise; stylised, simulated only.

Abstract Project page →

A stylised, mixed follow-up to ambient-drablate: averaging the cap-selection score over 5 random fold assignments (instead of one) with an uninformed prior, 20 seeds. At ε = 0.02 it lifts the IPS-score selector from 3.5 to 5.3 utility/h and halves its seed spread; at smaller ε it changes nothing beyond noise. Single-assignment results differ from the earlier project's, showing how much one fold permutation can matter. Every selector stays far below the label-matched control (about 12). Simulated and stylised only.

ambient-exploreonly5 tests

Does fitting only on the windows an assistant explored at random fix learning from its own feedback?

Fitting only on the windows an assistant explored at random fixes the uninformed-prior failure of learning from its own feedback (11.99 vs −13.08 utility/h at ε = 0.02), at an exploration cost (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-labelmatch and the reweighting and doubly robust fixes after it. The deployed learner already draws a random sample for free: the windows it spoke on only because its ε coin came up. Fitting on those windows alone, unweighted, reaches 11.99 utility/h at ε = 0.02 and 12.25 at 0.05 with an uninformed prior, against −13.08 and −71.85 for the fit on every spoken window (oracle 12.71; 20 seeds), and as a learner it earns 6.49/h online at ε = 0.005 against −2.04. Exploration costs dismissals (online utility falls at larger ε), and with an informed prior the plain fit is better at small ε. Stylised simulation only.

ambient-wearable8 tests

What limits the battery life of a pendant-style always-on audio wearable?

What limits battery life in a pendant-style always-on audio wearable: stylised nRF52840-class power model (mic floor ~170 h; speech-gated ~105 h vs 59 h always streaming) plus a 74-byte VAD gate that compiles for Cortex-M4; no hardware measured

Abstract Project page →

A stylised average-current model for an nRF52840-class pendant with a 150 mAh cell, built from a few vendor figures read on 2026-10-13 plus labelled assumptions. The always-on microphone is the floor (about 170 h alone); gating codec and radio on speech at a 30% speech fraction gives about 105 h against 59 h for always streaming. A 74-byte energy-gate routine compiles for Cortex-M4. Nothing is measured on hardware, the datasheets were not read in full and there is no numeric comparison with Omi.

13

Self-replicating manufacturing

How close can a small shop get to making copies of its own machines? Closure, growth and what to build next, in models that run on a CPU.

selfrep-closure8 tests

How much of a RepRap printer can a growing seed shop make itself?

Part, mass and cost closure of the RepRap Prusa Mendel (iteration 2) for three seed shops: printer alone makes 18 of 51 part lines (35%), plus router and laser 43%, assumed-mass closure 22%; casting helps only with brass bushings. Mass and cost inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

The RepRap Prusa Mendel (iteration 2) bill of materials (51 part lines, from the RepRap wiki) against three seed shops. A printer alone makes 18 of 51 lines (35%); adding a CNC router and laser cutter reaches 43% of lines and, under assumed masses and costs, about 22% of mass and 16% of cost; casting helps only if brass bushings replace LM8UU bearings (45% of lines, 24% of mass). Motors, electronics, rods, bearings and fasteners stay vitamins. Stylised: the wiki gives no masses or prices, so those inputs are assumed and shown with a sensitivity range, process assignments are judgement, and only the printer is decomposed.

selfrep-nextmachine6 tests

Which machine should a seed shop add next, and does a greedy rule find it?

Which machine a printer-only seed shop should add next under a budget: greedy closure-per-price vs exhaustive search; same choice on the real 3-machine instance, optimal in 72–94% of 500 synthetic instances. Machine prices assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Builds on the selfrep-closure part model. Choosing among a CNC router, laser cutter and casting setup under a budget, a greedy closure-per-price rule matches exhaustive search at every tested budget on the real three-machine instance (router first, then casting only if brass bushings replace LM8UU). On 500 random synthetic instances greedy is optimal in 72–94% of cases and loses up to about 38% of the closure gain in the worst case. Stylised: machine prices, masses and costs are assumed placeholders, machines have no bills of materials of their own, and the synthetic instances are random.

selfrep-growth9 tests

How fast does a replicating printer shop grow when its vitamins must be bought?

Discrete-event and fluid growth of a replicating printer shop with imported vitamins: doubling time falls roughly as 1/budget until machine time binds (about 53 h in the simulation), failed builds cost about 1/(1-f), and closure helps most when imports bind. All inputs assumed; Lackner and Wendt comparison not done. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Builds on the selfrep-closure part model. A discrete-event simulation of a fleet of printers that each build copies of themselves, checked against a closed-form fluid model. With a small import budget the doubling time falls almost in proportion to the budget (about 455 h at 4 units/h, 120 h at 16/h); above a crossover fleet size N* = BW/V machine time binds and doubling flattens near the 50 h build time. Failed builds raise the doubling time by about 1/(1−f), and raising closure helps most when imports bind. Every input (print rate, assembly time, costs, budget, failure rate) is assumed and the fleet is homogeneous. Stylised. The comparison with Lackner and Wendt’s growth model is not done.

selfrep-reinvest8 tests

When should a replicating shop stop copying itself and start making goods?

Optimal split of a replicating printer shop's time between copies and goods: copy flat out, then switch one e-folding time (about 50 h) before the horizon; constant splits get 9–27% of that value, smooth ramps no better. Cash-limited cases switch about 50 h from the end. All inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Builds on the selfrep-growth fleet model. A fluid optimal-control model splits machine time between building copies and making goods, scored on the total value of goods over 600 h. Copying flat out and then switching to goods one e-folding time (1/k = W/(1−f), 50 h with no failures) before the horizon matches the closed form; the best constant split earns only 9–27% of that value, and smooth ramps are no better than the sharp switch. When imports or goods sales fund vitamins, cash binds throughout and the switch lands about 50 h from the end. Every input is assumed, the fleet is a continuous fluid, goods demand is unlimited and the final fleet is worth nothing. Stylised. Piecewise policies are local search, not a proof of optimality.

selfrep-materials10 tests

How much imported material can recycling save a self-replicating printer shop?

Mass and energy balance of plastic and aluminium recycling for one RepRap copy (stylised, assumed process parameters): vitamins stay about 75% of imported mass, recycling the shop's own scrap cuts imports a median 3%, and only retired-machine plastic changes the plastic import much.

Abstract Project page →

Builds on the selfrep-closure part list. A stylised steady-state mass and energy balance for building one more RepRap Prusa Mendel, with shredding and re-extrusion of plastic and remelting of aluminium offcuts. With assumed process parameters, vitamins stay about 75% of imported mass for the largest shop (82% for the printer alone), and recycling the shop’s own scrap cuts imports by a median 3% (5–95% over parameter draws: 1–6%). Only plastic from retired machines changes the filament import much, and then the assumed recycled-share cap decides the result. Limitations: every yield, loss and energy figure is an assumption, recycling machines are not counted, and recycled-plastic quality is not modelled.

selfrep-recyclers8 tests

How many printer copies does it take for a shop's recycling machines to repay their own imports?

Payback of recycling machines with their own assumed part lists (stylised): about 100 printer copies on the shop's own scrap, 12–31 if retired machines' plastic is recycled.

Abstract Project page →

Builds on selfrep-materials. A shredder, a filament extruder and an aluminium furnace are given assumed part lists, split into vitamins and parts the shop can make. With the shop’s own scrap only, the plastic pair needs 99–116 printer copies to avoid as much imported mass as it costs (91–164 over part-mass draws) and the furnace about 94. Plastic from retired machines cuts this to about 12–31 copies, depending on an assumed recycled-share cap. Limitations: part lists and masses are placeholders, mass is the only currency (cost, time and energy are ignored), and retirement is a scenario knob. Stylised.

selfrep-costpayback8 tests

Does pricing a shop’s imports, instead of weighing them, change when its recycling machines repay themselves?

Recycler payback priced instead of weighed (stylised, assumed prices): plastic pair 98–111 printer copies on own scrap, furnace 203, 10–26 with retired plastic.

Abstract Project page →

Builds on selfrep-recyclers with assumed round-number prices for feedstock and for each vitamin of the machines. The plastic shredder and extruder repay in 98–111 printer copies on the shop’s own scrap (median 99, 45–235 over price draws), close to the mass-based 99–116, while the aluminium furnace worsens from 94 to about 203 copies because aluminium is cheap per kilogram. Recycling retired plastic brings the plastic pair to 10–26 copies. Stylised: every price and part list is an assumption, and labour and energy costs are ignored.

selfrep-singulararc8 tests

What is the closed form of a replicating shop’s smooth switch from copying to goods, and does it match dynamic programming?

Closed-form optimal copy share for a replicating printer shop with a saturating goods market (Pontryagin singular arc: goods output grows linearly, last 1/k hours all goods); earns 99.96–100% of the dynamic-programming policy's value. Necessary conditions only; all inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Builds on selfrep-satmarket. With concave revenue a c(1 − e−g/c), Pontryagin’s principle gives three arcs: copy flat out, a singular arc on which goods output grows linearly at rate kc, then goods only for the last 1/k hours. The entry time solves one scalar equation. In the Euler model the open-loop policy earns 99.96–100.00% of the dynamic-programming policy’s value over 7 market sizes and 4 failure shares. The conditions are necessary, not a proof of optimality, and depend on the assumed exponential revenue form. Stylised.

selfrep-satmarket8 tests

When the goods market saturates, does a replicating shop’s bang-bang switch turn smooth?

Reinvestment of a replicating printer shop when the goods market saturates, checked by dynamic programming: bang-bang is optimal with linear revenue, but with market capacity below about 10^4 machine-hours per hour the optimum ramps the copy share down over 90–300 h and bang-bang loses 4.5–7%. All inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Builds on the selfrep-reinvest fluid model, with concave goods revenue a c(1 − e−g/c) and a backward dynamic programme (Bellman) as a check on the local-search policies. With a large market the optimum is still copy-then-switch; once market capacity c is below about 104 machine-hours per hour the optimal copy share ramps down over 90–300 h, bang-bang loses 4.5–7% of the optimum and a logistic ramp recovers all but 1–1.5%. Slower growth from failed builds sharpens the switch again. Every input is assumed and the saturation form is a convenient choice; cash never binds. The DP value is the optimum of a discretised problem, within a few tenths of a percent of its simulated policy where it is accurate and several percent in near-linear cases. Stylised.

selfrep-wearout8 tests

What fleet can a replicating printer shop sustain when its machines wear out?

Fleet a replicating printer shop sustains when machines wear out (stylised, assumed inputs): short-lived machines die out from one seed; recycling gains need a correction for builds cut short.

Abstract Project page →

Extends the selfrep-growth fleet model with random machine lifetimes (Weibull) and a recovered share of vitamin value at retirement. With assumed inputs and a vitamin budget of 4 units/h, a lone seed machine died out in every run when mean life was 200 h or less (20% of runs at 500 h, 3% at 2000 h), while the fluid model predicted a small stable fleet; survivors held about 10 machines at 500 h. Wear-out lifetimes are safer than constant hazard at the same mean. The fluid equilibrium over-predicts fleet size at high recycling (235 vs 73 simulated at 95% recovery); charging for builds cut short by retirement closes the gap (76), though that correction was added after seeing the discrepancy. Stylised: every input is assumed.

selfrep-extinction6 tests

Can an exactly solvable birth-death chain explain why short-lived printer fleets die out?

Exact mean extinction time of a wearing-out printer fleet as a birth-death chain (stylised, assumed inputs): explains the die-outs in kind, within about 35% only after a post-hoc fix.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-wearout. The fleet is a birth-death chain with an absorbing state at zero, and its mean extinction time is solved exactly and checked against a closed form and Monte Carlo. From one seed machine it grows from 358 h (mean life 100 h) to 3967 h (200 h) to 41,602 h (300 h), but the wear-out simulation dies out 1.8–2.5× sooner. Scaling births by the chance a build outlives its machine brings the two within about 35% for a lone seed (16–18% at 200–300 h), a fit made after seeing the gap; it is 1.7–1.9× too short for four seeds at 300 h. Stylised, with assumed inputs; the 500 h rows are unusable.

selfrep-repairpay5 tests

Does paying for spares late rescue the long repair queue of a printer shop?

Does paying for spares at service start rescue the long repair queue of a printer shop (stylised, assumed inputs): yes, an unbounded queue then beats never repairing (488 against 458 at one bench) and queue caps stop mattering.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-repairlabour. That project found an unbounded repair queue is dead stock (414 working machines against 458 for never repairing, one bench, B = 40) when spares are bought at breakdown. Buying them when a bench frees up instead reverses it: 488 against 458, and 572 against 504 with four benches. The queue is as long (about 3400 machines) but ties up no vitamins, and capping it no longer helps (caps of 1–200 all give 484–492 at one bench; no standard errors computed, so no optimum cap is claimed). Stylised: assumed inputs, first-come service, a machine unaffordable at its turn is retired.

selfrep-repairlabour7 tests

What happens to a repairing printer shop when repairs need labour?

Repair labour as a limit on a repairing printer shop (stylised, assumed inputs): with few repair benches an unbounded queue of broken machines is dead stock and does worse than never repairing; capping the queue recovers most of the gain.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-repair. Repairs need one of K benches; broken machines queue after buying spares. The pre-run prediction that the working fleet is about min(import limit, K·L/h) fails: with B = 40 and one bench the fleet is 414 against a cap of 40, because most breakdowns are never served and the queue (2915 machines) is dead stock. An unbounded queue with one bench is worse than never repairing (414 against 458); retiring a breakdown when 1–20 machines already wait gives 487–492. Stylised: assumed inputs, benches are a count with no wages, no corrected closed form.

selfrep-repair8 tests

When is repairing a printer worth more than building a new one?

Repair versus replacement in a replicating printer shop (stylised, assumed inputs): repair wins iff its cost share is below its success probability, but only if spares are held back from new builds.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-wearout. Machines break down at a constant rate and the shop may spend spare-part vitamins to repair one instead of retiring it. A vitamin-balance formula predicts repair gives a bigger fleet exactly when the repair cost share is below the repair success probability; a discrete-event simulation with assumed inputs puts the crossing at that value, within about 9% of the formula in that sweep, but only when spares are held back from new builds (without a reserve the fleet was 70 against a formula value of 157). Repair also cuts die-out from one seed at short lifetimes (for example 55% against 100% at a mean life of 100 h) but does not remove it. Stylised: assumed inputs, memoryless breakdowns, repair returns the machine to new, no printed spares.

selfrep-spares7 tests

How much does making its own spare parts cut the cost of repairing a printer?

How much making its own spare parts cuts a printer shop's repair cost (stylised, assumed inputs): the printer alone makes none of the wear parts, so in-house spares barely move the fleet; the breakdown rate matters more.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-repair. The spare-part cost share of a repair is derived from the Prusa Mendel’s wear parts (belts, bearings, hot end, switches), each with an assumed life, and from which of them a seed shop can make. The printer alone makes none and adding a router and laser cutter makes only the pulleys, so the share stays near 0.021 and the fleet is unchanged (62.5 vs 63.0 machines, against 7.3 with replacement only). Swapping the linear bearings for a printed bushing lowers the share to 0.019, but if the bushing lasts half as long the fleet falls to 43, so breakdown rate matters more than where the spare comes from. Stylised: every life and cost is assumed.

selfrep-sparehours3 tests

Does a printer shop lose its printed-bushing gain once a printed spare takes print hours?

Does charging printed spares their print hours erase the printed-bushing gain (stylised, assumed inputs): the fleet ignores waits up to ~500 h per repair because it is import-limited, and the gain was within noise anyway.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-spares. A repair that needs a printed bushing waits extra print hours (mean-downtime approximation in the unchanged selfrep-repair simulation). At the assumed inputs the working fleet is flat up to about 500 h of wait per repair (62.7 vs 64.2 machines with none) and falls at 1000 h (58.5) to 36.0 at 5000 h, because the fleet is import-limited, not downtime-limited. The bushing’s gain over stock bearings (+1.8) was already inside the run-to-run spread. Stylised, assumed inputs; printing does not compete with building for machine time.

selfrep-extinction-kits7 tests

Is the lone-printer die-out an early birth-death accident?

Exact Markov-chain test of why a lone replicating printer dies out (stylised, assumed inputs): about a fifth die before a fleet forms at 500 h mean life; wear-out lives remove it.

Abstract Project page →

Tests the extinction explanation left open by selfrep-wearout with an exact continuous-time Markov chain of the same shop (Poisson vitamin kits, exponential builds and lives). With assumed inputs and a budget of 4 units/h, the chain gives a 0.194 chance that a lone seed machine is lost before the fleet reaches 6 machines at 500 h mean life (simulation 0.198 ± 0.006), of which 0.162 is the seed retiring before its first copy; relaxing the Markov assumptions moves this by at most about 0.03. Wear-out lives (Weibull shape 2 or more) cut it to under 3%. Exact mean extinction times for small equilibrium fleets match simulation (1464 h against 1511 ± 50 h at 200 h life), but with regular kits and lognormal builds long times roughly double, so the chain is a lower guide there. Stylised: every input is assumed; simulated only.

selfrep-extinction-qsd4 tests

Can a quasi-stationary approximation predict how long a small printer fleet lasts?

Quasi-stationary approximation of how long a small replicating-printer fleet lasts (stylised, assumed inputs): within 5% of the exact mean time once a correction for early die-out is applied, poor for the shortest lives.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-extinction-kits. The slowest decay rate of the exact Markov chain gives a quasi-stationary estimate 1/λ0 of the mean extinction time. Stylised, with assumed inputs, it overshoots a lone seed machine by 1.2 to 1.9 times (2388 h against 1465 h exact at 200 h life), but multiplied by the exact chance the fleet survives its start it lands within 5% in four of seven cases (for example 0.999 at 500 h life) and fails where the fleet rarely survives (ratio 1.4 at 200 h life, 42 at 75 h). Seed fleets help only up to the quasi-stationary time: 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 seeds give 1465 / 1983 / 2388 / 2666 h at 200 h life. The survival correction was chosen after seeing the overshoot, so it is a post-hoc fit. Stylised: every input is assumed; simulated only.

selfrep-reconcile4 tests

Why do two exact extinction chains of the same printer shop disagree?

Reconciles the two exact extinction chains of the lone printer shop (stylised, assumed inputs): the fleet-size chain is 1.5 to 7 times longer; adding the kit wait fixes small fleets but over-corrects large ones.

Abstract Project page →

Two sibling chains of the lone replicating printer shop, one on fleet size and one on machines and vitamin kits, give different mean extinction times for the same inputs. Stylised, with assumed inputs, the fleet-size chain is longer by 1.5 to 7 times because its birth law min(n/W, a) lets machines and kits never wait for each other. A fixed-in-advance repair that adds the two waits matches the kit chain within 5% when the fleet stays at 1 to 3 machines, but falls 24 to 60% below it for larger fleets, where kits pool in stock. No law right in both regimes was derived.

selfrep-redesign5 tests

Which part substitutions cut a printer's vitamins most, within a performance budget?

Which assumed part substitutions (printed bushings and nuts, wooden rods) cut the Prusa Mendel's vitamins most under a penalty budget: all seven take closure from 43/22/16% to 60/36/48% (lines/mass/cost); best set depends on the assumed penalties. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-closure that changes the machine instead of the shop. Seven assumed substitutions (printed bushings and nuts, wooden rods, a printed drive) are searched exhaustively, greedily and at random under an assumed penalty budget. All seven together take the Prusa Mendel’s vitamin lines from 29 to 19 and closure from 43/22/16% to 60/36/48% (lines/mass/cost) for the printer, router and laser shop; mass closure stays below 36% because motors, electronics and threaded rods remain. Cost closure responds most, and the best set depends on the assumed penalties. Stylised: substitutions, masses and penalties are all assumed and no part was tested.

selfrep-rodbeam6 tests

What does a wooden rod cost a printer in stiffness?

Beam model of the Prusa Mendel's smooth rods: a wooden rod sags 20 times a steel one at 8 mm and needs about 17 mm to match it, and selfrep-redesign's assumed dowel mass was twice the geometric one (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Replaces the assumed penalty of selfrep-redesign’s wooden-rod substitution with Euler–Bernoulli beam theory. At 8 mm a hardwood rod sags 20× a steel one (the modulus ratio) and a printed PLA rod 80×; matching steel stiffness needs about 17 mm of hardwood, outside the printer’s 8 mm hardware, while a 1–2 mm sag tolerance needs 9–11 mm. The earlier 30 g per dowel was about twice the geometric 13.8 g, moving mass closure from 35.8% to 34.6%; thicker dowels raise closure again, a quirk of counting imported feedstock as makeable. Stylised: properties and the 5 N load are assumed and no rod was tested.

selfrep-rodmodes5 tests

What natural-frequency target does a printer’s rod have to meet, and what does a wooden rod cost?

Carriage natural frequency on the Prusa Mendel's smooth rods: a vibration target, not a sag limit, sets the rod diameter; hardwood needs about twice steel's diameter (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-rodbeam that derives the rod spec from a vibration target instead of an assumed sag limit. A carriage mass on a simply supported rod (Rayleigh estimate with the 17/35 effective rod mass) gives a first mode of 42 Hz for 8 mm steel but 10 Hz for hardwood and 5 Hz for printed PLA, for an assumed 0.3 kg carriage. Matching steel’s frequency needs about 16 mm of hardwood, close to the sag-matching 17 mm; at equal frequency the dowel is 1.9–2.1× the steel diameter. Stylised: carriage mass and material constants are assumptions, one mode, no damping or bushing play.

selfrep-alurod6 tests

Does an aluminium rod fit the printer where a wooden one cannot?

Aluminium rods in the printer redesign: matching a steel rod's sag takes 10.4 mm aluminium (fits the assumed 12 mm holders) against 16.9 mm hardwood (does not), at 39.5% vs 37.8% mass closure (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-rodbeam that adds aluminium bar, cut to length on the router, as a rod substitution in selfrep-redesign. To match the sag of the 8 mm steel rod (0.19 mm at the assumed 5 N) aluminium needs 10.4 mm, inside the assumed 12 mm holder limit, while hardwood needs 16.9 mm and does not fit. Mass closure of the all-substitutions redesign is 39.5% with aluminium at a 0.2 mm spec, 37.8% with wood and 28.7% with steel rods kept as vitamins; the shop imports about 170 g more stock than with wood. Stylised: moduli, load and limit are assumed, and the surface of cut aluminium bar is taken to be adequate for the bushings.

selfrep-alufreq6 tests

How stiff a rod does a frequency target need, in aluminium and in wood?

Sizing printer rods to a first-mode frequency target instead of a sag spec: at 0.3 kg aluminium reaches 40 Hz with 10.0 mm (fits the assumed 12 mm holders) where hardwood needs 16.0 mm (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-alurod and selfrep-rodmodes: rods of the printer redesign are sized to a first-mode frequency target (Rayleigh estimate, assumed 0.3 kg carriage) instead of a sag spec. Aluminium reaches 40 Hz with 10.0 mm, inside the assumed 12 mm holder limit, where hardwood needs 16.0 mm; within 12 mm the highest reachable frequency is 56 Hz for aluminium and 23 Hz for hardwood. Closure by mass rises with the target only because thicker stock counts as makeable, while imported stock grows from 1946 g to 2596 g. Stylised: one mode, assumed carriage mass, moduli and holder limit.

selfrep-terminal6 tests

How does a resale value for the finished fleet move the switch from copies to goods?

A resale value s per machine at the horizon shortens the goods phase from one e-folding time 1/k to 1/k − s/a; at s ≥ a/k the shop never switches. Grid optimum matches the closed form. All inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-reinvest. Giving each machine left at the horizon a value s shortens the goods phase from one e-folding time 1/k to 1/k − s/a, so the switch moves later; at s ≥ a/k (50 per machine with no failures, 29% of the assumed vitamin cost) the shop copies to the end. The grid optimum of the Euler simulation agrees with this closed form to within 1 h, and ignoring a terminal value of 12.5–50 per machine costs 3–26% of the optimum. Every input is assumed; cash is free and demand unlimited. Stylised.

selfrep-terminalmarket5 tests

Does a resale value for the finished fleet still end copying late when the goods market saturates?

A resale value s per machine with a saturating goods market (DP): at capacity c = 1000 machine-hours per hour the copy phase runs to the horizon once s is 12.5 (a quarter of a/k), and the policy that ignores s earns 14% of the optimum; the DP loses to bang-bang by under 1% where the fleet is large, so it is a lower bound there; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-terminal and selfrep-satmarket: a backward dynamic programme with terminal reward s per machine on the saturating-market fluid model (W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed). With a linear market the DP reproduces the closed-form switch of selfrep-terminal. As the market capacity c falls, a small s moves the optimum from an early switch to copying until the horizon (c = 1000: switch near 400 h at s = 0, none at s = 12.5), and a policy tuned for s = 0 earns only 14% of the optimum. Where the final fleet is large the DP is not reliable: a bang-bang switch beats its policy by up to 0.7%, so it is a lower bound there. Stylised and preliminary; the resale value is assumed and does not itself saturate.

selfrep-dpgrid4 tests

Is the dynamic-programming table for the replicating shop with a resale value converged, and can its policy be trusted?

Grid-convergence check of the terminal-value DP: the policy's value is stable to about 0.15% from 800 to 1,600 grid points while the table value rises from 8–13% (400 points) to 2–3% (1,600) below it; a stylised fluid model, preliminary.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-terminalmarket, which found its DP table up to about 10% below the value of its own policy. This project refines the log-spaced fleet grid from 100 to 1,600 points and tries a second interpolation rule (linear in fleet size instead of in log fleet size), on the same fluid model (W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed). The simulated value of the DP policy changes by only about 0.15% between 800 and 1,600 points and stays within 0.2% of the best bang-bang switch, while the table value approaches it from below roughly in proportion to 1/(grid points): about 8–13% low at 400 points and 2–3% low at 1,600. The table is therefore a slowly converging lower bound, not a certificate; a first-order extrapolation puts it within about 0.8% of the bang-bang value in the three cases tried, but that rests on two grids. The cause of the bias is not diagnosed. Stylised fluid model, preliminary.

selfrep-resalecurve6 tests

How does a falling resale price for the finished fleet change when the shop stops copying?

A resale price for the finished fleet that falls with market depth m (stylised): with an unsaturated goods market the switch moves from 574 h (linear) to 549 h (m = 1e3) and a single switch matches the DP; with a saturating goods market the DP beats the best switch by up to 14%.

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to selfrep-terminalmarket: the fleet is sold at the horizon for sm(1 − e−N/m), so the first machine fetches s and the price falls with market depth m (W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed). With an unsaturated goods market a shallower resale market moves the optimal switch from 574 h (linear) to 549 h (m = 103), and a single switch matches the DP. With a saturating goods market (c = 104) the DP policy beats the best single switch by up to 14%. The DP table value is not a certificate (it overstates at 400 grid points); simulated policy values are reported. Stylised and preliminary; both market curves are assumed, not fitted.

14

Simulation-first design

Designs written as code, simulated, optimised and exported as manufacturing files with an open toolchain, on a CPU.

simdesign-bracket8 tests

Can a parametric L-bracket be sized by finite elements for minimum mass and come out printable?

Parametric L-bracket sized by 2D finite elements (scikit-fem) for minimum mass under a stress limit: differential evolution 19.6 g vs random 25.6 g vs grid 31.4 g at equal budget, exported as STL with a printability check. Assumed material inputs. Stylised.

Abstract Project page →

A 2D plane-stress scikit-fem model of an L-bracket with a filleted inner corner (arm width, fillet radius, depth) under a 100 N tip load. Differential evolution reaches 19.6 g against 25.6 g for random search and 31.4 g for a grid at 144–150 evaluations each, under a 20 MPa stress and 4 mm deflection limit. The design is exported as a binary STL and checked for minimum wall and overhang. Stylised: material properties and limits are assumed, the optimum stress rises about 7% on mesh refinement (just over the limit), the sharp-corner stress diverges, and the thin optimum was not checked for out-of-plane buckling.

selfrep-alusearch7 tests

Does an aluminium rod change which printer redesign the penalty-budget search picks?

With an aluminium rod option priced by sag, the penalty-budget search of the printer redesign picks the 12 mm aluminium rod and reaches 40.0% mass closure at budget 2.0 against 33.1% with the wooden rod (41.4% against 35.8% at full budget); the penalty curve is assumed and the metric favours heavy stock; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Project page →

A stylised, preliminary search over 448 designs: a rod choice (steel, hardwood or aluminium at 8, 10 or 12 mm) times subsets of six other part substitutions, with a rod penalty tied to mid-span sag by an assumed log curve. At every budget from 0.5 up the best mass-closure design uses the 12 mm aluminium rod: 40.0% at budget 2.0 against 33.1% for the wooden-rod search of selfrep-redesign, and 41.4% against 35.8% at full budget. The choice sits at the assumed holder limit because the closure metric counts heavier bar stock as makeable, so it says little about the best rod. The pick held for penalty scales from 0.05 to 1. Computed only; nothing was built.

selfrep-stockmass6 tests

Does the best printer redesign change when imported bar stock counts as an import, not as made?

Scoring the printer redesign by the mass the shop must still import (vitamins plus raw stock) instead of closure: the best design imports 5.85 kg against 6.72 kg for the baseline, while the closure-maximising 12 mm aluminium pick imports 6.79 kg (stylised; yield and prices assumed).

Abstract Project page →

A stylised, preliminary re-scoring of the 448-design search of selfrep-alusearch: the score is the mass (or cost) the shop must still import per printer copy, vitamins plus raw stock at an assumed 0.8 yield. The import-mass minimiser reaches 5.85 kg against 6.72 kg for the steel-rod baseline, with the light 8 mm hardwood rod; the earlier closure-maximising pick (12 mm aluminium) imports 6.79 kg, no better than baseline. By import cost the 12 mm aluminium rod stays best (147.5 against 173.3). Yield, stock price and penalties are assumed; computed only.

simdesign-topopt7 tests

Can Sigmund's 99-line topology optimisation be reproduced in Python and carried through to a printable part?

Python reproduction of Sigmund's 99-line SIMP topology optimisation (cantilever, half-MBB; filter removes 11.5% checkerboards) with the density field exported as a mirrored, extruded STL; stylised 2D compliance only.

Abstract Project page →

A Q4 plane-stress SIMP code with the 99-line sensitivity filter and optimality-criteria update, tested against Hooke's law and finite-difference sensitivities. It gives truss-like cantilever (compliance 351.9 → 52.4) and half-MBB (1007.0 → 203.3) designs. Without the filter 11.5% of 2×2 cells are checkerboards; with it none, at the same compliance within 0.03%. The thresholded MBB design is one connected body and is written as an extruded, mirrored STL. Stylised: dimensionless 2D compliance only, no stress or 3D check, not compared with the published codes.

simdesign-heaviside7 tests

Does a density filter with Heaviside projection close the gap between a topology-optimised density field and the black-and-white part?

Density filter and Heaviside projection added to the SIMP code: the optimiser's compliance matches the thresholded part's to 0.1% (sensitivity filter: 10% off) but the parts are equally stiff within 0.9%; β continuation needed (β=64 from the start: 344.8 vs 192.1); a minimum-length-scale check found no advantage (negative); stylised 2D.

Abstract Project page →

Adds a density filter, a tanh Heaviside projection and β continuation to the SIMP code of simdesign-topopt. On a 90×30 half-MBB beam the sensitivity and density filters leave 26–34% grey elements and a model compliance 10–15% above the thresholded part’s; with projection the two agree to 0.1% (192.1 vs 192.0). The thresholded parts are equally stiff within 0.9% (190.3–192.0), so the gain is an honest model, not a stiffer part. Starting at β = 64 without continuation gives 344.8 against 192.1. A minimum-length-scale check did not separate the formulations (negative): a single projection does not by itself fix a physical minimum feature. Stylised: 2D dimensionless compliance, one problem, one run per setting.

simdesign-fidelity6 tests

When does a cheaper beam model pick the same design as 3D finite elements?
