Layer-count sweep (2 to 12) of the constrained structural-colour coating: six to ten layers reach best angle shifts under 1 dE at C* 40 and 4 g/m2 where 2 and 4 layers stay near 3.4, but 12 layers did not search well at the same budget (stylised, 8 seeds).

Abstract Project page →

The constrained problem of garment-stackpareto with the layer count varied from 2 to 12 (Nelder–Mead restarts, 3000 calls, 8 seeds per cell). For the red target at C* ≥ 40 and 4 g/m2, 2 and 4 layers reach a best mean ΔE of about 3.4, while 6, 8 and 10 layers reach 0.5–0.8; medians are several times higher, so the ranking among 6–10 is within noise. At 12 layers few runs were feasible, probably a search limit at equal budget rather than a property of the stack. Stylised: flat substrate, three angles, no thickness tolerance; no coating was made.

garment-assist7 tests

Does an assistive garment pay for its own mass?

One-joint ankle exosuit model: active assist cuts modelled whole-body cost 3–14% (gain 0.1–0.5) but a few kg of garment mass erases it; break-even mass ∝ 1/(mass sensitivity). Stylised; assumed constants, no OpenSim/MyoSuite.

Abstract Project page →

A one-joint ankle model of an exosuit-style garment: a suit adding a fraction of the biological push-off torque cuts modelled whole-body metabolic cost by 3.1, 8.8 and 14.1% at gains 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5, but a delay of 0.25 of the gait cycle removes the benefit and a stiff passive spring raises ankle cost 17%. Added mass erases the saving at 8.9 kg if each kg costs 1% of whole-body power and at 1.8 kg if it costs 5%; the break-even scales as 1/sensitivity, a number the project does not supply. Stylised: lumped muscle, prescribed gait, assumed constants; not OpenSim or MyoSuite.

garment-assistpower5 tests

Is it the motor or the battery that decides whether an exosuit pays for its own mass?

Adds a motor and battery mass model to the ankle exosuit: at an assumed 8 N m/kg the motor (about 8 kg) makes a gain-0.3 suit raise cost 0.2–1.9%; the sign flips between 8 and 20 N m/kg, battery hours matter little. Stylised; assumed constants.

Abstract Project page →

Extends the ankle exosuit model with a power train: motor mass from peak torque and a torque density, battery mass from electrical energy and hours of use, and the resulting mass fed back into metabolic cost. With an assumed 8 N m/kg motor the gain-0.3 suit weighs about 9 kg, 8.4 of it motor, and raises whole-body cost 0.2–1.9%; the sign flips between 8 and 20 N m/kg, while eight hours of battery add under 2 kg. Stylised: every power-train constant is assumed, not sourced.

garment-protective8 tests

What would a suit-like protective garment weigh and cost, and what limits it?

Cunniff-style scaling for nylon, aramid and UHMWPE: at equal weight UHMWPE gives 1.49× aramid's V50 and needs 0.20–0.67× the areal density depending on an unknown exponent; a 3 mm, 1 kg suit-like panel falls short of a 4 kg/m² aramid reference except under optimistic assumptions. Stylised; recalled formula, assumed properties and prices, no protection claim.

Abstract Project page →

A Cunniff-style specific-toughness scaling (U*) for nylon, aramid and UHMWPE with a 0.5 m2 torso-panel mass, cost, thickness and stiffness model. At equal weight UHMWPE gives 1.49× aramid's V50 in this scaling, and needs 0.20–0.67× the areal density depending on an unknown exponent. Under a 3 mm, 1 kg suit-like limit the panel falls short of a 4 kg/m2 aramid reference except for UHMWPE with an optimistic exponent. Stylised: recalled formula, assumed properties and unsourced prices, no ballistic physics and no protection claim.

garment-smart8 tests

Which sensors in a smart garment recognise what you are doing, and how fragile is that to garment slip?

Activity recognition from simulated chest/thigh/wrist IMUs and knee/elbow strain: two sensors reach ~99% and all five 99.9% on easy synthetic classes, but a clean-trained model falls to 45% under 1 rad garment slip (94% when trained with slip). Stylised; invented signals, no real dataset.

Abstract Project page →

Synthetic chest, thigh and wrist accelerometers and knee and elbow strain channels, six activities, a softmax classifier on spectral features and unseen simulated people. Two sensors reach about 99% and all five 99.9%, because the invented classes are easy to separate. A model trained on clean data falls to 81, 61 and 45% when the IMUs rotate by 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0 rad (a garment slipping), while training with 0.6 rad of slip holds 94–99%. Strain-only stays at 97% under slip by construction. Stylised: sinusoidal signals, no real dataset, no drift or hysteresis.

16

Task-specific AI accelerators

Small accelerators designed together with the model for one task: accuracy, cycles, area and energy per inference, checked in open RTL flows.

accel-kws13 tests

How small can a keyword-spotting accelerator get, and what does each bit of precision cost?

Keyword-spotting accelerator: quantised MLP on Speech Commands, serial-MAC RTL bit-exact against an integer reference, accuracy vs cycles, cells and modelled energy over width and weight bits (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A one-hidden-layer MLP on pooled MFCC features of Speech Commands v0.02 (10 keywords plus unknown), quantised to 2–8 bit weights, mapped to a serial-MAC RTL engine that matches an integer NumPy reference bit for bit on all 40 swept configurations. Test accuracy saturates near 75% (0.752 at 128 hidden units, 4 bits); 4-bit weights are within 0.4 points of 8-bit at 64 and 128 units, 2 bits collapses at small width, and a 64-unit 4-bit design (0.722) uses about 31% of the best design’s modelled energy. Modelled classifier energy is 0.0045–0.19 µW at 4 inferences per second, far below the 1.8 mW microphone floor in ambient-wearable. Stylised: assumed 45 nm energy constants not re-checked, generic-gate area without memories, no front end, a third-party dataset mirror, and a weak feature set.

accel-codesign6 tests

Under a latency deadline, how much engine area does picking the most accurate model first cost, compared with choosing model and lane count together?

Model-first vs joint choice of model and MAC lane count under a latency deadline, on the 40 measured accel-kws models; accepting 2 validation points less cuts engine area 31–42% (stylised, table-based, cycles for more than one lane analytic).

Abstract Project page →

Exhaustive joint search over the 40 measured accel-kws keyword-spotting models and six MAC lane counts (240 designs), against a model-first flow, at deadlines of 2,000–20,000 cycles. The most accurate model (validation 0.775, test 0.752) needs 16 lanes at 2,000 cycles and 7,667 generic cells; accepting 2 validation points less (test 0.738) cuts area by 31–42%, and 3 points by 35–56%. Stylised and only partly the milestone: models are a fixed measured table (the dataset was unreachable), cycles for more than one lane are analytic and not RTL-simulated, memory bandwidth is not counted, area is generic gates, and no NSGA-II or Bayesian search was run (the space is small enough to enumerate).

accel-dataflow4 tests

Which dataflow should a small keyword-spotting accelerator use, and does the answer survive allowing an input buffer?

Weight-, output-, input-stationary and reduction-tree dataflows of a P-lane MAC array on the 40 accel-kws models, from a cycle-by-cycle schedule simulator that matches closed forms exactly and the P = 1 RTL cycles; output-stationary wins on SRAM energy at batch 4 until an input buffer is allowed, then input-mapped flows win at 32 lanes (stylised, assumed energy constants, no RTL for more than one lane).

Abstract Project page →

Four dataflows (output-, weight-, input-stationary and reduction-tree) of a P-lane MAC array, as schedules walked cycle by cycle on the 40 accel-kws models, with SRAM-access counts that match closed forms exactly and, at P = 1, the measured RTL cycles of accel-kws. At batch 1 output-stationary is best (input-stationary is a median 1.2× to 4.1× worse, falling with lanes); at batch 4 it wins every model while weight-stationary is a median 4.5–9.0× worse through partial-sum traffic. Allowing an activation buffer flips the batch-4 winner to the input-mapped flows at 32 lanes (1.37× better), so the ranking rests on a modelling choice. Stylised: assumed energy constants, a one-cycle register model, no RTL beyond one lane, Timeloop not tried.

accel-plane6 tests

Does a loop-nest cycle model of a P-lane MAC array match RTL at more than one lane, tails included?

P-lane output-stationary and reduction-tree matrix-vector engines in Verilog, bit-exact against NumPy at 1 to 32 lanes, with RTL cycles equal to accel-dataflow's schedule model plus a constant 2 or 3 at every point, tails included (stylised, generic-gate area, batch 1, no memories).

Abstract Project page →

Output-stationary and reduction-tree matrix-vector engines written in Verilog for the two accel-kws layer shapes (64×70 and 11×64), simulated in Icarus Verilog at 1 to 32 lanes. All 36 sweep points are bit-exact against NumPy, and RTL cycles equal the accel-dataflow schedule model plus a constant 2 (3 with a registered adder tree), including ragged last tiles: output-stationary needs 66 cycles against 46 for the reduction tree on the 11-output layer at 16 lanes, and 142 against 194 on the 70-input layer at 32 lanes. Yosys generic-gate area grows faster for the output-stationary engine (11,799 against 8,216 cells at 32 lanes), partly because of its registered output vector. Stylised: batch 1, generic gates not a library, no memories, no timing.

accel-planebatch5 tests

Does the weight-stationary advantage in the dataflow model survive RTL at batch above 1, and what does it cost in gates?

Output- and weight-stationary batched RTL engines at batch 1 to 16: bit-exact, cycles and operand-fetch counts equal accel-dataflow's schedule model, and weight-stationary's saved weight fetches cost up to 4x the generic gates (stylised, P = 8, no memories).

Abstract Project page →

One parameterised Verilog engine implements output- and weight-stationary batched matrix products (P = 8 lanes) for the two accel-kws layer shapes, simulated in Icarus Verilog at batch 1 to 16. All 20 points are bit-exact against NumPy, RTL cycles equal the accel-dataflow schedule model plus a constant 2, and RTL weight and activation fetch counts match the model exactly. Weight-stationary fetches the 4,480 weights of the 64×70 layer once instead of B times at identical cycles, but keeping its partial sums in registers grows the design from 3,024 to 12,284 generic cells (about 192 flops per extra batch element) against a flat ~3,000 for output-stationary. The model's ‘weight-stationary is worst’ ranking came from partial-sum SRAM traffic that this RTL trades for area. Stylised; generic gates, no memories, no energy figures.

accel-fetchprice6 tests

How cheap must idle flops be, relative to a weight fetch, for register-file weight-stationary to beat output-stationary?

Breakeven price ratios from accel-planebatch's RTL counts: register-file weight-stationary beats output-stationary only if an idle flop costs under ~1% of a weight fetch per cycle at batch 4 (falling ~1/B); no energy constant measured (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Breakeven price ratios solved from the RTL-measured counts of accel-planebatch (P = 8, batch 1 to 16, two accel-kws layers). Register-file weight-stationary beats output-stationary on energy only if an extra flop costs under about 1% of a weight fetch per cycle at B = 4 (2.6×10−3 at B = 16), a bar that falls roughly as 1/B unless idle flops are clock-gated. Weight-stationary with partial sums in SRAM wins only if a 24-bit partial-sum access costs under 0.25 to 0.48 of a weight fetch, which looks implausible. Stylised: no energy constant is measured or sourced, so which side real technology falls on is left open.

accel-pdkprice12 tests

At SKY130's own energy prices, does register-file weight-stationary scheduling beat output-stationary?

Places accel-fetchprice's breakevens against SKY130 liberty energies (idle flop 46 fJ per cycle; OpenRAM macro 10 to 90 pJ per access): with weights packed into SRAM words register-file weight-stationary loses to output-stationary at nearly every batch; partial sums in SRAM lose everywhere. Library values, not measurements.

Abstract Project page →

Takes the breakeven price ratios of accel-fetchprice and prices them with the SKY130 HD liberty file (an idle dfxtp_1 flop costs 46 fJ per cycle, almost all clock-pin power) and the four OpenRAM SRAM macros shipped with OpenROAD-flow-scripts (10 to 90 pJ per access). If one 4-bit weight is fetched per access, weight-stationary wins at most batches; if weights are packed into the SRAM word (0.8 to 2.9 pJ per weight) output-stationary wins at nearly every batch, and weight-stationary with partial sums in SRAM loses in every case since a word holds fewer 24-bit sums than 4-bit weights. Library characterisation values, not measurements; the per-edge versus per-cycle reading of the OpenRAM figure is unresolved.

accel-gatedprice9 tests

Does clock-gating the extra accumulators make register-file weight-stationary scheduling beat output-stationary?

Prices clock-gated register-file weight-stationary scheduling from SKY130 and GF180 liberty files: an idle clock gate costs 0.86 of an idle flop (SKY130; 0.99 to 1.02 in GF180), so one gate per 24-bit accumulator cuts the idle cost about 28-fold and flips register-file WS from losing to winning against packed SRAM weight fetches in 35 of 64 cells, in all but one cell at 24 flops per gate. Library values, not measurements.

Abstract Project page →

Follows up accel-pdkprice, where idle flops made weight-stationary (WS) lose to output-stationary (OS) once weights are packed into SRAM words. Reads the idle clock energy of a flop and of an integrated clock gate (ICG) from the SKY130 HD and GF180MCU liberty files: an idle SKY130 dlclkp_1 costs 0.86 of an idle dfxtp_1 (39.7 against 46.4 fJ per cycle), and GF180 gates cost 0.99 to 1.02 of its flops at 3.3 and 5 V in both track heights. One gate shared by G accumulator flops therefore cuts the idle cost about G-fold. With one gate per 24-bit accumulator, WS needs a weight fetch of only 0.08 to 0.9 pJ (ungated: 2.2 to 26 pJ) and beats OS against every packed SKY130 macro in all 64 macro, layer and batch cells but one (an 80-bit macro on the 11×64 layer at B = 16 needs 27 flops per gate). Library characterisation values, a gate-per-group model with the enable logic, area and the register-file read mux unpriced; no RTL built or synthesised.
Stylised.

accel-gatedrtl6 tests

Does the clock-gated weight-stationary engine hold up once it is written in RTL and synthesised?

The clock-gated register-file weight-stationary engine in RTL and SKY130 synthesis: bit-exact, same accumulator writes as output-stationary, clock-pin energy 1.0 to 1.07x OS with a gate per set, but area only 7 to 18 % below ungated WS and 1.2 to 5.3x OS (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Writes the register-file weight-stationary (WS) engine of accel-planebatch with clock gates (one per 24-bit accumulator, or one per set of eight) and synthesises it to SKY130 HD with Yosys. All 32 points are bit-exact against NumPy and write exactly as many accumulator bits as the output-stationary engine, confirming the assumption of accel-gatedprice. A gate per set brings the accumulator clock-pin energy to 1.00–1.07× output-stationary (ungated WS: B×), but area falls only 7–18 % against ungated WS, and gated WS is still 1.2× to 5.3× the output-stationary area at batch 2 to 16 because the extra accumulator sets are flops either way. Stylised: synthesis only, no place and route, clock tree or timing; energy is a liberty-based clock-pin model.

accel-gatedlanes3 tests

Does the gated weight-stationary engine's verdict depend on how many lanes it has?

The gated weight-stationary engine's lane count swept from 2 to 16 (32 ran out of synthesis memory): bit-exact, clock-pin energy 1.01 to 1.07x OS with a gate per set at every P, area 1.6 to 1.9x OS at B = 4 and flat from P = 4, so the verdict depends on the batch, not the lanes (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Sweeps the lane count P (2 to 16, with a failed attempt at 32) of the four engine modes from accel-gatedrtl on the 64×70 keyword-spotting layer, in RTL simulation and Yosys synthesis to SKY130 HD. All 29 points are bit-exact and write the same accumulator bits in every mode. Accumulator clock-pin energy stays at B× OS for ungated WS and at 1.01 to 1.07× with a gate per set, independent of P; gated WS stays 1.6 to 1.9× OS area at B = 4 (2.9 to 3.0× at B = 8), flat from P = 4. So the earlier conclusion (cheap to clock, not small) is a property of the batch, not the lane count. Stylised: synthesis only, clock-pin energy only; Yosys exceeded 7 GB at P = 32, so wider engines are not covered.

accel-gatedmux4 tests

Why did the gated weight-stationary engine need so much synthesis memory, and does fixing it change its area verdict?

Why the gated weight-stationary engine needed so much synthesis memory: one variable-index read of the accumulator bus; an AND-OR read mux gives bit-exact, same-cycle engines 17 to 28 % smaller, gated WS 1.5x OS area at B = 4 and 2.2x at B = 8 (was 1.6 to 1.9x and 2.9 to 3.0x), and lets P = 64 synthesise (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

The accumulator read in the engine of accel-gatedrtl indexed the whole accumulator bus with a variable, which Yosys builds as one wide shifter per lane and which stopped accel-gatedlanes at 16 lanes. An AND-OR read mux over the batch sets gives the same cycles, fetches, accumulator writes and flop count, bit-exact against NumPy at all 48 points (P = 2–64, B = 4 and 8), but weight-stationary engines come out 17–28% smaller in SKY130 HD synthesis (output-stationary unchanged). Gated weight-stationary is 1.45–1.50× the output-stationary area at B = 4 and 2.1–2.2× at B = 8, flat in P, against 1.6–1.9× and 2.9–3.0× before; every point now synthesises under the old 7 GB cap. Stylised: synthesis only, one layer shape, random data, clock-pin-only energy; the cause is inferred from the before-and-after effect.

accel-policy6 tests

Does a small control network need an accelerator to meet the control-rate deadline?

Can a small behaviour-cloned control network meet the control-rate deadline on a microcontroller or a P-lane accelerator for a two-link arm? Stylised and preliminary: the int8 policies track 300+ times worse than their teacher, so policy accuracy, not hardware speed, is the limit; the latency model (assumed constants) shows hardware matters only above about 10 kHz.

Abstract Project page →

Small MLP policies, cloned from a computed-torque controller for a two-link arm with DAgger and quantised to 8 and 4 bits, with inference latency modelled for microcontroller loops and P-lane accelerators (assumed constants) and the closed loop simulated with that latency. Preliminary and mostly negative: the int8 policies track at least 300× worse than the teacher, which itself barely notices a sample of delay, so policy accuracy rather than hardware speed limits control; the deadline model says hardware only matters above about 10 kHz or for larger networks. Stylised; hardware figures are not measured.

accel-fpga5 tests

Does the keyword-spotting engine fit a small open-toolchain FPGA, and how fast does it clock?

The accel-kws serial-MAC engine through Yosys and nextpnr-ice40 on UP5K and HX8K for 15 geometries (random weights, synthesis only): all fit in at most 22% of the UP5K's logic, weights land in block RAM, Fmax 15–22 MHz on UP5K. Stylised; no board, no power.

Abstract Project page →

The accel-kws serial-MAC engine, wrapped with on-chip weight ROMs and run through Yosys and nextpnr-ice40 for 15 geometries (hidden width 8–128, 2/4/8-bit weights) on the iCE40 UP5K and HX8K, 3 seeds each. All 15 fit: at most 1,138 of the UP5K’s 5,280 logic cells (22%) and 24 of its 30 block RAMs, because Yosys put the weights in block RAM, so logic grows with weight bits rather than width. Post-route Fmax is 15–22 MHz on UP5K and 37–54 MHz on HX8K, so one inference takes 0.04–0.70 ms. Stylised: the weights are random (Speech Commands was unreachable), accuracies are borrowed from accel-kws, and nothing was run on a board or measured for power.

accel-sparse7 tests

When does a task's accuracy tolerance let an accelerator drop its multipliers?

Pruning, int4/int8, ternary and binary MLPs on scikit-learn digits (substitute task) with a modelled-energy engine: when does the accuracy slack let the hardware drop multipliers? Stylised; at 1–2 points tolerance, pruned int8 still beats multiplier-free.

Abstract Project page →

Pruning, int4/int8, ternary and binary variants of a 64-32-10 MLP on scikit-learn's 8×8 digits (a substitute task: Speech Commands was unreachable), with a modelled energy per inference for a zero-skipping serial engine, over 10 splits. Pruning 75% of int8 weights costs 0.2 points and cuts modelled energy to 36% of dense int8; ternary costs 1.4 points and binary 3.0. Within 1–2 points of float32 the cheapest design still has multipliers, because operand reads dominate in the assumed model; multiplier energy must be about 10× the assumed value before dropping it clearly pays. Stylised: assumed 45 nm constants, no RTL or synthesis, no lookup-table variant, toy task.

accel-lut6 tests

Does weight-sharing lookup-table inference beat a multiply-accumulate engine for a small accelerator?

Weight-sharing product-table inference against int8 MAC engines on the digits MLP: negative at this size, break-even only for wide layers with cheap table reads. Stylised, modelled energy.

Abstract Project page →

A k-means weight-sharing codebook with a per-input product table (no multiplier per weight) against int8 serial MAC engines, on the 64-32-10 digits MLP of accel-sparse, dense and 75% pruned, over 10 splits. Negative: within 2 points of float32 the table engine does not beat int8 (dense: 3.51 nJ for 8 shared values against 3.56 nJ for int8; pruned: 1.55 against 1.51 nJ), and it only looks better against a baseline that rereads activations per weight. An analytic sweep puts the break-even at layers of about 128 outputs or more, and then only if table reads cost a quarter of an array read. Stylised: assumed 45 nm constants, no retraining or RTL, substitute task.

accel-lutwide6 tests

Does a wider hidden layer make weight-sharing product-table inference beat an int8 MAC engine?

Product-table inference on trained wide digits MLPs (32, 128, 512 hidden): at best 14% under int8 energy, only with an assumed cheap table read. Stylised, modelled energy.

Abstract Project page →

Tests the break-even accel-lut predicted analytically, on trained 64-N-10 digits MLPs (N = 32, 128, 512, 10 splits), with the table engine on the wide layer and an int8 MAC on the 10-output layer. Mostly negative: the best table design is 14% below int8 modelled energy at width 512 only if a table read costs a quarter of an array read per bit (assumed), and 2× or worse at the array-cost read. Accuracy cost of sharing shrinks with width (K = 8: 1.6 points at 32, 0.4 at 512). Stylised, modelled energy, no synthesis.

accel-lutft4 tests

Does fine-tuning the shared weight values rescue low-K lookup-table inference?

Fine-tuning the shared values of accel-lut's product-table engine: rescues K=2 in the 75%-pruned digits MLP (14% under int8 energy only at an assumed cheap table read), not the dense network. Stylised, modelled energy.

Abstract Project page →

accel-lut left its shared values untrained. Here the codebook is kept in the loop for 60 epochs (straight-through, k-means re-fit each step) on the same 64-32-10 digits MLP, dense and 75% pruned, over 10 splits. Mixed: in the pruned network 2 shared values go from a 6.5-point to a 1.7-point accuracy drop, and with an assumed cheap table read (0.04 pJ/bit) that is 1.30 nJ against 1.51 nJ for int8; at 0.16 pJ/bit it loses. In the dense network fine-tuning does not help (8 shared values: 3.2 points down against 1.6 without it). Stylised: assumed energy constants, one fine-tuning recipe, no RTL, substitute task.

accel-lutrtl4 tests

What does a product-table inference engine cost in RTL, against a serial MAC engine?

The product-table engine and a serial MAC engine in Verilog, bit-exact against NumPy and synthesised with Yosys: negative, the table needs an accumulator per output (stylised)

Abstract Project page →

Both engines for a 64×N dense layer with 4-bit activations and int8 shared weights, written in Verilog, checked bit for bit against an integer NumPy reference, and synthesised with Yosys to generic gates (assumed gate-equivalent weights). Negative and stylised: the table engine keeps one accumulator per output, so its datapath is 2.4× (N=8) to 11.6× (N=128) the MAC engine's and it takes 1.1× to 3.0× the cycles, even though it stores half the weight bits. Random weights, area only, no energy measured.

17

Algorithmic chip-design loops

Chip-design loops that need no LLM: algorithms propose designs and flow settings, open tools score them.

eda-harness3 tests

Can one harness check, score, cache and log candidate chip designs for any proposer?

Unattended design loop (lint, bit-exact RTL sim, gate-netlist check, Yosys synthesis, hash cache, JSONL log, pluggable proposers) run on chip-accel's 40-design grid: synthesis and the gate check are 99% of wall time (stylised, generic-gate counts, no place and route).

Abstract Project page →

A loop that takes a parameterised generator and a search space and runs each candidate through lint, bit- and cycle-exact RTL simulation, a gate-netlist simulation check and Yosys synthesis, caching by design hash and logging every evaluation as JSON. On chip-accel’s MAC engine (40 designs) all candidates pass; synthesis and the gate-level check take 99% of the 424 s of wall time and RTL simulation under 1%. The Pareto front matches chip-accel’s. Stylised: one design family, generic-gate counts, simulation-based (not formal) equivalence, no place and route.

eda-gridorder7 tests

Does the order a grid proposer walks a chip-design space change how quickly it finds the Pareto front?

Does the order a grid walks a design space matter? The harness's lexicographic grid trails every random order to 30 evaluations; Halton reaches 90% of the front in 7 evaluations against 17 for random (stylised, one table, deterministic orders are single draws).

Abstract Project page →

The lexicographic grid that the harness ships is replayed against Halton, farthest-point and Latin orders and random shuffles on the 80-design table from eda-proposers (stdlib only, nothing new simulated). Lexicographic scores worse than all 300 random orders up to 30 evaluations and needs 75 evaluations for the whole front; a Halton order reaches 90% of the front's hypervolume in 7 evaluations against a median 17 for random, while random-start farthest-point and Latin orders gain only +0.010 to +0.042 over random from 8 to 20 evaluations and nothing by 40. Stylised: one small table, and the deterministic orders are single draws with no interval.

eda-proposers10 tests

Which search method finds a chip design's Pareto front with the fewest evaluations?

Random, grid, annealing, GA, NSGA-II and TPE at equal budgets by Pareto hypervolume on an 80-design logged space: TPE and NSGA-II lead random from about 16 to 30 evaluations, annealing trails it (stylised, tiny space, untuned).

Abstract Project page →

Random search, a grid, simulated annealing, a genetic algorithm, NSGA-II and a TPE-style Bayesian method are compared at equal evaluation budgets on an 80-design space (MAC lanes × bit width × ABC script) of a toy quantised-MLP accelerator, using Pareto hypervolume over 100 seeds. TPE reaches 0.917 of the true-front hypervolume at 16 evaluations against 0.891 for random, and 0.980 against 0.943 at 30; annealing trails random throughout. Stylised: the space is tiny (random search at 40 evaluations already scores 0.965), hyperparameters are untuned, objectives are generic-gate counts, and nothing is said about real chips.

eda-fidelity7 tests

Do cheap rungs of the chip-design tool ladder rank designs like synthesis, and how much synthesis time does screening save?

A three-rung fidelity ladder (analytic model, RTL simulation, synthesis) over 40 logged designs: the free rung ranks the objective at Spearman 0.74, and successive halving finds the optimum at 20 s of tool time against 205 s to synthesise everything (stylised, toy design family, no place and route).

Abstract Project page →

A three-rung ladder over 40 logged MAC-engine designs: a free analytic model (cells ≈ lanes×bits2), cycle-accurate simulation, and Yosys synthesis. The analytic rung ranks the cells×cycles objective with Spearman 0.74 against synthesis (0.95 for cells alone) and finds 2 of the 5 best designs. Successive halving that screens on the cheap rungs reaches the optimum with certainty at 20 s of tool time, against 0.10 for random search at the same budget and 205 s for synthesising everything. Stylised: one toy design family with its optimum at a corner, no place-and-route rung, and the search is a replay over the committed log.

eda-surrogate12 tests

Can cheap word-level RTL features predict synthesised cell counts well enough to screen a design search, and does that survive a new design family?

A cell-count surrogate from cheap word-level RTL features over 133 designs in four generator families: 3.9% median error on families it saw (non-negative linear model), 11% to 210% on a held-out family with rank agreement staying at Spearman 0.75 to 1.00, and it cuts syntheses to find a near-best design in a 36-design pool from 12.4 to 1-5 (stylised, synthesis-only target, no place and route).

Abstract Project page →

A surrogate for Yosys generic-gate cell counts, trained on 24 word-level features (multiplier, adder, mux and register sizes read after proc; opt, about 30× cheaper than synthesis) over 133 designs in four generator families I wrote: MAC engines, FIR filters, ALUs and sorting networks. On families it saw, a non-negative linear cost model has a 3.9% median error and within-family Spearman 0.995, beating boosted trees (8.5%). When a whole family is held out, median errors run from 10.5% to 210.7% and the best model changes with the family, but rank agreement stays at Spearman 0.75–1.00. Ordering a 36-design pool by predicted cells×cycles found a design within 2% of the best after 1–5 syntheses against 12.4 (MAC) and 18.6 (FIR) for random order, both optima sitting at an edge of the space, so the test is weak. Stylised: synthesis-only target, no place and route, small designs.

eda-flowtune11 tests

Does the best ABC recipe for one design transfer to another?

All 400 ABC pass sequences on eight small SKY130-mapped designs: one design's best recipe scores a mean 1.31× the other's optimum, and a transferred warm start helps only one design (stylised, toy designs, no place and route).

Abstract Project page →

All 400 ABC pass sequences (up to three passes of seven) mapped to SKY130 on eight small datapath designs, so every optimum is known. The best recipe differs per design and transfers badly: one design’s best recipe scores a mean 1.31× (worst 2.06×) the other’s optimum, and score rankings of recipes correlate only weakly across designs (Spearman −0.51 to 0.46). A leave-one-out consensus recipe is only slightly better than a median sequence (1.22× against 1.26×), and warm-starting a hill climber with it helps one design (mac4) but is within noise of random search on average at budgets 10 to 40. Stylised: eight hand-picked toy designs, ABC’s static delay, no place and route; the OpenROAD-settings half of the milestone is not done.

eda-verify5 tests

How many injected RTL bugs do random, coverage-directed and formal checks catch, and at what cost?

Mutation study of random, coverage-directed and bounded-formal RTL checks on the MAC accelerator: 64 random vectors kill 99% of killable mutants, formal 71% (timeouts), at ~50x the CPU cost (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

Mutation study on the MAC accelerator: 91 compilable mutants (operator, literal, deletion and ROM edits), of which 66 are killable and 16 are proved equivalent by induction. 64 random vectors kill 99% of the killable ones, 16 coverage-directed vectors 97% (16 random: 95%), and bounded Yosys formal checking 71% because 19 SAT runs timed out. Cost per kill: about 1 s for simulation against 52 s for a formal kill. Stylised: one design, one bound, one solver.

eda-checkorder5 tests

In what order should an automated design loop run random, directed and formal checks?

Replays the eda-verify mutation log to cost check cascades: random simulation before formal cuts CPU by 54% with more kills; the order among cheap stages barely matters (stylised re-analysis).

Abstract Project page →

Replay of the eda-verify mutation log (91 mutants, 20 seeds), costing each check cascade in CPU seconds. Formal alone takes 16,354 s for 47 kills and 16 equivalence proofs; random simulation first and formal only on the survivors takes about 7,500 s and finds 66 of 66 killable mutants, a 54% saving. The order among the cheap stages changes the total by under 2%; the remaining cost is formal working on equivalent or timed-out mutants, which no ordering removes. Stylised: a re-analysis of one design, one solver and its timeouts; nothing new was simulated.

eda-earlystop7 tests

When can a check cascade stop formal verification early without losing kills?

Replays the eda-verify log with a time cap on formal: a 170 s cap loses no kill and saves 41% of cascade CPU but forfeits every equivalence proof; a 230 s cap keeps 15 of 16 proofs and saves 23% (stylised re-analysis).

Abstract Project page →

Replay of the eda-verify mutation log with a time cap on the formal stage. Every formal kill in the log finished within 164 s, while equivalence proofs take about 222 s, so a 170 s cap loses no kill (66 of 66 killable mutants still found) and saves 41% of the cascade's CPU, but gives up all 16 equivalence proofs; a 230 s cap keeps 15 of them and saves 23%. Caps of 30 s or less start losing kills. A cap learned from half the mutants worked on the other half when the training half contained formal kills and failed (1.6 of 29 kills lost) when it contained none. Stylised: one design, one solver, 91 mutants; nothing new was simulated.

eda-equivpredict8 tests

Can cheap features say which simulation survivors formal can prove equivalent?

Predicts from the mutated source line which simulation survivors formal can prove equivalent: nearest-line prediction cuts formal CPU 55% and finds 14 of 16 proofs on one design (stylised, 27 mutants).

Abstract Project page →

Replay of the eda-verify log on the 27 mutants that 16 directed vectors do not kill (16 provably equivalent, 9 timeouts, 2 formal kills). Predicting from the mutated source line and running formal only on predicted-equivalent survivors costs 3,298 CPU-s against 7,414 s for always running formal (−55%) and still finds 14 of 16 proofs, 93% accurate under leave-one-line-out; smoother rules (3-NN, a one-split rule) find 12 of 16 and operator kind is no better than guessing. The signal is the design region the solver finds hard, not a transferable rule. Stylised: 27 mutants, one design, one solver; nothing new was simulated.

eda-equivinterval5 tests

How sure is the 93% nearest-line equivalence predictor?

Puts a line-clustered interval on eda-equivpredict's 93%: 25 of 27 survivors right, 95% CI 76.5–100% over 11 distinct lines, permutation p = 0.012 (stylised, one design).

Abstract Project page →

Uncertainty for eda-equivpredict, replayed from the same eda-verify log. The 27 survivors sit on only 11 distinct source lines, so a line-cluster bootstrap gives a 95% interval of 76.5–100% around the observed 25 of 27 (92.6%), against a 59.3% majority-class baseline, and a permutation test that shuffles line groups gives p = 0.012. One design, one solver, predictors chosen with the log in view. Stylised.

eda-conefeat3 tests

Do synthesized-netlist features predict which simulation survivors Yosys can prove equivalent?

Tests whether Yosys netlist features (cell-count change, miter size) predict which eda-verify survivors are provably equivalent: none beats the 59.3% majority class under leave-one-line-out, against 92.6% for source line (negative, stylised, one design).

Abstract Project page →

Follow-up to eda-equivpredict on the same 27 survivors, now with Yosys installed. Position-free features (cell-count change after synthesis, miter size, identical cell histogram) are scored under leave-one-line-out. None beats guessing the majority class (16 of 27, 59.3%); the source-line rule gets 25 of 27. The nine solver timeouts barely change the netlist (|Δcells| 0 for six), but equivalent mutants span 0 to 178, and miter size is nearly constant (1,188–1,199). A negative result on one design; cone depth and fan-in were not tried (see eda-conehash).

eda-conehash5 tests

Do fan-in cone features of a mutant predict which simulation survivors Yosys can prove equivalent?

Fan-in cone features (changed sinks, cone gates and depth, registers reached) from hashed gate-level netlists vs which eda-verify survivors are provably equivalent: none beats the 59.3% majority class under leave-one-line-out (best 13 of 27; negative, stylised, one design).

Abstract Project page →

The next step eda-conefeat named. Golden and mutant are lowered to gate level without ABC, and each flip-flop and output is compared by a Merkle hash of its fan-in cone. Features of the changed cones (count, gates, depth, leaves, registers reached downstream) are scored under leave-one-line-out on the same 27 survivors. None beats the 59.3% majority class (best 13 of 27). One observation, found after looking at the table: all seven survivors that change exactly one sink are literal edits on two lines, and none is provably equivalent (six of the nine solver timeouts are among them). One design, one solver, stylised.

18

Open-source purpose-built robots

Robots built for one job and designed from the task outward: when a specialised body beats a general-purpose arm, on cost, speed and reliability.

osrobot-specialise10 tests

When does a purpose-built gantry beat a general two-link arm at tray pick-and-place?

When does a purpose-built gantry beat a general two-link arm at tray pick-and-place? At 2 mm tolerance the arm wins only between 0.36 and 0.99 m of work area, and the band depends on assumed costs (stylised).

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib model compares an XY gantry with an equal-link planar arm over a square work area, on cost per good pick per hour. At 2 mm tolerance the gantry wins up to 0.35 m and above about 1.0 m; the arm wins between 0.36 and 0.99 m. Tolerance below 1 mm removes the arm’s band, and the band depends heavily on the assumed cost coefficients (halving the gantry’s removes it). Stylised: every cost, mass, speed and accuracy figure is assumed, and only one task is modelled.

osrobot-morph8 tests

Does co-designing an arm's link lengths and controller beat tuning the controller on a fixed body?

Does co-designing an arm's link split and controller beat tuning the controller on a fixed body? Co-design gained 1.9% in held-out move time (0.283 against 0.289 s), within three-seed noise; tuning the controller mattered about 37%. Stylised, preliminary, mostly negative.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib planar two-link arm model searches the split of a fixed 0.50 m reach together with PD gains, against an equal-link body with tuned gains, at equal search budget. The tray is reachable only for splits of 0.40 to 0.60. Co-design gained 1.9% in held-out move time (0.283 against 0.289 s), within three-seed noise, while tuning the controller cut hand-set gains' 0.460 s by about 37%. Stylised, preliminary and mostly negative: one body parameter and an assumed torque limit.

osrobot-lab10 tests

Can a small twin of a liquid-handling bench catch protocol errors before they run, and how much pipetting error does a serial dilution tolerate?

Can a small twin of a liquid-handling bench catch protocol errors before they run, and how much pipetting error does a serial dilution tolerate? It flags 366 of 522 injected faults against 100 for a syntax-only baseline, and an assumed error curve gives a final-well CV of 0.187 at 10 µL and 0.035 at 100 µL transfers (stylised, circular fault set).

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib deck-and-pipette twin tracks tips, well volumes, liquid labels and straight-line travel over labware, and checks protocols before they run. On 522 injected faults across three reference protocols it flags 366 (355 with the intended code) where a syntax-only baseline flags 100; the misses are mostly equivalent mutants. Collisions appear only where a move crosses taller labware (a tube rack in one protocol; forced travel heights up to 70 mm collide, 90 mm and above do not). With an assumed pipetting-error curve, a 12-well two-fold serial dilution has a final-well CV of 0.187 at 10 µL transfers, 0.100 at 20 and 0.035 at 100 µL. Stylised and circular by construction: the faults match the checks, and every geometry, timing and error value is assumed.

osrobot-bodysearch9 tests

Does searching an arm’s joint count, link lengths and mount, with its controller tuned in the loop, beat a fixed three-link body at the same cost?

Does searching a planar arm's joint count, links and mount, with its controller tuned, beat a fixed three-link body at equal cost? On a shelf task with a tool-down constraint, 0.95 held-out success against 0.26; on a long position-only reach, no gain (stylised, kinematic).

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib model searches link lengths, joint count and mount position of a planar arm, with its inverse-kinematics controller tuned in the loop, against a fixed three-link body at an equal cost budget (300 evaluations, 10 seeds, held-out targets). On a shelf task that needs the tool pointing down, the search reaches 0.95 success against 0.26 for the fixed body with a tuned controller and 0.50 with the mount also tuned; on a long position-only reach the fixed body already succeeds and the search adds nothing. Random search beat a (1+4) evolution strategy here, weakly. Stylised: kinematics and static torque only (no MuJoCo dynamics), and every cost, mass and limit is assumed.

osrobot-uav8 tests

How heavy must a purpose-built UAV for targeted observation be, and when does a hover-capable airframe stop being worth its weight?

How heavy must a purpose-built UAV for targeted observation be, and when is a hover-capable airframe worth its weight? At 3 km out and 20 min on station a fixed wing closes at 1.27 kg against 2.14 kg for a quadrotor and 2.08 kg for a VTOL wing, and the quadrotor stops closing at 45 min (stylised, assumed constants, no flight stack run).

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib mass-closure sizing model closes a quadrotor, a fixed wing and a fixed wing with a vertical-lift system for the same mission, choosing rotor diameter or wing area for least mass. For 3 km out, 20 min on station and a 0.5 kg payload the plain fixed wing is lightest (1.27 kg), against 2.14 kg for the quadrotor and 2.08 kg for the VTOL wing. The quadrotor does not close at 45 min on station; the VTOL wing is lighter than it from 30 min or beyond about 10 km. Stylised: every technology constant is assumed, no flight stack was run, and a fixed wing cannot hover or launch unaided.

osrobot-uavwind8 tests

Does a steady wind change which purpose-built observation UAV is lightest, and what is wind worth to a multirotor?

Does a steady wind change which purpose-built observation UAV is lightest? At 3 km and 20 min on station the fixed wing stays lightest from 0 to 18 m/s (1.27 to 1.50 kg) while the quadrotor goes 2.14 to 7.0 kg; the multirotor's still-air win at 1 min on station ends near 10 m/s. Stylised, steady known wind only.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib extension of the osrobot-uav mass-closure sizing adds a steady wind: headwind out, tailwind back, airspeed re-optimised, and station-keeping at airspeed equal to the wind. For 3 km out, 20 min on station and 0.5 kg the plain fixed wing stays lightest at every wind from 0 to 18 m/s (1.27 kg at 0, 1.30 at 10, 1.50 at 18); the quadrotor goes 2.14 → 2.33 → 2.86 → 7.0 kg at 0, 10, 15 and 18 m/s and the VTOL wing 2.08 → 2.54. The multirotor’s one win in still air (1 min on station) lasts to about 8 m/s. Designs sized for still air keep 17.2 (fixed wing) and 18.5 min (multirotor) of 20 at 9 m/s and 8.8 and 13.8 at 15 m/s; building for 15 m/s costs 34% (multirotor) and 9% (fixed wing) in mass. Crediting the multirotor with translational lift makes its mass fall to 1.71 kg at 10 m/s, an optimistic artefact of a steady known wind. Stylised: assumed coefficients, no gusts, crosswind or launch limits, nothing flown.

osrobot-uavgust8 tests

How much heavier must an observation UAV be if the wind is uncertain, and is designing to a wind quantile cheaper than a bigger battery reserve?

How much heavier must an observation UAV be if the wind is uncertain? Designing to the 95th-percentile of wind ~ N(8, 3) m/s costs the fixed wing +3.7% and the multirotor +11.7% mass, and a bigger battery reserve buys about the same reliability for about the same mass; stylised, one steady wind per mission.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib extension of osrobot-uavwind draws one along-track wind per mission from a normal distribution (exact discretisation, no sampling noise) and sizes the airframe for a quantile of it. For a 3 km, 20 min, 0.5 kg mission with wind ~ N(8, 3) m/s, designing to the 95th-percentile wind (12.9 m/s) costs the fixed wing +3.7% mass (1.333 against 1.286 kg) and the multirotor +11.7% (2.518 against 2.254 kg). The standard 20% reserve, if it may be spent, already lifts a mean-wind design to 0.95 (fixed wing) and 0.99 (multirotor) success, and a larger reserve and a quantile design cost within a few percent of each other. At a 1 min stay the 95th-percentile design flips the lightest airframe from multirotor to fixed wing. Stylised: one steady wind per mission, assumed constants, no turbulence, no launch limit, and no flight.

osrobot-uavnogo5 tests

If an observation UAV only launches when the forecast wind is below a limit, how much does forecast error bring failures back, and what does it cost in scrubbed missions?

If an observation UAV launches only when the forecast wind is under a limit, how much does forecast error bring failures back? A perfect forecast turns every failure into a scrub (fixed wing, wind ~ N(5, 4) m/s: 4.6% scrubbed at the 95th-percentile limit); a 2 m/s error gives 6.8% failures at the median limit but 1.1% at the 95th. Stylised, one steady wind per mission.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib extension of osrobot-uavgust sizes the airframe for a launch limit wind and launches only if the forecast of the wind is at most that limit, with a normal forecast error (exact discretisation, no sampling noise). With a perfect forecast every failure becomes a scrub (fixed wing, wind ~ N(5, 4) m/s: 48% scrubbed at the median limit, 4.6% at the 95th percentile, 1.274 to 1.313 kg). A 2 m/s forecast error brings the failure rate to 6.8% at the median limit but only 1.1% at the 95th-percentile limit. Stylised: one steady wind per mission, assumed constants, normal forecast error, no cost put on a scrub.

osrobot-uavvalue4 tests

What is a UAV launch wind limit worth in money, and should the launch threshold sit below the design limit when the forecast is wrong?

What is a UAV launch wind limit worth in money, and should the launch threshold sit below the design limit when the forecast is wrong? With an assumed expensive airframe and a 2 m/s forecast error the best threshold sits 1 to 6 m/s below the design limit, worth up to $284 per attempt, with failures at or below 0.1%; with a cheap airframe the best design covers nearly every wind. Stylised, assumed prices.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib extension of osrobot-uavnogo puts a money value on a completed observation, the loss of an aircraft on a failure and a scrubbed day, then searches the design wind limit L and the launch threshold T together (exact probabilities, no sampling noise). With a cheap airframe ($1,500/kg, assumed) the best design is for nearly every wind (L at 14 m/s or more in 17 of 18 cases, 11 on the grid edge) and the rule barely matters. With an expensive one ($30,000/kg, assumed) the optimum is interior, and with a 2 m/s forecast error the best T sits 1 to 6 m/s below L in all 9 cases, worth up to $284 per attempt over tying T to L, with failures at or below 0.1%. Money figures are assumptions, many optima sit on the grid edge, and a failure is assumed to lose the whole airframe. Stylised, no aircraft designed or flown.

osrobot-assist6 tests

When a spoon-feeding arm meets a moving mouth, what sets the force on the lips: the sensor, the approach speed or a force cap?

What sets the force on the lips when a spoon-feeding arm meets a swaying mouth: the sensor, the approach speed or a force cap? Peak force tracks approach speed (1.0 N at 0.05 m/s, 4.0 N at 0.20), a camera cuts how often the lips are touched (0.40 against 0.72 of trials) but not how hard, and latency erodes that gain. Stylised point-mass model, assumed constants.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib planar point-mass twin of a feeding arm and a swaying mouth, with 200 paired trials per row. With a 0.05 s forward lead the push on a blocked tip is 20 N·s/m × speed, so peak lip force tracks approach speed (1.0 N at 0.05 m/s, 4.0 N at 0.20). A camera lowers the share of trials that touch the lips (0.40 against 0.72 at 30 mm sway) without lowering the peak, and its advantage fades with latency (touch share 0.07 at no delay, 0.71 at 0.4 s). A 1 N force cap trims the worst peak but not the share of comfortable feeds. Stylised: all constants are assumed, the peak-force result is largely an identity of the chosen controller, and no human model or Assistive Gym was used.

osrobot-lipsweep5 tests

Is the peak force of a feeding arm on the lips set by the lips' stiffness, the arm's force loop, or its approach lead?

Is the peak force of a feeding arm on the lips set by lip stiffness, the force loop or the approach lead? Lip stiffness moves the mean peak from 0.32 to 2.02 N at 0.20 m/s (stylised; extends osrobot-assist).

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib sweep of osrobot-assist's feeding-arm twin over lip stiffness, loop stiffness and forward lead (200 paired trials per row, 30 mm sway, camera arm at 0.20 m/s). Mean peak lip force rises from 0.32 N at 100 N/m to 1.15 N at 800 and 2.02 N at 6400; the worst trial reaches 6.7 N, above the controller's 4.0 N stall push, so that push is a ceiling only for soft and medium lips. At 0.05 m/s every stiffness stays under 2 N. Stylised: assumed constants, a point mass and a passive user.

osrobot-field7 tests

For a weeding robot with a cheap camera, is it better to treat weeds as it drives or to scout first and come back, and what does a weak sensor cost?

For a weeding robot with a cheap camera, is it better to treat weeds as it drives or to scout first? Scouting then touring killed the same share (0.399 against 0.401 at 1 m/s) and was slower in all 23 paired rows; lane overlap repays a weak sensor (0.40 to 0.86 killed) at 3.5 times the time. Stylised, constants assumed.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib simulation of a lane-following weeding robot on a 60×30 m field with clustered weeds, a motion-blurred noisy detector and muddy squares. Scouting then touring the targets kills the same share of weeds as treating inline (0.399 against 0.401 at 1 m/s) and is slower in all 23 paired rows, by 2.8 to 7.8 min. Lane overlap repays a weak sensor at a steep price: 0 to 0.75 overlap raises the kill share from 0.40 to 0.86 and the time from 52 to 178 min; no grid configuration reaches a 0.9 kill share at a 0.5 hit rate. Stylised: every constant is assumed, the speed results move with the blur assumption, and the planner comparison is a statement about this cost model.

19

The software-engineering loop

Measuring and optimising the agent loop that builds this portfolio: what the run log records, what a run costs, and which work is worth the budget.

swe-ledger8 tests

What can the run log measure about the agent loop today?

What can the run log measure about the agent loop today? Cost fields are present in at most 1% of 189 runs, a third of listed projects are follow-up families, and every recorded CI-failure count is zero. Preliminary first step of track 10.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib reader of a snapshot of prompts/runs.jsonl (189 runs, 184 listed projects) reports coverage and throughput proxies. Token, cost and tool-call fields are present in at most 1% of runs and wall time is derivable for only 15, so no cost-per-project figure is possible yet. About a third of listed projects sit in follow-up families of three or more, and 24 slugs appear in more than one run. All 143 recorded CI-failure counts are zero, which looks like a success-only field, not a clean record. Preliminary: first step of the ledger milestone; no git-history backfill, no value or correctness scoring.

swe-backfill9 tests

What does git history say about the agent loop that the run log cannot?

What does git history say about the agent loop that the run log cannot? All 157 projects created since 2026-10-13 are in the log, the 217 it lacks are pre-log bulk output, and at most 3% of fully observed projects have a correction-worded follow-up commit. Preliminary second step of track 10.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib reader of 517 commits touching research/<slug>/ (396 projects, 2026-09-28 to 2026-10-15) fills in what the run log lacks. All 157 projects created since 2026-10-13 are in the log; the 217 it never lists were made in two bulk days (09-29 and 09-30) before the log began. Half of all projects (49%) sit in follow-up families, creations arrive in bursts (median gap 4 minutes), and only 6 of 234 fully observed projects (2.6%, 95% interval 1% to 5%) have a later commit whose subject says it corrects something, a lower bound on defects, not an estimate. No tokens, cost, pull request or CI data; preliminary.

swe-value8 tests

Can two independent passes agree on what a portfolio project is worth?

Can two passes agree on what a project is worth? A three-level value rubric scored two automated ways over 408 projects agrees at chance (kappa 0.07, 95% 0.01 to 0.13), partly from a name-family flaw fixed after the fact (0.25); a blind 30-project hand sample agrees better (0.45 to 0.57, wide intervals). Preliminary, track 10 milestone 3; no correctness term.

Abstract Project page →

A three-level value rubric (follow-up, new question, listed milestone) scored over all 408 research/ projects by two automated passes, one from names and order and one from README text, plus a blind 30-project hand sample. The two automated passes agree at chance level (linear Cohen’s kappa 0.07, 95% bootstrap 0.01 to 0.13); a flaw in the name pass (108 *-twin projects counted as one follow-up chain) explains part, and fixing it after the fact lifts kappa to 0.25. Against the hand sample the text pass reaches 0.45 (0.24 to 0.65) and the fixed name pass 0.57 (0.24 to 0.81), n = 30, scored by the rubric’s author. Follow-ups add about as many lines as new projects (median 318 vs 328), so by the rubric they return less per line, a ratio that is largely built in. Preliminary and negative on the automated passes; no correctness term.

swe-prompt7 tests

How many runs does a prompt experiment need, and is it safe to peek at it?

When can a prompt experiment stop? Fixed-n, peek-every-pair and a mixture SPRT simulated on ledger-shaped outcomes: peeking declares an identical brief different in 21% (success rate) to 40% (value) of experiments, the mixture test stays under 5% but needs far more runs than a 97% success rate allows. Stylised, no candidate brief run; track 10 milestone 6, partial.

Abstract Project page →

Three stopping rules for a champion-versus-candidate brief experiment were simulated on outcome distributions drawn from the run ledger (success rate 237/244) and from swe-value’s project values: one look at the end, a look after every pair, and a mixture sequential probability ratio test. Looking after every pair declared an identical brief different in 21% of 2,000 experiments on success rate and 40% on value (nominal 5%); the mixture test stayed at 0.4% and 3.9%, at the price of power (92% against 99% at a +0.2 shift in value, stopping after 181 of 400 pairs on average). At a 97% success rate a fixed test needs about 2,200 runs to see a 0.971 to 0.991 change, so success rate is a poor primary metric. Stylised and preliminary: all 244 ledger rows are the same prompt, effects are hypothetical, and the value scores are weak; no candidate brief has been run.

swe-allocate6 tests

Which track should the next run work on, and does a smarter pick beat a uniform one?

Which track should the next run work on? Four allocation policies (uniform, greedy, bootstrap Thompson, knapsack-UCB) replayed offline on 7 tracks' scored projects: greedy and Thompson reach about 80% of the best-arm oracle against 60% for the current uniform pick, but value per line falls with order in 4 of 7 tracks, so the stationary replay overstates the gain. Stylised, offline only, no live trial; track 10 milestone 4, partial.

Abstract Project page →

Four track-allocation policies (uniform, greedy value per line, bootstrap Thompson sampling, and a knapsack-style UCB) were replayed offline on 7 tracks, using the 408-project scores from swe-value (value 1 to 3, cost in lines added) under a 20,000-line budget and 300 seeds. Greedy and Thompson reach about 79–83% (pass A) and 75–79% (pass B) of the best-single-track oracle, against 58–60% for the current uniform pick; the UCB variant explores too much to help (62–66%). This is a stylised, preliminary result: arms are assumed stationary, yet value per line falls with order in 4 of 7 tracks (Spearman −0.36 to −0.57), the value scores themselves agree only weakly, lines are a poor proxy for tokens, and no live trial was run, so no policy is adopted.

swe-audit6 tests

Do the portfolio's committed results reproduce when the code is re-run?

Do committed results reproduce? A seeded sample of 40 projects with a runnable experiment was re-run: 36 (90%, 95% Wilson 77% to 96%) matched their committed results.txt, 3 timed out under load and 1 needed a missing voice model. Preliminary first pass of track 10, milestone 2; it checks reproduction only, not citations. Second sample of 60 (92 distinct projects pooled): 81 reproduced (88%), no finished run differed; re-running the 5 timeouts serially reproduced all, giving 86 of 92 (93%).

Abstract Project page →

A seeded sample of 40 research/ projects with a runnable experiment was re-run on a clean copy and diffed against the committed results.txt. 36 of 40 (90%, 95% Wilson interval 77% to 96%) reproduced: 34 byte-identical and 2 differing only in a timing line. Three timed out at 300 s (four jobs in parallel) and one needs a voice model that is not in the repository, so those four are inconclusive, not failures. Of 713 decimal numbers in the sampled READMEs, 85% appear verbatim in committed result files (the rest are derived or in prose). A second sample of 60 (8 overlapping) brought the pooled total to 92 distinct projects: 81 reproduced (88%, Wilson 80% to 93%), none of the 81 finished runs gave different numbers, and the 11 others are missing tools (Yosys, MuJoCo, a voice model) or timeouts. Re-running the five timeouts one at a time (no parallel load) reproduced all five (two differing only in timing lines), lifting the pooled figure to 86 of 92 (93%, Wilson 86% to 97%); the 6 left are missing tools or the voice model. A mechanical reproduction check on a small sample, with no citation audit, so the correctness term is only partly estimated. Preliminary.

swe-cleanbroken6 tests

When research merges collide cleanly, is the result still right?

When research merges collide cleanly, is the result still right? None of 92 clean replays was broken (28.7% of pairs within 60 min conflict); found and removed two duplicate README bullets the build missed.

Abstract Project page →

Replays pairs of research merges that touched the shared index files within 10, 30 and 60 minutes of each other (67 merges, 2026-10-14 to 10-16) and checks the merged tree against the homepage build’s rules. Of 129 pairs within 60 min, 37 (28.7%) conflicted textually and the other 92 merged with no new inconsistency; none was clean but broken. The same checker found two projects with duplicate README.md bullets since the repository fold-in, which build.py missed; they are removed and the build now fails on duplicates. Preliminary: three days, an approximate replay, and consistency rules rather than the full build.

swe-prlifetime9 tests

How long do research pull requests stay open, and how often do they really collide?

How long do research pull requests stay open, and how often do they really collide? Median 0.9 min open (95% merged within 30 min); replayed from real creation times, 2 of 58 shared-file PRs (3.4%) conflict.

Abstract Project page →

Joins 122 merged pull requests that touched research/ (2026-10-16 to 10-17) to their real creation times from the GitHub API. The median pull request was open 0.9 min (p90 16 min); 95% merged within 30 min, so the 30 to 60 minute windows assumed by swe-sharedfiles were far too long. Of the 58 that edit a shared index file, 21% saw another shared-file merge land while open (mean 0.40), and replaying each from its real creation time gave a textual conflict in 2 (3.4%, 95% Wilson 1.0% to 11.7%). Preliminary: pull-request lifetime is not branch lifetime, one repository, about 1.5 days.

swe-branchlife6 tests

Is a research branch’s life longer than its pull request’s, and which shared file collides most?

Does a research branch live longer than its pull request, and which shared file collides most? Median 1.1 min from first commit to merge (vs 0.9 for the PR); research/PROJECTS.md conflicts in 5 of 44 PRs that edit it, more than the index files (3 of 58).

Abstract Project page →

Adds each of the 122 research pull requests’ first-commit time (GitHub API) to the swe-prlifetime data. Branch lifetime is almost the same as pull-request lifetime (median 1.1 vs 0.9 min, p90 16.1 vs 16.0), because sessions commit at the end of their work; commit dates cannot see the earlier working time. Replayed from the branch start, 3 of 58 shared-index-file PRs (5.2%, 95% Wilson 1.8–14.1%) conflict, versus 2 from pull-request creation. The larger finding: research/PROJECTS.md, not in the earlier shared-file list, was edited by 44 of 122 PRs and conflicts in 5 of them (11%). Preliminary: 1.5 days, one repository.

swe-sharedfiles7 tests

How often do research merges collide on the shared index files?

How often do research merges collide on the shared index files? 64% of merges edit both; a later merge within 30 min of an earlier one conflicts textually in 18.6% of 59 replayed pairs (assumed branch times, preliminary).

Abstract Project page →

Measured from git history (101 research merges, 2026-10-14 to 10-16): 64.4% edit both README.md and projects.json, the median gap between such merges is 30.6 min, and replaying a later merge against an earlier one within 30 min gives a textual conflict in 18.6% of 59 pairs (15.3% in a shared file). Branch times are assumed, not measured; textual conflicts only; preliminary.

swe-schedule6 tests

How many parallel agent runs duplicate each other when they start in the same minute, and what removes the waste?

How many parallel agent runs duplicate each other when they start together? 12.8% of runs at four blind starts; a start gap past the claim latency or scheduler slots remove it (stylised, assumed timings).

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib Monte Carlo of start-time collisions among runs that pick from a pool of 11 tracks. Four blind simultaneous starts leave 12.8% of runs redundant (closed form agrees), claim-checking alone barely helps because all runs read before any claim is pushed, a start gap longer than the claim latency drives waste to about 1–2%, and scheduler-assigned slots remove it entirely up to the pool size. Every timing constant is assumed, the pool is uniform, and queueing against usage limits is not yet modelled. Stylised; first step of milestone 5 of track 10.

swe-pickmix10 tests

Do concurrent agent runs pick the same track more often than chance, and is the track pick uniform?

Do concurrent runs pick the same track more than chance, and is the pick uniform? Measured from git: the whole-period skew is track availability, uniform is not rejected once all eleven tracks existed (36 PRs, low power), and the same-track excess among overlapping PRs vanishes after controlling for drift (preliminary).

Abstract Project page →

Measured from git history rather than simulated: 218 merged projects since the tracks were set. Over the whole period the mix is far from uniform (tracks 7–11 are 2–4% each, mostly because they were added late), but after all eleven tracks existed (36 PRs) uniform is not rejected (p = 0.25, low power). Same-track pairs among overlapping PRs are 17.9% against 12.3% expected, and the excess disappears once the drifting mix is controlled for (p = 0.115 within merge days). Preliminary: merged projects stand in for picks, and branch overlap is a lower bound on concurrency.

swe-prflow6 tests

What do 526 closed pull requests say about how the agent loop lands work?

What do 526 closed pull requests say about how the agent loop lands work? 87.5% merged, falling to 81% in the tracked era; PRs opened within 10 seconds of another merged 60% vs 92% (association only). Preliminary third step of track 10.

Abstract Project page →

A stdlib analysis of the creation and merge times of every closed PR here (#1 to #526). 87.5% merged (Wilson 84.3–90.0%), falling from 93.8% for PRs opened by 10-01 to 81.2% from 10-05 on. Median time to merge is 0.6 minutes, 4.3% of merges happen in four same-second batches after long waits, and PRs opened within 10 seconds of another merged only 60% of the time against 92% for the rest. The last is an association, not a cause. No CI, review or closure-reason data, and the timestamps were hand-transcribed. Preliminary third step of track 10.

swe-orgs7 tests

Which practices of engineering organisations that ship could help an agent loop, and what is there to fix?

Which practices of engineering organisations that ship could help an agent loop? A cited catalogue of 47 practices from 46 sources (batch 14 adds Reason and Vaughan on organisational accidents; batch 13 adds Rigby and Bird on lightweight review, Humble and Farley's deployment pipeline and Beck's Extreme Programming), scored against the 758-run ledger: no new proposal clears a 5% ceiling (negative, preliminary). Ongoing, with a research log; track 10, milestone 7.

Abstract Project page →

A cited, growing catalogue of 51 practices from 50 sources (Perrow on normal accidents, the DevOps Handbook, Reason on layered defences, Vaughan on normalization of deviance, Rigby and Bird, Humble and Farley, Beck, Allspaw and Hammond on Flickr, Parnas, Nygard, Conway, Nagappan et al., Skelton and Pais, Brooks, Fowler, Reinertsen, Toyota, the Rogers Commission, 37signals, Instagram, Google, Microsoft, Facebook, Netflix, Amazon, Etsy, Basecamp, Spotify, Stripe (twice, including its online-migrations post), Shopify, Linear, and postmortems from GitLab and Cloudflare, the SEC’s order on Knight Capital and others), each tagged with company stage, evidence type (four measured, the rest case studies, postmortems, accounts or opinion), the loop element it maps to, how far it transfers to a fleet of agent sessions, and the assumption that does not carry over. The failure reports agree: a safety mechanism or a cost nobody measured before it shipped. Scored against the 758-row run ledger, the failure classes runs report are small (1.1–2.5% of runs, self-reported keyword matches), so no practice clears the 5% ceiling as a new proposal: a negative result. Sources were checked by web search only. Thirteenth batch of standing milestone 7 of track 10; the research log below records each batch.
